Machine Learning

AIMLZG565 / DSEZG565 · Syllabus tree, instructor's analysis and a graded problem bank

Try each problem first. Open the Hint only when stuck, and read the Key insight in every answer.

345 problems11 modules 5 levels L1→L57 cross-module capstones

Source: Machine Learning_Watermarked_ppts_Nov2026.pdf (750 slides, BITS Pilani WILP, S1‑2026‑27). The deck is organised by the instructor's own Course Plan into eleven modules M1–M11, delivered across 15 contact sessions (CS‑1 … CS‑15). Each module below is tagged with the session(s) and the approximate slide range it came from.
Primary textbook: T1 Tom M. Mitchell, Machine Learning (McGraw‑Hill). References: R1 Bishop, Pattern Recognition & Machine Learning; R2 Tan/Steinbach/Kumar, Introduction to Data Mining; R3 Burges, A Tutorial on Support Vector Machines.

How to use this document:

  1. Part 1 is the syllabus broken down as a tree. Every node has an ID such as 5.2.3, and every problem lists the IDs it trains.
  2. Part 2 is the instructor's analysis: the main ideas that run through the course, which topics depend on which, the misconceptions students most often bring, and errata found in the slides.
  3. Parts 3–13 are the problem sets, one per course module (M1–M11), followed by a cross‑module capstone part. Problems climb through five levels:
Level Name What it trains
L1 Foundation Definitions and concept checks. Answer "true or false, and why".
L2 Computation Applying a formula directly to clean, small data.
L3 Application Multi‑step word problems at exam / assignment level.
L4 Analysis Derivations, proofs, edge cases, "what breaks if…", comparing methods.
L5 Synthesis / Mastery Combining topics, model‑building judgement, misconception traps, open‑ended design.

Each problem has a collapsible Hint and a collapsible Answer & Key Insight. Attempt the problem before you open either one. The Key Insight line is the reason the problem exists, so read it even when your answer was right.

PART 2 — Instructor's Analysis of the Tree

2.1 The spine of the course: the big ideas that keep coming back

Students who treat this course as eleven unrelated algorithms struggle. Students who see these threads find that most modules are the same handful of ideas, reapplied.

# Big idea Where it appears
A A loss function is a hidden distributional (or geometric) assumption. Squared error \(\Leftrightarrow\) Gaussian noise (MLE of linear regression); cross-entropy \(\Leftrightarrow\) Bernoulli labels (MLE of logistic regression); counting \(\Leftrightarrow\) MLE of Naïve Bayes's tables. Change the assumption, change the "right" loss. 3.1, 4.2, 8.1, 8.3.2
B Bias–variance trade-off, under one name or another, in every module. Regularisation strength (3.5, 4.3), tree depth/pruning (5.3), \(k\) in k-NN (6.3.2), \(C\) in SVM (7.3.2), bagging-reduces-variance vs boosting-reduces-bias (9.1.2). 3.4.2, 3.5, 5.3, 6.3.2, 7.3.2, 9.1.2
C Conditioning and reversal via Bayes' theorem. Bayes' theorem \(\to\) Bayes-optimal classifier \(\to\) Naïve Bayes \(\to\) the GMM E-step responsibility \(\gamma(z_{nk})\), which is the same formula with mixing weights playing the role of priors. 8.2.1, 8.3, 10.5.3
D Distance is the basic primitive of "similar". The same Minkowski/Gower toolkit drives k-NN's neighbours, k-means's cluster assignment, and (implicitly, through \(\lVert w \rVert\)) the SVM margin. 6.2, 7.1.2, 10.2
E A linear score \(w^\top x + b\), thresholded or squashed, is the common skeleton of discriminative classifiers. Logistic regression squashes it with a sigmoid; the linear SVM thresholds it with \(\operatorname{sign}()\); both draw a hyperplane decision boundary. 4.1.2, 7.1.1
F Weak learners combine into strong ones, three different ways. Bagging averages independent high-variance learners; boosting re-weights to serially fix a high-bias learner's mistakes; stacking lets a meta-model blend heterogeneous learners. 9.1–9.4
G The test set is not a tuning knob. Hyper-parameters (\(\lambda\), \(k\), \(C\), tree depth, number of estimators) must be chosen on a validation split or by cross-validation; touching the test set during tuning silently inflates the reported generalisation error. 2.4.1, 6.5, 11.1, 11.2

8.1 MLE  (logistic reg. MLE has no closed form, 4.2.1 explains why) ──► 8.3 Naïve Bayes ──────────┘

5.1-5.3 Decision trees (entropy/Gini, pruning) ──► 9.2 Bagging/Random Forest ──► 9.3 Boosting (AdaBoost,
                                                                                  Gradient Boosting, XGBoost)

Critical bottlenecks (weak here and the damage spreads downstream):

  1. Gradient descent mechanics — the update rule, the role of the learning rate, and why feature scaling changes the shape of the descent path. Needed verbatim in Module 3, reused in Module 4, and reappears conceptually as "functional gradient descent" in Gradient Boosting (Module 9).
  2. Computing a score from a small table by hand — entropy/Gini (Module 5), a Gaussian density or a Naïve Bayes product of likelihoods (Module 8), a Minkowski/Gower distance (Module 6). All four are "plug numbers into a formula, then \(\arg\max\)/\(\arg\min\)", and all four show up again inside ensembles (Module 9) and clustering (Module 10).
  3. Bayes' theorem, in the direction you actually need it. \(P(\text{class} \mid \text{evidence})\) is not \(P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{class})\); getting this backwards breaks Naïve Bayes (8.3), the Bayes-optimal classifier (8.2), and the GMM E-step (10.5.3) identically.
  4. Train / validation / test discipline. Introduced in Module 2, tested again in Module 6 (k-NN's choice of \(k\)), and made explicit in Module 11 as "the test set is not a tuning knob" — the single most common practical mistake in applied ML.

2.3 The most common misconceptions (targeted by L1 and L5 problems)

Misconception Reality Targeted in
"A classifier with 99% accuracy is obviously good." Not under class imbalance — predicting the majority class every time can reach 99% accuracy while missing every rare case (fraud, disease, defect). M4
"Tuning hyper-parameters on the test set is fine, as long as I don't retrain on it." It still leaks information: the reported generalisation error becomes optimistic because the model/hyper-parameters were selected to do well on that exact set. The slides state this directly: "the test data can't be used for parameter tuning." M2, M6, M11
"A decision tree that gets 100% training accuracy is the best tree." It is very likely overfit: a perfectly pure tree has memorised noise. Pre-/post-pruning trade a little training accuracy for better test accuracy. M5
"Larger \(k\) in k-NN is always safer." \(k\) trades bias and variance: \(k = 1\) overfits to noise (high variance); \(k \to N\) underfits to the global majority class (high bias). The elbow method exists precisely to find the middle. M6
"More regularisation can only help." Too much regularisation underfits (high bias); the strength must be tuned, typically via validation/cross-validation, like every other hyper-parameter. M3, M4
"Bagging and boosting do the same thing, just with different names." Bagging trains independent learners in parallel to reduce variance (good with high-variance, low-bias base learners such as deep trees). Boosting trains learners sequentially, re-weighting mistakes, to reduce bias (good with high-bias, low-variance base learners such as shallow stumps). M9
"Naïve Bayes's conditional-independence assumption is harmless in practice." It is frequently violated (e.g. Plan and Usage are correlated given churn in the slides' own telecom example) yet the classifier often still ranks the classes correctly, because only the \(\arg\max\) over classes needs to be right, not the exact probabilities. M8
"A Gaussian Mixture Model assigns every point to one cluster, like k-means." GMM gives soft responsibilities \(\gamma(z_{nk})\) that sum to 1 across clusters for each point; a hard assignment (if needed) is a separate, later decision. M10
"\(P(\text{class} \mid \text{evidence}) = P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{class})\)." They differ unless the prior and evidence probabilities happen to coincide; conflating them is the same base-rate error that breaks medical-test and spam-filter reasoning if not corrected by Bayes' theorem. M8
"A Lagrange multiplier \(\alpha_i\) in an SVM can be negative, or the set of multipliers found by any system of equations through the support vectors is automatically a valid solution." A genuine dual solution requires every \(\alpha_i \ge 0\) and \(\sum \alpha_i y_i = 0\); a system of equations that merely forces the margin to pass exactly through the chosen support vectors can produce a negative \(\alpha_i\), which is not a valid Lagrange multiplier (see errata item 1 below). M7
"Feature scaling is a formality; gradient descent converges to the same place either way." It converges to the same minimiser, but the path and the number of iterations differ enormously: unscaled features give elongated, skewed cost contours and a zig-zagging, slow descent. M3

2.4 Errata and ambiguities spotted in the slides (do not copy these into exams)

  1. Module 7 (SVM), Session 10, "Numerical Example" (the three-support-vector hyperplane problem): solving the three linear equations through the support vectors \(S_1 = (1, 0, y = -1)\), \(S_2 = (3, 1, y = +1)\), \(S_3 = (3, -1, y = +1)\) gives \(\alpha_1 = -3.5\), \(\alpha_2 = 0.75\), \(\alpha_3 = 0.75\). This is not a valid dual solution: every Lagrange multiplier must satisfy \(\alpha_i \ge 0\), and the KKT stationarity condition requires \(\sum \alpha_i y_i = 0\), but here \(\sum \alpha_i y_i = (-3.5)(-1) + 0.75(1) + 0.75(1) =\) \(5.0 \ne 0\). The slide's shortcut (solve "\(w \cdot x_i + b = y_i\)" through the three support vectors as a plain \(3 \times 3\) linear system) skips the dual's own constraints and should not be used as a template for solving a general SVM dual by hand.
  2. Module 3, Session 3&4, "Numerical Exercise" + its "Answer" slide (regularisation with gradient descent): after one ridge-regression update the weights shrink slightly (as expected — ridge's multiplicative shrink factor \((1 - \eta \cdot \lambda)\) is applied), but the slide's own Lasso answer (\(w_1 = 0.1477\), \(w_2 = 0.2793\)) comes out larger than both the unregularised weights (0.0477, 0.1793) and the ridge weights (0.0507, 0.1823), directly contradicting the slide's own interpretation line "Lasso Adds fixed penalty → can push weights toward zero faster." The slide never actually states the correct L1 subgradient update (\(w \leftarrow w(1 \text{ at non-zero}) - \eta \cdot \nabla \text{MSE} - \eta \cdot \lambda \cdot \operatorname{sign}(w)\)); treat the given Lasso numbers as unreliable.
  3. Module 10, Session 14, GMM worked example ("VI Maximization Step" page, the document-membership calculation): the responsibility of document 1 to the second cluster is printed with the same label as the first — "\(P(Z_{\text{Doc1‑Cluster1}}) = 0.006\)" followed immediately by "\(P(Z_{\text{Doc1‑Cluster1}}) = 0.994\)" — the second line should read \(P(Z_{\text{Doc1‑Cluster2}}) = 0.994\) (the two responsibilities for a point must sum to 1, which \(0.006 + 0.994\) does, confirming the value is right and only the cluster label is wrong).
  4. Module 2, Session 2, IQR outlier worked example (page 96, data 10,11,11,11,12,12,13,14,14,15,17,22): \(Q_1 = 11\) and \(Q_3 = 14.5\) are obtained by the median-of-halves method (median of the lower six values, median of the upper six values), not by the position formula \(k(n+1)/4\) used elsewhere in the slides (which would give \(Q_1 = 11\), \(Q_3 = 14.75\) — close but not identical). Both conventions are legitimate; state which one you are using in an answer, exactly as for the ISM course's quartile ambiguity.
  5. Module 9, AdaBoost worked numeric example: the total error is \(\varepsilon = 2/7\), which is often rounded to 0.28 on the way. With the exact value the ratio \((1 - \varepsilon)/\varepsilon\) is exactly 2.5 and the stump performance is \(\alpha = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln 2.5 \approx \mathbf{0.458}\). Rounding \(\varepsilon\) to 0.28 first turns the ratio into \(0.72/0.28 \approx 2.571\) and \(\alpha\) into \(\approx 0.472\), which is a visible change in the third digit. The lesson is general: carry exact fractions (or at least four significant figures) through intermediate steps and round only the final answer.

2.5 How the problem bank is designed

  • Every leaf of the tree is hit by at least one problem. Bottleneck nodes (gradient descent mechanics, hand-computed scores, Bayes' direction, train/validation/test discipline) are hit several times at increasing levels across different modules.
  • L1 problems check vocabulary and catch misconceptions before computation starts.
  • L2 problems use small, clean numbers, so mechanics are separated from reading comprehension.
  • L3 problems mirror the style of the worked "Problem Type" exercises embedded in the slides themselves.
  • L4 problems make you derive results: why least squares is the MLE under Gaussian noise, why a Lagrange multiplier must be non-negative, why Lasso's gradient does not exist at 0, why Random Forest's feature subsampling decorrelates trees. Once you can derive a result, you no longer need to memorise it.
  • L5 problems connect a topic to real model-building judgement (choosing a metric under imbalance, diagnosing why a model overfits, picking an ensemble strategy for a given base learner) or set a deliberate misconception trap.
  • Each module ends with a module capstone that uses the whole module. Part 14 holds cross-module capstones that combine three or more modules, the way an actual ML project does.

Suggested study loop per topic: do all L1 \(\to\) all L2 \(\to\) L3 \(\to\) L4, checking each answer as you go, then attempt L5 without hints. Re-attempt anything you got wrong after 48 hours.

PART 3 — Module 1: Introduction to Machine Learning

3.A What & Why of ML (1.1)

P1.1 L1 · Foundation

The three blanks in Mitchell's definition

Tom Mitchell defines a learning program as one that improves its performance \(P\) at task \(T\) through experience \(E\). For each scenario, write down \(T\), \(P\) and \(E\):

(a) A spam filter that gets better at sorting mail the longer it runs.
(b) A thermostat that always switches off at exactly 22 °C.

Hint

One of these two is not a learning program at all — ask whether its behaviour changes with experience.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(T\) = classify an incoming e-mail as spam/not-spam. \(P\) = fraction of e-mails correctly classified. \(E\) = a stream of e-mails, each later labelled by the user as spam or not. This is a genuine \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\) triple.

(b) There is no \(E\). The thermostat's rule ("switch off at 22 °C") never changes no matter how many times it runs — nothing it does ever updates from experience. It is not a learning program, just a fixed rule; it has a \(T\) and an implicit \(P\) but no \(E\), and without \(E\) there is nothing to "learn."

Key insight: All three of \(T\), \(P\) and \(E\) must be present and \(E\) must actually feed back into a change in behaviour for something to count as "learning" in Mitchell's sense — a system that only executes a fixed rule, however well, is not an ML system.

P1.2 L1 · Foundation

When a rule beats a model

True or false, with a one-line reason: "If you can write down the exact rule a task requires, you should still use ML for it, because ML will always generalise at least as well as the hand-written rule."

Hint

Think about what ML buys you when the mapping is already perfectly known and unambiguous.

Answer & Key Insight

False. If a correct, closed-form rule is already known and does not depend on anything the business expects to drift over time (e.g. "\(\text{VAT} = 18\%\) of price"), coding that rule directly is faster to build, perfectly accurate, fully explainable, and has no training data requirement or drift risk. ML earns its cost when (i) no one can state the rule explicitly (image recognition), (ii) the rule would need to be personalised per user at a scale no one can hand-write, or (iii) the pattern itself is expected to shift and should be re-learned from fresh data.

Key insight: "Could I write this as an if/else rule a domain expert agrees with?" is a genuine filter question before reaching for ML — ML is a tool for problems that resist being stated as explicit logic, not a universal upgrade over one that doesn't.

P1.3 L2 · Computation

ML or rule? Five quick calls

For each, answer "ML" or "rule-based", in one line each:

(a) Deciding whether a credit-card transaction's amount exceeds the cardholder's stated daily limit.
(b) Deciding whether a credit-card transaction looks fraudulent given location, amount, merchant category and time, when genuine fraud patterns keep changing.
(c) Converting a temperature reading from Celsius to Fahrenheit.
(d) Recommending which of 50,000 products a given shopper is most likely to buy next.
(e) Tagging whether a photo contains a cat.

Hint

Ask: is there a known, stable formula, or does the mapping depend on patterns too complex/too personalised/too shifting to write down?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Rule-based — a direct numeric comparison, known and stable.

(b) ML — the fraud pattern is complex, high-dimensional, and known to drift as fraudsters adapt.

(c) Rule-based — an exact, unchanging formula \({}^\circ\text{F} = {}^\circ\text{C} \times 9/5 + 32\).

(d) ML — personalised at a scale (50,000 items \(\times\) every shopper) no rule set could realistically encode.

(e) ML — no one can write down the pixel-level rule for "cat."

Key insight: The same surface domain (finance, e-commerce) can contain both rule-based and ML sub-problems side by side; the decision is made task-by-task, not company-by-company.

P1.4 L3 · Application

Specifying \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\) for a messy real problem

A bank wants to "use AI to reduce loan defaults." Turn this vague pitch into a precise \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\) specification, and name which broader application domain (from: vision, NLP, recommendation, security/fraud, forecasting) it belongs to.

Hint

"Reduce defaults" is a business goal, not a task definition — the task is a prediction the bank can act on before the fact.

Answer & Key Insight

\(T\): predict, at the time of application, whether a given loan applicant will default within the loan's term (a binary classification). \(P\): a classification-quality metric appropriate to the (likely imbalanced) default rate — e.g. AUC-ROC, or precision/recall on the default class, rather than raw accuracy. \(E\): a historical dataset of past applicants' intake features (income, credit history, loan amount, etc.) paired with their eventual known outcome (defaulted / repaid). Domain: this is closest to forecasting/risk-scoring, with structure similar to security/fraud screening (predicting a rare, costly, adversarial-adjacent outcome from tabular features).

Key insight: "Reduce defaults" is an outcome the bank wants, not something a model can be trained to directly output — a learning task must be a predictable quantity available at decision time, with a measurable \(P\) and a concrete, already-existing \(E\).

P1.5 L4 · Analysis

Comparing two \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\) formulations of one problem

Two data scientists both try to formalise "detect when a factory machine is about to fail":

  • DS1: \(T\) = classify each hourly sensor reading as "healthy" or "about to fail", \(P\) = classification accuracy, \(E\) = historical hourly readings labelled healthy/failed at the moment of failure.
  • DS2: \(T\) = predict, from the current sensor reading, the number of hours remaining until the next failure, \(P\) = mean absolute error (MAE) of that prediction in hours, \(E\) = historical sensor-reading streams each ending in a recorded failure time.

Which formulation is more useful to a maintenance team, and what is the specific flaw in DS1's choice of \(P\)?

Hint

How many of the hourly readings in a typical dataset are actually labelled "about to fail", versus "healthy"? What does that do to a model that is rewarded purely on accuracy?

Answer & Key Insight

DS2 is more useful: a maintenance team needs a lead time to act (e.g. "schedule service within 6 hours"), and a continuous remaining-life estimate (regression) gives exactly that, while DS1's binary flag gives no sense of urgency. The flaw in DS1's \(P\): machine failure is rare, so the "healthy" class vastly outnumbers "about to fail" in \(E\); a model that predicts "healthy" on every single reading can reach 99%+ accuracy while never once catching a real failure. DS1 needed a metric robust to class imbalance (e.g. recall on the failure class, or precision-recall AUC), not plain accuracy.

Key insight: Choosing \(P\) is not a formality after \(T\) is fixed — an badly chosen \(P\) (accuracy on a rare class) can make a model that is useless in practice look excellent on paper, and the choice of \(T\) itself (classification vs. a regression that gives a lead time) changes how actionable the output is.

P1.6 L5 · Mastery

Does "AI" even apply here?

A startup pitches: "We're building AI to tell users the exact sales tax owed on any purchase in any of the 50 US states." Is this an ML problem? If yes, specify \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\) and the application domain; if no, explain what it actually is and what a correct build looks like instead.

Hint

Is the mapping from (state, item category, price) to tax owed something that is already fully and precisely known, or something that must be inferred from examples?

Answer & Key Insight

This is not an ML problem. Sales tax rates and category exemptions in every US state are published, exact, legally-defined rules — there is no uncertainty to resolve from data, no pattern to generalise, and no \(E\) in Mitchell's sense (performance does not improve with more "experience," because there is nothing to learn: the rate for (state, category) is a lookup, not an inference). The correct build is a rule-based lookup table/engine keyed by (state, category, date-of-change), kept current by tracking legislative updates — the hard engineering problem here is data maintenance, not learning.

Key insight: "AI" in a pitch does not make a problem an ML problem; the test is always the same one from 1.1.2 — is there a known, stable rule, or genuine uncertainty that must be inferred from experience? A plausible-sounding AI pitch can still fail this test completely.

3.B Types of ML by Feedback Signal (1.2)

P1.7 L1 · Foundation

Match the definition

Match each definition to one of: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, semi-supervised learning.

(a) Learn from a small labelled set plus a much larger unlabelled set.
(b) Learn a mapping from inputs to known, correct outputs provided for every training example.
(c) Learn to group similar objects together without being told what the groups mean.
(d) Learn, through trial and sequential interaction with an environment, which actions earn the most cumulative reward.

Hint

Ask: is there a label at all? If yes, is it present for every example? If there's no label, is there instead a reward signal that arrives after acting?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Semi-supervised learning.

(b) Supervised learning.

(c) Unsupervised learning (clustering).

(d) Reinforcement learning.

Key insight: The four types sit on a single spectrum of "how much, and what kind of, feedback is available" — full per-example labels, no labels at all, a partial mix of the two, or a delayed scalar reward instead of a label — and that spectrum, not the algorithm used, is what defines the category.

P1.8 L1 · Foundation

True or false: classification vs regression

True or false, with a reason: "Classification and regression are really the same problem; the only difference is that classification happens to have a discrete-valued target."

Hint

Is that actually the definition used, or just usually true? Think of a target that is discrete but the problem is still regarded as regression, or ordered-discrete and still neither classic classification nor regression cleanly.

Answer & Key Insight

Essentially true, and it is exactly the definition used: both are supervised learning; the target function \(f(x)\) is discrete-valued for classification (a label from a finite set of classes) and real-valued (continuous) for regression. The only wrinkle is ordinal targets (e.g. star ratings 1–5): these are discrete, so they are often handled as classification, but because the classes are ordered, treating a "4" misclassified as "5" the same as "4" misclassified as "1" throws away information — this is why ordinal regression exists as a distinct third approach that is neither plain classification nor plain regression.

Key insight: The classification/regression split is genuinely just "discrete vs continuous target," but real targets aren't always cleanly one or the other, and ordinal data is the clearest example of a target type the clean dichotomy doesn't fully capture.

P1.9 L2 · Computation

Classify eight scenarios by feedback type

Classify each as supervised–classification, supervised–regression, unsupervised, reinforcement learning, or semi-supervised:

(a) Predicting a house's sale price from its features.
(b) Grouping news articles into topics with no predefined topic list.
(c) A warehouse robot learning, through repeated attempts and a reward for successful stacking, how to stack boxes without toppling them.
(d) Diagnosing a disease from an X-ray using a large archive of X-rays, only 2% of which have been reviewed and labelled by a radiologist.
(e) Predicting whether an e-mail is spam.
(f) Predicting tomorrow's maximum temperature.
(g) Finding unusual spending patterns in a transaction log with no "fraud/not fraud" labels at all.
(h) A game-playing agent learning a strategy purely from win/loss outcomes at the end of each game.

Hint

(d) and (g): is there any label present, and if so, how much of it? (c) and (h): is there a label for the "correct" action at each step, or only an outcome?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Supervised–regression (continuous price).

(b) Unsupervised (clustering, no predefined labels).

(c) Reinforcement learning (reward after actions, sequential).

(d) Semi-supervised (98% unlabelled, 2% labelled).

(e) Supervised–classification (discrete spam/not-spam).

(f) Supervised–regression (continuous temperature).

(g) Unsupervised (no labels at all — this is anomaly detection via clustering/density, not classification, precisely because there's nothing to supervise with).

(h) Reinforcement learning (delayed, sparse win/loss reward, not a per-move label).

Key insight: The presence of some human-provided outcome (a final game result, a reward) is not automatically a "label" in the supervised sense — a label tells you the correct answer directly and immediately for a given input; a reward only tells you how good an entire sequence of actions turned out to be.

P1.10 L2 · Computation

Is semi-supervised learning justified here?

A company has 500 labelled and 2,000,000 unlabelled customer-support tickets. Explain in one or two sentences why semi-supervised learning is a sensible choice here rather than training a supervised model on only the 500 labels, and rather than discarding the labels and clustering the full 2,000,500 unsupervised.

Hint

Consider what is lost if you throw away either part of the data.

Answer & Key Insight

With only 500 labelled tickets, a purely supervised model would be trained on a tiny, likely unrepresentative sample and would generalise poorly. Throwing the labels away and clustering all 2,000,500 unsupervised would discard the one thing that tells the model what the categories actually mean (the 500 labels), leaving clusters with no guaranteed correspondence to the categories the company cares about. Semi-supervised learning uses the small labelled set to anchor what the categories mean while the enormous unlabelled set helps the model learn the overall shape/structure of ticket text, getting the benefit of both.

Key insight: Semi-supervised learning is specifically the right tool exactly when labelled data is small and expensive to get but unlabelled data is large and nearly free — the common situation in practice, which is why it sits as its own named category rather than a minor variant.

P1.11 L3 · Application

Stating the clustering objective informally

A retailer wants to segment 50,000 customers by purchasing behaviour into groups, with no predefined segment names. State, informally but precisely, the two-part objective any good clustering of these customers should satisfy, and explain what would be wrong with a clustering that puts every single customer into their own, individual cluster.

Hint

One part of the objective is about customers within a cluster; the other is about customers across different clusters.

Answer & Key Insight

A good clustering should minimise intra-cluster distance (customers assigned to the same cluster should be as similar to each other as possible) while maximising inter-cluster distance (customers in different clusters should be as dissimilar as possible). Putting every customer in their own cluster trivially satisfies "minimise intra-cluster distance" (there's only one point per cluster, so intra-cluster distance is exactly zero) but is useless: there is no inter-cluster separation to speak of because there's no grouping happening at all — the retailer learns nothing they didn't already know (every individual customer is themselves).

Key insight: A clustering objective can't be optimised one-sided — a trivial solution (one cluster per point, or one giant cluster for everyone) always exists for whichever half of the objective you ignore, which is exactly why both halves are stated together.

P1.12 L3 · Application

Formalising an RL scenario

An elevator-dispatch system learns, through experience, to decide which elevator car to send when a call button is pressed, aiming to minimise average passenger wait time. Identify its agent, environment, state, action set, and reward signal.

Hint

The "state" needs to capture everything the dispatcher currently knows that's relevant to the decision — think about what changes between one call and the next.

Answer & Key Insight

Agent: the dispatch controller. Environment: the building — all elevator cars, their current floors/directions/occupancy, and the pattern of passenger call requests. State: (current floor and direction of each car, which floors currently have pending calls, time of day, etc.). Action set: \(\{\text{send car } 1, \text{send car } 2, \ldots, \text{send car } k\}\) for the newly pressed call. Reward: a signal that penalises wait time — e.g. a negative reward equal to the wait time once the passenger is picked up (so the agent is trained to minimise cumulative negative reward, i.e. minimise total wait time), possibly with an extra penalty for extreme individual waits.

Key insight: Formalising an RL problem is mostly the discipline of naming these five pieces explicitly — a vague goal ("minimise wait time") only becomes trainable once it is turned into a reward the agent receives after each action, tied to a well-defined state and action set.

P1.13 L3 · Application

Diagnosing a classification-dressed-as-regression mistake

A team wants to predict customer satisfaction, originally measured on a continuous 0–100 survey scale, but they decide to bucket it into "Low" (0–40), "Medium" (41–70), "High" (71–100) and train a classifier, because "classification models are easier to evaluate with accuracy." A model is trained and reports 91% accuracy. What is lost by this choice, and what would you recommend instead?

Hint

Think about what happens to a true score of 40 predicted as 41, versus a true score of 40 predicted as 95, under the bucketed scheme.

Answer & Key Insight

Bucketing throws away the ordering and magnitude information in the original continuous target: a prediction of "Medium" when the truth is "Low" is counted as simply "wrong," identically whether the true score was 40 (a near-miss, one point from the Medium boundary) or 2 (a disastrous miss). The 91% accuracy figure also hides how badly wrong the misclassified 9% actually are. Recommendation: keep the problem as regression on the original 0–100 scale (evaluated with MAE/RMSE/\(R^2\)) if the application genuinely needs the numeric score, or at minimum use ordinal classification/ordinal-aware metrics if buckets are truly required by the business, rather than plain multi-class accuracy.

Key insight: Converting a naturally continuous target into discrete buckets to make evaluation "easier" is a common but costly shortcut — easier-to-compute accuracy is not the same as a metric that actually reflects what the business cares about.

P1.14 L4 · Analysis

Can RL always be reformulated as supervised learning?

A colleague argues: "Reinforcement learning is unnecessary — any RL problem can just be reformulated as supervised learning, by recording the action taken at each state and the eventual reward, and training a classifier to predict 'the best action given the state.'" Identify the two things this reformulation is missing that make it not equivalent to RL.

Hint

In supervised learning, the label given for an example is assumed to be the correct answer. Is "the action that was taken" the same as "the best action"? And where would the labels for actions never tried come from?

Answer & Key Insight

First gap — credit assignment: a supervised "label" is assumed correct, but "the action taken, plus the eventual reward" does not tell you that the action was good; it only tells you what happened afterward, which may be due to many other actions in the sequence (the reward is delayed and depends on a whole trajectory, not one step). Simply mimicking actions associated with high eventual reward conflates correlation with that action's true contribution. Second gap — exploration: supervised learning is purely passive — it can only learn from labels it's given, and here, there are no labels at all for actions that were never tried; RL's agent must actively explore untried actions to discover whether they're better, which is a fundamentally different data-generation process than learning from a fixed labelled dataset.

Key insight: The thing that makes RL genuinely distinct from supervised learning is not just "no label was given" — it is the two-sided problem of credit assignment over delayed reward and active exploration of untried actions, neither of which a passive supervised reformulation can solve by construction.

P1.15 L4 · Analysis

Why semi-supervised learning needs an assumption

Explain, with a concrete counterexample, why semi-supervised learning cannot work for arbitrary unlabelled data — i.e. what assumption about how the labelled and unlabelled data relate must hold for the unlabelled data to help at all.

Hint

Imagine the unlabelled examples come from a completely different, unrelated distribution than the labelled ones (e.g. labelled cat/dog photos plus unlabelled satellite images).

Answer & Key Insight

If the unlabelled data's underlying structure has nothing to do with the labelled task's class boundaries, it cannot help, and can actively hurt. Counterexample: 500 labelled cat/dog photos plus 2,000,000 unlabelled satellite images — the unlabelled data's "clusters" (urban areas, farmland, coastline) tell you nothing about where the cat/dog decision boundary lies; a model that tries to use that unlabelled structure to inform its labelled task will at best waste effort and at worst be actively misled. Semi-supervised learning implicitly assumes something like the cluster assumption (points in the same natural cluster of the unlabelled data tend to share the same label) or the manifold assumption (the data lies on a lower-dimensional structure along which the label varies smoothly) — and this must genuinely hold between the labelled and unlabelled sets, not be assumed by default.

Key insight: Semi-supervised learning's extra signal from unlabelled data is not "free information that always helps" — it is a bet that the unlabelled data's natural structure lines up with the labels, and that bet needs to be true of your specific data, not just true in general.

P1.16 L5 · Mastery

Misconception trap: "RL is just supervised learning with a weird label"

A student says: "Reinforcement learning's reward is basically just a label, so RL is a special case of supervised learning." Construct a short scenario (2–3 sentences) that makes the flaw in this statement obvious, and in your own words state precisely what distinguishes a reward from a label.

Hint

Think of a game where the agent makes 40 moves and only finds out whether it won or lost at the very end.

Answer & Key Insight

Scenario: a chess-playing agent makes 40 moves in a game and receives a single reward (\(+1\) win / \(-1\) loss) only after the 40th move. Supervised learning would need to know, for each of the 40 individual moves, whether that specific move was correct — but the \(+1/-1\) signal says nothing about which of the 40 moves were good and which were mistakes the opponent failed to punish. A label in supervised learning is (i) available per-example, (ii) assumed correct for that specific example, and (iii) given without the learner having to act first. A reward in RL is (i) often delayed and received only after a whole sequence of actions, (ii) a measure of overall outcome quality, not a per-action correctness signal, and (iii) only observed because the agent chose to act in a particular way — changing the action changes what reward is even available to observe.

Key insight: The deep difference is the credit-assignment problem (P1.14) hiding inside "a reward is basically a label": a reward tells you how a whole trajectory of decisions turned out, not which individual decision in that trajectory deserves the credit or the blame — and that gap is exactly what RL's machinery (and nothing in supervised learning) is built to solve.

P1.17 L5 · Mastery

A business problem that resists a single, clean label

A payments company wants to flag fraudulent transactions. Their data: 50,000 transactions confirmed fraudulent (by chargeback), 2 million confirmed legitimate (never disputed within the dispute window), and 3 million more that are too recent to know yet, plus the ability to act (block a transaction) and later observe whether the customer complained. Which feedback type(s) genuinely apply here, and how would you combine them into one practical plan?

Hint

Notice this problem actually has three different kinds of signal available at once — don't force it into exactly one textbook category.

Answer & Key Insight

This scenario genuinely blends three types. (1) Supervised classification on the 50,000 confirmed-fraud + 2,000,000 confirmed-legitimate transactions (a label exists, even though heavily imbalanced). (2) Semi-supervised learning, treating the 3,000,000 not-yet-resolved transactions as the large unlabelled pool that can still inform the model's sense of the data's overall structure while their eventual labels catch up. (3) A reinforcement-learning-flavoured feedback loop for the acting part: once the model blocks a transaction, the customer's later complaint (or lack of one) is a delayed, action-dependent outcome signal that should feed back into retraining — blocking changes what gets observed, exactly as acting changes the state in RL. A practical plan trains the initial classifier supervised on confirmed data, optionally folds in the unresolved transactions semi-supervised, and continuously monitors the outcomes of the model's own block/allow decisions as an ongoing feedback loop that must account for the fact that blocked transactions no longer generate the same complaint signal a false positive would.

Key insight: Real deployed systems rarely fit cleanly into exactly one of the four textbook categories — the categories are a vocabulary for naming the kind of signal present in each part of a problem, not a forced single label for the whole system.

3.C Types of ML by Data Usage & Inductive Learning (1.3–1.4)

P1.18 L1 · Foundation

Vocabulary check: how training data is used

True or false, with a reason, for each:

(a) "Online learning updates the model on one example (or a small stream) at a time, as data arrives."
(b) "Instance-based learning builds an explicit, compact model during training, then discards the training data."
(c) "Model-based learning stores every training example and compares new queries against all of them at prediction time."

Hint

(b) and (c) have the definitions of instance-based and model-based learning deliberately swapped — read carefully.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True.

(b) False — this is the definition of model-based (eager) learning: fit a model, then the raw training data is no longer needed. Instance-based learning does the opposite.

(c) False — this is the definition of instance-based (lazy) learning: store the training data itself and compare at query time. Model-based learning fits parameters once and discards the raw data.

Key insight: "Instance-based vs model-based" is about whether the raw training data is kept and consulted at prediction time (instance-based/lazy) or compressed into parameters and then discarded (model-based/eager) — not about how the data was fed in during training (that's the separate batch/online axis).

P1.19 L2 · Computation

Classify six scenarios by data-usage type

For each, name (i) batch, mini-batch, or online, and (ii) instance-based or model-based, where determinable from the description:

(a) A spam filter retrained once a month on all mail collected that month.
(b) A recommendation engine that updates its model after every single click a user makes, in real time.
(c) A \(k\)-nearest-neighbour classifier used to tag new support tickets by comparing them against the full archive of previously tagged tickets.
(d) A neural network trained by repeatedly sweeping through shuffled batches of 256 images at a time.
(e) A linear regression model fit once on a fixed historical dataset and then used, unchanged, for a year.
(f) A stock-price anomaly detector that must incorporate each new tick of market data the instant it arrives.

Hint

(c) and (e) are about instance-based vs model-based; the others are about batch/mini-batch/online.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Batch (monthly, all data at once); instance-based/model-based not determinable from this description alone.

(b) Online.

(c) Instance-based (explicitly compares against the stored archive at query time); batch/online not specified.

(d) Mini-batch.

(e) Model-based (fit once, data then unused); this is also, by how it's described, a batch fit.

(f) Online (must incorporate each new tick immediately).

Key insight: "How was the model trained" (batch/mini-batch/online) and "how does the model make predictions" (instance-based/model-based) are two independent axes — a given scenario description might answer one question clearly while leaving the other unspecified, and it's a mistake to force an answer the description doesn't support.

P1.20 L2 · Computation

Checking the inductive learning hypothesis against a tiny example

A model is trained on 4 examples and achieves 100% training accuracy, but scores only 52% (near chance) on a held-out test set drawn from the same underlying population. Does this training set satisfy the inductive learning hypothesis, in the sense needed for the model to generalise? Explain.

Hint

The inductive learning hypothesis is a hypothesis about the training data itself, not about the model.

Answer & Key Insight

No. The inductive learning hypothesis states that a hypothesis which approximates the target function well over a sufficiently large sample of training examples will also approximate it well over unseen examples. 4 examples is far too small a sample for this hypothesis to be expected to hold for anything but the simplest target functions — the near-chance test performance is exactly the symptom of the hypothesis's precondition ("sufficiently large sample") not being met, not a flaw in the learning algorithm itself.

Key insight: The inductive learning hypothesis is a working assumption, not a guarantee — it depends on the training sample being large and representative enough, and when it visibly fails (\(\text{train} \gg \text{test}\) performance, as here), the first thing to question is the size/representativeness of the training set, not necessarily the model's capacity.

P1.21 L3 · Application

Most general and most specific hypothesis

A hypothesis space consists of conjunctions over two attributes, \(\text{Sky} \in \{\text{Sunny}, \text{Cloudy}, ?\}\) and \(\text{Wind} \in \{\text{Strong}, \text{Weak}, ?\}\), where "?" means "any value is acceptable" for that attribute. Given two positive examples — \((\text{Sunny}, \text{Strong})\) and \((\text{Sunny}, \text{Weak})\) — both labelled "\(\text{EnjoySport} = \text{Yes}\)" and no negative examples, state the most specific hypothesis consistent with the data and the most general hypothesis consistent with the data.

Hint

Most specific: only generalise an attribute when the positive examples actually disagree on its value. Most general: with no negative examples to rule anything out, how unconstrained can you be?

Answer & Key Insight

Most specific hypothesis: \((\text{Sunny}, ?)\) — Sky stays "Sunny" because both positive examples agree on it, but Wind must generalise to "?" because the two positive examples disagree (Strong vs Weak), so no single specific value for Wind is consistent with both. Most general hypothesis: \((?, ?)\) — with no negative examples at all to rule anything out, nothing forces either attribute to be constrained, so the most general consistent hypothesis accepts every instance.

Key insight: The most specific hypothesis is driven entirely by where the positive examples agree or disagree; the most general hypothesis is constrained only by the negative examples (there's none here, so it's maximally unconstrained) — this is the seed idea behind version-space learning algorithms like candidate-elimination.

P1.22 L3 · Application

Batch or online for a drifting fraud model?

A fraud-detection model's underlying pattern of fraud changes week to week as fraudsters adapt to whatever the current model catches. Recommend batch or online learning, and name the specific risk the alternative choice would create.

Hint

Think about the lag between "the pattern changes" and "the model notices."

Answer & Key Insight

Recommend online (or at least frequent mini-batch retraining). The specific risk of batch learning here is staleness: if the model is only retrained monthly, fraudsters who adapt week-to-week will have roughly three weeks of free rein each cycle in which the model is working against a pattern that has already moved on, directly costing the business money for the gap between pattern-shift and retraining. Online learning (or high-frequency retraining) keeps the decision boundary tracking the adversary's current behaviour much more closely, at the cost of a model that is more sensitive to short-term noise and that needs careful monitoring for sudden swings.

Key insight: Batch vs online isn't just an engineering/infrastructure choice — it directly trades off "stability and simplicity" against "how quickly the model can respond to a changing world," and adversarial, fast-drifting domains like fraud are the textbook case where that trade-off tips toward online.

P1.23 L4 · Analysis

Why instance-based and model-based trade training cost for query cost

Explain, in terms of what happens at training time versus at prediction (query) time, why an instance-based learner has near-zero training cost but expensive queries, while a model-based learner has the reverse pattern. Then state one practical situation where each tradeoff direction is clearly preferable.

Hint

What does "training" actually consist of for each type, if instance-based learning just stores the data?

Answer & Key Insight

Instance-based: "training" is just storing the data — essentially free. Every query then has to compare the new point against some or all of the stored examples (e.g. compute distances to every training point for \(k\)-NN), so query cost grows with the size of the stored dataset and can be substantial. Model-based: training does real work — fitting parameters by optimisation over the whole dataset, which is the expensive step — but once fit, a query is typically a single cheap function evaluation of the (usually small, fixed-size) parameters, independent of how large the original training set was. Instance-based preferable: when the data changes constantly and retraining a model-based learner from scratch each time would be too costly (e.g. a small, frequently-updated reference database where new points just need to be added to storage). Model-based preferable: when queries must be answered extremely fast and at huge volume (e.g. a real-time ad-ranking system serving millions of requests per second), where a one-time, amortised training cost is a far better trade than paying a per-query cost against a huge stored dataset.

Key insight: "Training cost vs. query cost" is a real engineering trade-off, not just a theoretical curiosity — which side of it you want depends entirely on whether your system's bottleneck is "the data changes often" or "queries must be answered fast and at scale."

P1.24 L4 · Analysis

Hypothesis-space size and inductive bias

Two learners are given the exact same small training set. Learner A's hypothesis space is "any Boolean function of the input attributes" (extremely large/unrestricted). Learner B's hypothesis space is "conjunctions of at most 2 attribute tests" (small/restricted). Explain what each learner's choice of hypothesis space costs or buys it, in terms of fitting the training data versus generalising to new data.

Hint

An unrestricted hypothesis space can always fit the training data perfectly — ask what that perfect fit is actually worth.

Answer & Key Insight

Learner A (unrestricted Boolean functions) can always find a hypothesis that fits the training data perfectly — including one that does nothing more than memorise exactly those training examples and predict arbitrarily (even randomly) elsewhere. This is because an unrestricted space contains no inductive bias at all: with no restriction on which hypotheses are "preferred" ahead of time, there's no basis to prefer a generalising hypothesis over a memorising one, so the hypothesis space alone guarantees nothing about performance on unseen data. Learner B (conjunctions of \(\le 2\) attributes) cannot necessarily fit noisy or complex training data perfectly, but its restriction is an inductive bias — it only considers hypotheses of a specific, simple form, so if the true target function (or a good approximation of it) happens to be expressible that way, Learner B is far more likely to land on something that generalises, precisely because it was never free to memorise arbitrarily in the first place.

Key insight: A hypothesis space's size is not "more is always better" — an unrestricted space can always match the training data with zero generalising power, while a well-chosen restricted space trades some training fit for an inductive bias that is actually necessary for generalisation to be possible at all (this is the no-free-lunch intuition behind every "bias–variance" discussion later in the course).

3.D Module 1 Capstone

P1.25 L5 · Mastery

Full classification of a new product idea

A startup describes their product: "A smart thermostat that (i) learns each household's comfort preferences from a handful of manual temperature overrides the owner makes in the first two weeks, combined with months of ambient sensor data that was never manually labelled, and (ii) continuously adjusts heating/cooling schedules in real time as it runs, trying to minimise energy cost while keeping the number of manual overrides low (a signal it only finds out about after it acts)."

(a) Is this an ML problem, a rule-based problem, or both?
(b) Which feedback type(s) from 1.2 genuinely apply to (i) and to (ii) separately?
(c) Is (ii) better described as batch, mini-batch, or online learning, and why?
(d) Briefly state a \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\) for the comfort-learning part described in (i).

Hint

Treat (i) and (ii) as two separate sub-problems with potentially different feedback types — don't force one label onto the whole system.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) ML, specifically because "comfort preference" is not something that can be stated as a simple fixed rule — it differs per household and must be inferred from behaviour.

(b) (i) is semi-supervised: a handful of manually-overridden temperatures act as the small labelled set, and months of ambient sensor data (with no explicit "this is the ideal temperature" label) act as the large unlabelled set that helps the model learn the household's broader comfort-relevant patterns (time of day, occupancy, outdoor conditions). (ii) is reinforcement learning: the thermostat acts (adjusts the schedule), and only afterward observes a delayed, action-dependent outcome signal (did the owner override it, and how much energy was used) — exactly the agent/environment/reward structure of 1.2.3, not a label available in advance.

(c) (ii) is best described as online learning: it must continuously adjust in real time as it runs, incorporating each new override-or-not outcome as it happens, rather than waiting to batch up data over weeks before updating.

(d) \(T\): predict the owner's preferred temperature setpoint at a given time of day/condition. \(P\): a measure that penalises manual overrides (e.g. rate of overrides per week, or a weighted combination of override frequency and the size of the correction made). \(E\): the household's manual override events from the first two weeks, together with the ambient sensor stream collected continuously.

Key insight: This single product description mixes at least two different feedback types (semi-supervised for the initial preference-learning, reinforcement-learning-flavoured for the ongoing adaptive control loop) and an online data-usage pattern — exactly the kind of composite system P1.17 pointed at, and the discipline of naming each piece separately (rather than forcing one label on the whole product) is the actual skill this module is building.

P1.26 L5 · Mastery

Find the three planted errors

A junior analyst writes up this case study. It contains three distinct errors drawn from this module's content. Find and correct all three.

"Our company wants to automatically compute each employee's gross pay from their hours worked and hourly rate, so we built a supervised regression model trained on last year's payroll records. Separately, we want to teach a warehouse robot to pick the fastest route between shelves; since the robot gets a label at every single step telling it the one correct next move, this is just ordinary supervised classification. Finally, because our sales data changes a little every single day, we decided to retrain our demand-forecasting model once every three years in a single giant batch, to be maximally thorough."

Hint

One error is about whether ML was even the right tool to reach for; one is about mislabelling a feedback type; one is about a batch/online mismatch with the stated update frequency of the data.

Answer & Key Insight

Error 1 (1.1.2): gross pay from \(\text{hours} \times \text{rate}\) is an exact, known, stable arithmetic rule — it should be computed directly, not learned from a trained model; there is no genuine uncertainty for ML to resolve here, and a model could even learn the wrong rule if the historical payroll data contains any errors or exceptions.

Error 2 (1.2.1 / 1.2.3): a warehouse robot finding the fastest route generally does not get told the one correct next move at every step — it typically only discovers whether a sequence of moves was good via delayed feedback (time taken, or a collision). If it genuinely did receive a correct-next-move label at every single step, it actually would be supervised learning; the error here is calling it "ordinary supervised classification" as if that's the typical/obvious setup for this kind of task, when in reality this class of problem (sequential decisions, outcome discovered after the fact) is the canonical reinforcement-learning setting, and the case study should have flagged the per-step-label assumption as the unusual, specific premise it is rather than stating it as the default.

Error 3 (1.3.1): data that changes "a little every single day" calling for retraining only "once every three years" is a severe mismatch — this guarantees the model operates on badly stale information for most of its three-year life. A changing-daily signal calls for frequent retraining (daily/weekly batch, mini-batch, or online), not an extremely infrequent giant batch; "maximally thorough" is the wrong framing — thoroughness of a single retrain does not compensate for staleness between retrains.

Key insight: Each of this module's core distinctions (ML vs rule, feedback type, batch/online frequency) has a specific, checkable failure mode, and a surprising number of real-world mistakes in applied ML are exactly these three kinds of category error rather than anything to do with model architecture or tuning.

PART 4 — Module 2: Machine Learning Workflow

4.A Data Fundamentals (2.1)

P2.1 L1 · Foundation

Objects, attributes and the target

A lender keeps the following table.

Loan ID Amount (₹ lakh) Period (months) Credit rating Defaulted?
L-101 35 60 Good No
L-102 12 6 Poor Yes
L-103 70 36 Good No
L-104 18 48 Fair No
L-105 25 12 Poor Yes

(a) How many objects and how many attributes does the table contain? Give two other names the course uses for each.

(b) The lender wants to predict Defaulted? for new applicants. Which column is the target, and which columns are candidate input features?

(c) True or false: "Loan ID is a numeric-looking attribute, so it should be fed to the model as a feature."

Hint

Rows are one kind of thing and columns another. For (c), ask whether the ID carries any property of the loan or only names it.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) 5 objects and 5 attributes. Objects are also called records, points, samples, instances or entities. Attributes are also called variables, fields, characteristics, dimensions or features.

(b) The target is Defaulted?. The candidate input features are Amount, Period and Credit rating.

(c) False. Loan ID is a nominal identifier. It distinguishes one loan from another and says nothing about the loan's risk. A model given the ID could at best memorise the training rows, which does not generalise to new loans whose IDs it has never seen.

Key insight: A column being present in the table does not make it a feature. An attribute is useful only if it describes a property of the object that can plausibly relate to the target.

P2.2 L1 · Foundation

Name the measurement level

For each attribute, give its Stevens level (nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio) and say whether it is discrete or continuous.

(a) Postal PIN code.

(b) T-shirt size {S, M, L, XL}.

(c) Calendar year of birth.

(d) Number of children in a household.

(e) Air temperature in °F.

(f) Body mass in kg.

(g) Customer satisfaction on a 1–5 star scale.

(h) Blood group {A, B, AB, O}.

Hint

Check the four operations in order: can you test equality, order the values, take meaningful differences, and take meaningful ratios? Ratios need a true zero meaning "none of the quantity".

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Nominal, discrete. It is a number in form only; \(560001 - 110001\) means nothing.

(b) Ordinal, discrete. \(\text{S} < \text{M} < \text{L} < \text{XL}\), but "\(\text{L} - \text{M}\)" has no fixed size.

(c) Interval, discrete. Differences between years are meaningful, but year 0 is an arbitrary origin, so "born in 2000 is 1.0005 times born in 1999" is meaningless. (Age, by contrast, is ratio.)

(d) Ratio, discrete. Zero means no children, and 4 children is twice 2.

(e) Interval, continuous. 0 °F is not "no heat".

(f) Ratio, continuous. 0 kg means no mass, so 80 kg is twice 40 kg.

(g) Ordinal, discrete. The gap from 1 to 2 stars need not equal the gap from 4 to 5.

(h) Nominal, discrete. Only equality tests make sense.

Key insight: The level is decided by which operations are meaningful (\(=\), then \(<\), then \(+\,-\), then \(\times\,\div\)), not by whether the values happen to be written as numbers. Discreteness is a separate axis: a count is discrete and still ratio-level.

P2.3 L2 · Computation

Is 30 °C twice as hot as 15 °C?

(a) Compute the ratio \(30/15\) after converting both temperatures to Fahrenheit (\(F = 1.8C + 32\)) and to Kelvin (\(K = C + 273.15\)). Report each ratio to four decimals.

(b) Now take three readings, 15 °C, 20 °C and 30 °C, and compute the ratio of differences \((30 - 15)/(20 - 15)\) in Celsius and in Fahrenheit.

(c) Use (a) and (b) to explain which statements about Celsius temperature are meaningful.

Hint

An interval scale allows any transformation of the form \(\text{new} = a \cdot \text{old} + b\). Ask which quantity survives such a transformation and which does not.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) In Fahrenheit the temperatures are 86 °F and 59 °F, so the ratio is

\[ \frac{86}{59} = \mathbf{1.4576} \]

In Kelvin they are 303.15 K and 288.15 K, so the ratio is 1.0521. In Celsius it was 2. The "twice as hot" claim gives three different answers depending on the unit.

(b) In Celsius and in Fahrenheit:

\[ \frac{30 - 15}{20 - 15} = \frac{15}{5} = \mathbf{3}, \qquad \frac{86 - 59}{68 - 59} = \frac{27}{9} = \mathbf{3} \]

The ratio of differences is the same.

(c) Under \(\text{new} = a \cdot \text{old} + b\), the offset \(b\) cancels in any difference and the scale \(a\) cancels in any ratio of differences, so statements like "the rise from 15 to 30 was three times the rise from 15 to 20" are meaningful. A ratio of raw values keeps \(b\), so it changes with the unit and is meaningless. Only Kelvin, which has a true zero, supports "twice as hot", and physically 30 °C is only about 5% hotter than 15 °C in absolute terms.

Key insight: Celsius is interval, not ratio. Differences and ratios of differences are invariant under the permitted transformation \(a \cdot x + b\), but ratios of raw values are not; that is exactly what separates the interval level from the ratio level.

P2.4 L2 · Computation

Which statistic is legal?

For each proposal, say whether it is meaningful, and if not, name a statistic that is.

(a) The mean of customers' PIN codes, to find the "average location".

(b) The median T-shirt size sold last month.

(c) The arithmetic mean of 1–5 star ratings.

(d) The geometric mean of annual incomes.

(e) The standard deviation of daily temperatures in °C.

(f) The coefficient of variation (\(\sigma/\bar{x}\), "percent variation") of daily temperatures in °C.

Then decide whether each transformation is permitted for the attribute's level:

(g) Recoding the ordinal grades {good, better, best} from {1, 2, 3} to {0.5, 1, 10}.

(h) Converting a ratio attribute "length in metres" to "length in feet plus 2".

Hint

Use the slide table: nominal allows mode and entropy; ordinal adds median and percentiles; interval adds mean and standard deviation; ratio adds geometric mean, harmonic mean and percent variation.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Not meaningful. PIN codes are nominal. Use the mode (the most common PIN code), or work with real latitude and longitude if location is what matters.

(b) Meaningful. Size is ordinal, so the median is defined.

(c) Strictly not meaningful, because the rating is ordinal and the gaps between stars are not known to be equal. The median (or the percentage of 4–5 star ratings) is the safe summary. The mean is common in practice, but only under the extra assumption that the scale is equally spaced.

(d) Meaningful. Income is ratio-level (₹0 means no income), so the geometric mean is allowed.

(e) Meaningful. The standard deviation uses only differences, which interval data supports.

(f) Not meaningful. \(\sigma/\bar{x}\) divides by a raw value, so it depends on where zero is placed. It would change if the same days were recorded in °F. Compute it only on a ratio scale such as Kelvin.

(g) Permitted. Any order-preserving (monotonic increasing) recoding is allowed for ordinal data.

(h) Not permitted. A ratio attribute allows only \(\text{new} = a \cdot \text{old}\). Adding 2 moves the true zero and turns the attribute into an interval one.

Key insight: Each Stevens level is defined by the transformations it tolerates, and a statistic is meaningful only if its conclusions survive those transformations. That is why the allowed statistics grow as you move up from nominal to ratio.

P2.5 L3 · Application

Classifying a bank's customer table

A bank wants to segment customers for a premium-card campaign. Its extract looks like this.

Name Gender Is Priority Customer? Card Type Credit Score No. of Accounts Income Level Region
Asha F Yes Platinum 742 3 Upper BGLR
Ravi M No Gold 655 1 Middle DELHI
Meena F No Titanium (blank) 2 Lower BGLR
Karan M Yes Gold 701 4 Upper PUNE

(a) For every column, state the Stevens level, discrete or continuous, and (for two-valued columns) whether it is symmetric or asymmetric binary.

(b) Which column should not be used as a model input, and why?

(c) Assume the card tiers are ordered \(\text{Gold} < \text{Titanium} < \text{Platinum}\). Can you then compute "the average card type" of priority customers? What should you report instead?

(d) What data type (relational, transactional, document, time series, and so on) is this table?

Hint

A binary attribute is symmetric when both values carry equal weight (such as gender) and asymmetric when only one value is the event of interest (such as "is priority").

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The columns classify as follows.

  • Name: nominal, discrete. It is an identifier.
  • Gender: nominal, discrete, symmetric binary.
  • Is Priority Customer?: nominal, discrete, asymmetric binary. "Yes" is the rare, interesting state.
  • Card Type: ordinal, discrete, given the tier order in (c).
  • Credit Score: interval, and continuous in concept even though it is reported as integers. It has no true zero (a score of 0 does not mean "no creditworthiness"), so differences are meaningful but ratios are not.
  • No. of Accounts: ratio, discrete. It is a count.
  • Income Level: ordinal, discrete (\(\text{Lower} < \text{Middle} < \text{Upper}\)).
  • Region: nominal, discrete.

(b) Name. It identifies a person and carries no generalisable signal. It also raises privacy concerns.

(c) No. Card type is ordinal, so a mean is not meaningful. Report the median tier (or the mode). For the two priority customers, Platinum and Gold, the "median" falls between them, so the mode or a frequency table is more informative here.

(d) Relational (record) data. Each row is an object with a fixed set of attributes. Meena's blank credit score is a missing value to be handled later in cleaning.

Key insight: One small table usually mixes all four Stevens levels. Classifying every column first tells you which summaries, distances and encodings are legal before you build anything.

P2.6 L3 · Application

Dimensionality, sparsity and resolution of a document collection

A news archive is turned into a document–term matrix: 20,000 articles (rows) by a 40,000-word vocabulary (columns), where each cell is the count of that word in that article. On average an article contains 150 distinct vocabulary words.

(a) What is the dimensionality of each object?

(b) What fraction of the cells are non-zero, and what is the sparsity (the fraction that are zero)?

(c) Storing every cell as a 4-byte float, how large is the dense matrix? A compressed sparse row format stores, for each non-zero, a 4-byte value and a 4-byte column index, plus one 4-byte row pointer per row (20,001 of them). How large is that, and roughly how many times smaller?

(d) Is each cell discrete or continuous?

(e) The same archive also has an hourly click count per article. Give one example of a pattern that is visible at hourly resolution but invisible at monthly resolution.

Hint

Count the non-zeros first: articles times average distinct words per article.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) 40,000 dimensions per article.

(b) The non-zeros and the total cells are

\[ 20{,}000 \times 150 = 3{,}000{,}000 \quad \text{out of} \quad 20{,}000 \times 40{,}000 = 800{,}000{,}000 \]

The density is 0.375%, so the sparsity is 99.625%.

(c) Dense and sparse storage are

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{dense} &= 800{,}000{,}000 \times 4 \text{ bytes} = \mathbf{3.2\ GB} \\ \text{sparse} &= 3{,}000{,}000 \times 8 + 20{,}001 \times 4 \text{ bytes} \approx \mathbf{24.08\ MB} \end{aligned} \]

That is about 133 times smaller.

(d) Discrete. Word counts are non-negative integers.

(e) A daily rhythm, such as clicks peaking at 9 a.m. and 9 p.m., is visible hourly but averages away at monthly resolution. Conversely, a slow seasonal trend may be clearer at monthly resolution, because hourly noise hides it.

Key insight: For sparse data, "only presence counts". The zeros dominate, so both storage and similarity measures should be built on the non-zeros. Resolution is a modelling choice: the pattern you find depends on the scale at which you look.

4.B Data Quality, Cleaning & Outliers (2.2–2.3)

P2.7 L1 · Foundation

Noise, outlier, wrong data, disguised missing or duplicate?

Name the data-quality problem in each case. Choose from noise, outlier, wrong data, disguised missing value, inconsistent data and duplicate data.

(a) A heart-rate sensor's readings jitter by \(\pm 3\) bpm around the true value because of electrical interference.

(b) In an HR table, a salary of \(-10\) appears.

(c) In a sign-up form, 41% of users have date of birth 01-Jan-1970, the form's default value.

(d) After two CRM systems are merged, "R. Sharma, r.sharma@x.com" and "Rahul Sharma, rahul.s@y.com" have the same phone number and address.

(e) One customer's record shows \(\text{Age} = 42\) and \(\text{Birthday} = 03/07/2010\).

(f) Among 5,000 retail customers who spend ₹2,000–₹20,000 a year, one corporate buyer spends ₹4.5 crore a year, and the figure is correct.

Hint

Ask whether the value is genuine but unusual, impossible, a placeholder for "unknown", contradicted by another field, or the same entity recorded twice.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Noise. It is a random modification of the original values.

(b) Wrong data (a noisy, invalid value). A salary cannot be negative.

(c) Disguised missing value. The default date stands in for "not provided".

(d) Duplicate data. It is the same person recorded twice, which is typical when heterogeneous sources are merged.

(e) Inconsistent data. The two fields contradict each other, so at least one is wrong.

(f) Outlier. It is a genuine object very different from the rest. It is not an error.

Key insight: Different problems need different treatment. Noise is smoothed, wrong values are corrected or set to missing, disguised missing values are first converted to real missing values, duplicates are merged, and genuine outliers are kept or modelled separately. Mixing these up (for example, deleting a genuine outlier as if it were an error) loses information.

P2.8 L1 · Foundation

"Outliers should always be deleted"

True or false, with a reason: "Any point outside the IQR fences is bad data and should always be deleted before training."

Hint

The slides list two cases for outliers. In one of them, the outlier is exactly what you are looking for.

Answer & Key Insight

False. The fences flag points that are unusual, not points that are wrong.

In case 1, the outlier is noise or an error, such as a typing slip that turns 100K into 10000K. It should be corrected, set to missing or removed.

In case 2, the outlier is the goal of the analysis, as in credit-card fraud or network intrusion detection. Deleting those points would delete the very class the model must learn.

Even a genuine but irrelevant extreme value may be better handled by capping (winsorising), a log transform or binning than by deletion. The decision needs domain knowledge, and it must be made using training data only.

Key insight: An outlier rule is a detector, not a verdict. Always ask "a mistake or a millionaire?" before deciding what to do with a flagged point.

P2.9 L2 · Computation

IQR fences by hand

The waiting times (minutes) at a clinic on eleven days were

29, 23, 31, 26, 48, 27, 25, 30, 26, 33, 28.

(a) Find \(Q_1\), the median and \(Q_3\) using the median-of-halves method that the course slides use. With \(n\) odd, leave the median out of both halves.

(b) Compute the IQR and the fences \(Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR}\) and \(Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}\), and list any outliers.

(c) NumPy's default percentile (linear interpolation at position \(p \cdot (n - 1)\)) gives \(Q_1 = 26\) and \(Q_3 = 30.5\) for the same data. Recompute the fences with these values. Does the verdict change?

Hint

Sort first. With 11 values the median is the 6th value, and each half has 5 values.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Sorted, the data are 23, 25, 26, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33, 48. The median is 28.

The lower half is 23, 25, 26, 26, 27, so \(Q_1 = 26\).

The upper half is 29, 30, 31, 33, 48, so \(Q_3 = 31\).

(b) \(\text{IQR} = 31 - 26 = \mathbf{5}\). The lower fence and the upper fence are

\[ Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} = 26 - 7.5 = \mathbf{18.5}, \qquad Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR} = 31 + 7.5 = \mathbf{38.5} \]

The only outlier is 48.

(c) With \(Q_1 = 26\) and \(Q_3 = 30.5\), \(\text{IQR} = 4.5\) and the fences are 19.25 and 37.25. The outlier is still 48, so the verdict does not change here. A borderline point between 37.25 and 38.5 would have been flagged by one method and not the other.

Key insight: Quartile conventions differ (median-of-halves, \(n + 1\) position, linear interpolation). They usually agree on clear outliers but can disagree near the fence, so always state the method you used.

P2.10 L2 · Computation

\(3\sigma\) fences on a production line

A filling machine has been monitored for 250 fills. The fill weights look roughly bell-shaped, with mean \(\bar{x} = 50.2\) g and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1.6\) g.

(a) Compute the \(3\sigma\) fences.

(b) Classify the new fills 44.9 g, 46.0 g, 55.3 g and 54.8 g.

(c) If the process really is normal and stable, what fraction of fills fall outside the fences purely by chance? How many such false alarms do you expect in 250 fills and in 10,000 fills?

Hint

The fences are \(\bar{x} \pm 3\sigma\), and about 99.73% of a normal distribution lies inside them.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The lower fence and the upper fence are

\[ \bar{x} - 3\sigma = 50.2 - 4.8 = \mathbf{45.4\ g}, \qquad \bar{x} + 3\sigma = 50.2 + 4.8 = \mathbf{55.0\ g} \]

(b) 44.9 g and 55.3 g are outliers. 46.0 g and 54.8 g are inside the fences.

(c) The fraction outside is

\[ 2 \times P(Z > 3) \approx \mathbf{0.27\%} \]

That gives about 0.67 false alarms in 250 fills and about 27 in 10,000 fills.

Key insight: The \(3\sigma\) rule is a probability statement about a normal distribution. On a large, genuinely normal stream it will still flag about 3 points per thousand that are perfectly fine, so a flag is a prompt to investigate, not proof of a fault.

P2.11 L3 · Application

Aggregating daily sales into weekly averages

A café records daily sales (in ₹ thousand) for four weeks, Monday to Sunday.

Week Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat Sun
1 42 38 45 51 60 88 95
2 40 44 47 49 63 84 90
3 39 41 50 52 58 91 99
4 45 37 44 55 61 86 93

The 28 daily values have mean 60.25 and population standard deviation 20.53.

(a) Aggregate to four weekly average daily sales. Compute their mean and population standard deviation.

(b) By what factor did aggregation reduce the standard deviation? Compare it with the factor \(1/\sqrt{7} \approx 0.378\) you would expect if the daily values were independent random noise around one mean. Explain the difference.

(c) Name two benefits and one cost of this aggregation for a model that forecasts the café's demand.

Hint

Most of the day-to-day spread in this table is not random. Look at what happens on Saturday and Sunday every week.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The weekly totals are 419, 417, 430 and 421, so the weekly averages are 59.857, 59.571, 61.429 and 60.143. Their mean is 60.25, the same as before, and their population standard deviation is 0.71.

(b) The reduction factor is

\[ \frac{0.71}{20.53} \approx \mathbf{0.035} \]

roughly ten times stronger than \(1/\sqrt{7} \approx 0.378\). The daily spread is dominated by a systematic weekly cycle (weekdays near 45, weekends near 90). Averaging over one full cycle removes that pattern entirely, leaving only the small week-to-week noise. The \(1/\sqrt{7}\) rule applies only to independent noise.

(c) Benefits: data reduction (28 records become 4) and more stable values with less variability, which gives smoother trend estimates. A third benefit is a change of scale to the level at which decisions such as weekly ordering are made. Cost: the day-of-week pattern is lost, so a model trained on weekly averages cannot tell the café how many staff it needs on Saturday.

Key insight: Aggregation trades resolution for stability. It is the right move when decisions are taken at the coarser scale, and the wrong move when the fine-scale pattern is itself the signal.

P2.12 L3 · Application

Cleaning a merged tax-records table

Two branch offices' files were merged into the table below. Income is in thousands.

Tid Refund Marital Status Taxable Income (K) Cheat
1 Yes Single 125 No
2 No Married 100 No
3 No Single 70 No
4 Yes Married 120 No
5 No Divorced 10000 Yes
6 No NULL 60 No
7 Yes Divorced 220 No
8 No Single NULL Yes
9 No Married 75 No
10 No Single 90 Yes
11 No Single 90 No

Records 10 and 11 refer to the same taxpayer.

(a) List every data-quality problem in the table.

(b) Treat record 10/11 as one record, and use the nine known incomes. Find \(Q_1\), the median and \(Q_3\) by median-of-halves (\(n\) is odd, so leave the median out of both halves). Compute the IQR fences and list the outliers.

(c) Record 8's income is missing. Compute the mean and median imputation values (i) using all nine known incomes, and (ii) after record 5's income has been confirmed as a typing error and set to missing. Which imputation would you use, and why?

(d) Impute record 6's marital status with the mode of the other records, counting record 10/11 once.

Hint

The slide's question about the extreme income is "a mistake or a millionaire?". For (c), notice how far a single extreme value moves the mean compared with the median.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The table has four problems.

  • A suspicious extreme value: 10000K in record 5.
  • Missing values: Marital Status in record 6 and Taxable Income in record 8.
  • Duplicate records: 10 and 11.
  • Inconsistent duplicates: records 10 and 11 disagree on Cheat. The label conflict has to be resolved from source documents, or the record dropped from training.

(b) Sorted, the incomes are 60, 70, 75, 90, 100, 120, 125, 220, 10000. The median is 100.

The lower half is 60, 70, 75, 90, so \(Q_1 = 72.5\). The upper half is 120, 125, 220, 10000, so \(Q_3 = 172.5\).

\(\text{IQR} = \mathbf{100}\), so the fences are

\[ Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} = \mathbf{-77.5}, \qquad Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR} = \mathbf{322.5} \]
