(e) Suppose the current error is \((\theta_1 - \theta_1^*, \theta_2 - \theta_2^*) = (-1, -0.001)\), which in prediction terms is an equal mismatch of one unit per standard deviation of each feature. In which direction does the negative gradient point, and why does this produce zig-zagging rather than a straight path?

Hint

When \(H\) is diagonal, gradient descent splits into two independent one-dimensional problems, each like P3.14 with its own curvature \(a = s_j^2\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The entries of \(\frac{1}{n} X^\top X\) are \(\frac{1}{n} \sum x_{ij} x_{ik}\). On the diagonal these are the variances \(s_j^2\), because the features are centred. Off the diagonal they are covariances, which are 0. So \(H = \operatorname{diag}(1, 10^6)\).

Because \(J\) is quadratic with minimiser \(\theta^*\), \(\nabla J = H(\theta - \theta^*)\), so \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j} = s_j^2 (\theta_j - \theta_j^*)\).

(b) \(\theta_j \leftarrow \theta_j - \eta \cdot s_j^2 (\theta_j - \theta_j^*)\), so

\[ e_j \leftarrow (1 - \eta \cdot s_j^2) \cdot e_j. \]

Stability requires \(\lvert 1 - \eta \cdot s_j^2 \rvert < 1\) for both coordinates, and the binding one is \(s_2^2 = 10^6\). So \(\eta < 2 \times 10^{-6}\).

At such an \(\eta\) the bedrooms factor is \(1 - \eta \cdot 1 \ge 1 - 2 \times 10^{-6}\). Each step removes at most two millionths of the \(\theta_1\) error, so \(\theta_1\) barely moves.

(c) We need \((1 - 10^{-6})^k = 10^{-3}\), so \(k = \frac{\ln(10^{-3})}{\ln(1 - 10^{-6})} \approx\) 6.9 million iterations. Meanwhile \(\theta_2\) converges almost instantly, because its factor is \(1 - 1 = 0\).

(d) After standardising, \(H = I\), and \(\eta = 1\) makes both factors 0, so gradient descent converges in one step. Any \(\eta\) in \((0, 2)\) now converges at the same rate in both coordinates.

The contours of \(J\) are the level sets of \(\sum_j s_j^2 (\theta_j - \theta_j^*)^2\). With \(s_1^2 = s_2^2\) these are circles. With variances 1 and \(10^6\) they are ellipses whose axis lengths are in the ratio 1 : 1000, so they are very elongated.

(e) \(-\nabla J = -(1 \cdot (-1), 10^6 \cdot (-0.001)) =\) (1, 1000), which points almost entirely along \(\theta_2\) even though both coordinates are "equally wrong". The step overshoots in the steep \(\theta_2\) direction and makes almost no progress in the shallow \(\theta_1\) direction. The next gradient then flips sign in \(\theta_2\), and the path zig-zags across the narrow valley instead of heading down its long axis.

Key insight: Rescaling feature \(j\) by a factor \(c\) rescales its curvature by \(c^2\). One shared \(\eta\) cannot suit coordinates whose curvatures differ by a factor of \(10^6\). Standardising equalises the curvatures, so a single learning rate fits every direction.

5.D Basis Functions & Bias–Variance (3.4)

P3.16 L1 · Foundation

What counts as a "linear" model?

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "\(y = w_0 + w_1 x + w_2 x^2\) is a linear model, so it can be fitted with the normal equation."

(b) "\(y = w_0 + w_1 \sin(x) + w_2 \exp(-x^2)\) is a linear basis-function model."

(c) "\(y = w_0 + \sin(w_1 x)\) is a linear basis-function model."

(d) "A model with high bias typically shows a high training error and a high test error."

(e) "A model with high variance typically shows a low training error and a test error close to it."

Hint

"Linear" in "linear model" refers to the weights \(w\), not to the input \(x\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. With basis functions \(\Phi = (1, x, x^2)\), the model is \(w^\top \Phi(x)\), which is linear in \(w\). Fit it with

\[ w = (\Phi^\top \Phi)^{-1} \Phi^\top y. \]

(b) True. The basis functions are \(\Phi_0 = 1\), \(\Phi_1 = \sin(x)\) and \(\Phi_2 = \exp(-x^2)\). They are fixed in advance and contain no unknowns, so the model is linear in \(w\).

(c) False. \(w_1\) sits inside the sine, so the model is not linear in \(w\) and the normal equation does not apply.

(d) True. A model that is too simple cannot fit even the training data, so both errors are high and close to each other. This is underfitting.

(e) False. High variance means a low training error but a much higher test error. The large gap between the two is the signature of overfitting.

Key insight: Any fixed non-linear transformation of \(x\) can be used as a feature, and the model stays linear in \(w\). Polynomial regression is linear regression run on the features \((1, x, x^2, \dots)\), so everything from 5.A–5.C applies to it unchanged.

P3.17 L2 · Computation

Fitting a quadratic with a basis-function design matrix

Data: \((x, y) = (-1, 3), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 5)\). Fit \(y = w_0 + w_1 x + w_2 x^2\) by least squares.

(a) Build the design matrix \(\Phi\) with rows \((1, x, x^2)\), and compute \(\Phi^\top \Phi\) and \(\Phi^\top y\).

(b) Using \((\Phi^\top \Phi)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 11/20 & 3/20 & -1/4 \\ 3/20 & 9/20 & -1/4 \\ -1/4 & -1/4 & 1/4 \end{pmatrix}\), compute \(w\).

(c) Compute the residuals and the SSE. The best straight line for the same data is \(y = 2.2 + 0.6x\), with \(\text{SSE} = 9.2\). Which model fits better?

(d) Predict \(y\) at \(x = 3\) with the quadratic.

Hint

The third column of \(\Phi\) is just the second column squared. After that, everything is the same normal equation as in 5.B.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\Phi\) has rows \((1, -1, 1)\), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 4).

\[ \Phi^\top \Phi = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & 6 \\ 2 & 6 & 8 \\ 6 & 8 & 18 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \Phi^\top y = \begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 8 \\ 24 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(b)

\[ \begin{aligned} w_0 &= (11 \cdot 10 + 3 \cdot 8)/20 - 24/4 = 6.7 - 6 = 0.7, \\ w_1 &= (3 \cdot 10 + 9 \cdot 8)/20 - 24/4 = 5.1 - 6 = -0.9, \\ w_2 &= (-10 - 8 + 24)/4 = 1.5. \end{aligned} \]

So \(w = (0.7, -0.9, 1.5)\). A cross-check with sklearn's PolynomialFeatures(2) and LinearRegression gives the same coefficients.

(c) The predictions are 3.1, 0.7, 1.3, 4.9, so the residuals are \((0.1, -0.3, 0.3, -0.1)\) and \(\text{SSE} = 0.2\). The quadratic fits far better than the line (0.2 against 9.2), because the data clearly curves upward.

(d) \(0.7 - 0.9 \cdot 3 + 1.5 \cdot 9 =\) 11.5.

Key insight: Moving from a line to a polynomial changes only the design matrix. The estimator, the convexity of \(J\), and the gradient-descent update all stay exactly the same.

P3.18 L2 · Computation

Reading a train/test table across model complexity

Polynomials of increasing degree are fitted to the same 30 training points and evaluated on 200 held-out test points:

Degree Training MSE Test MSE
1 18.4 19.1
2 4.2 4.6
4 3.9 4.4
8 2.1 9.8
12 0.3 41.7

(a) Which degrees underfit, which overfit, and which degree would you choose?

(b) Training MSE falls at every step. Why is it not a good guide for choosing the degree?

(c) Explain the change from degree 4 to degree 8 in terms of bias and variance.

Hint

Look at the level of each error and at the gap between them, row by row.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Degree 1 underfits: both errors are high and close to each other, which is high bias. Degrees 8 and 12 overfit: the training error keeps falling while the test error climbs, and the gap widens from 7.7 to 41.4, which is high variance. Degree 4 is the choice, because it has the lowest test MSE (4.4). Degree 2 is almost as good and simpler, so it is a reasonable alternative if simplicity is valued.

(b) A more flexible model can always fit the training data at least as well as a less flexible one (every lower-degree polynomial is a special case of a higher-degree one), so training MSE can only fall as the degree rises. It measures the ability to fit, not generalisation. Model complexity must be chosen on held-out (validation) data.

(c) From degree 4 to degree 8, bias barely decreases (training MSE improves only from 3.9 to 2.1), while variance rises sharply. The extra wiggles start fitting the noise in these particular 30 points, so the test MSE more than doubles.

Key insight: The diagnosis comes from two numbers, the size of the errors and the gap between them. High and close means underfitting. Low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Low and close is the target.

P3.19 L3 · Application

Underfit, good fit and overfit on the same data

Training data: \((x, y) = (0, 1.4), (1, 1.6), (2, 5.4), (3, 9.8)\).

Test data: \((x, y) = (0.5, 1.2), (1.5, 3.3), (2.5, 7.2), (3.5, 13.1)\).

(a) Fit a straight line to the training data by hand (normal equation or the slope formula). Compute its training MSE and test MSE.

(b) The least-squares quadratic is \(y = 1.25 - 0.25x + 1.05x^2\), and the cubic through all four training points is \(y = 1.4 - 2.6x + 3.3x^2 - 0.5x^3\). Compute the training MSE and test MSE of each.

(c) Put all three models into a table and diagnose each as underfit, good fit or overfit. Which would you deploy?

Hint

The cubic has 4 parameters and there are 4 training points, so think about what its training error must be before computing anything.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\bar{x} = 1.5\) and \(\bar{y} = 4.55\).

\[ \sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y}) = 4.725 + 1.475 + 0.425 + 7.875 = 14.5 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 5. \]

So the slope is 2.9, the intercept is \(4.55 - 4.35 = 0.2\), and the line is \(y = 0.2 + 2.9x\).

Training residuals are \((-1.2, 1.5, 0.6, -0.9)\), so training MSE = 1.215.

Test predictions are 1.65, 4.55, 7.45, 10.35, with errors \((0.45, 1.25, 0.25, -2.75)\), so test MSE = 2.3475.

(b) Quadratic: training residuals are \((-0.15, 0.45, -0.45, 0.15)\), so training MSE = 0.1125. Test predictions are 1.3875, 3.2375, 7.1875, 13.2375, so test MSE \(\approx\) 0.0145.

Cubic: it passes through every training point, so training MSE = 0. Test predictions are 0.8625, 3.2375, 7.7125, 11.2875, so test MSE \(\approx\) 0.9164.

(c) The results are:

Model Train MSE Test MSE Diagnosis
Line 1.215 2.348 Underfit (both errors high)
Quadratic 0.113 0.015 Good fit; deploy this
Cubic 0 0.916 Overfit (perfect training, test \(60\times\) worse than the quadratic)

The cubic's \(-0.5x^3\) term bends the curve down at \(x = 3.5\), where it predicts 11.29 against a true 13.1. It has learned the noise in the four training points.

Key insight: A model with as many parameters as training points can always reach zero training error, so a perfect training score is a warning sign, not an achievement. Only the held-out error tells you which model has captured the real pattern.

P3.20 L3 · Application

Learning curves: will more data help?

Two models are trained on growing subsets of a large dataset whose irreducible noise gives an MSE floor of about 1.0. Validation MSE is measured on a fixed held-out set.

Training size \(n\) Model A train Model A validation Model B train Model B validation
20 4.1 5.0 0.2 9.5
200 4.6 4.8 0.8 3.1
2000 4.7 4.75 1.0 1.3

(a) Diagnose each model at \(n = 20\).

(b) For which model did collecting more data help, and why does it help that one but not the other?

(c) The team can either collect 20,000 more examples or add quadratic and interaction features to Model A. Which action helps Model A, and why?

Hint

Look at where each pair of curves converges, and compare that level with the noise floor of 1.0.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Model A has high bias: its training and validation errors are close but both far above the floor of 1.0. Model B has high variance: its training error is near 0 but its validation error is 9.5, a huge gap.

(b) More data helped Model B: its validation error fell from 9.5 to 1.3, close to the floor, and its gap shrank from 9.3 to 0.3. A flexible model has more room to memorise noise when data is scarce; with more examples the noise averages out and the true pattern dominates. Model A did not improve: its curves have already met at about 4.7, and more data only confirms that the model is too simple.

(c) Add the features. Model A's errors have converged far above the noise floor, so 20,000 more examples would leave it at about 4.7. Only extra model capacity (richer basis functions, or less regularisation if any is applied) can lower its bias.

Key insight: More data reduces variance but not bias. Before paying to collect data, check whether the training and validation curves have already met: if they have, and are well above the noise floor, the model needs more capacity, not more data.

5.E Regularization: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net (3.5)

Conventions for this subsection: the intercept \(w_0\) is never penalised. "Ridge with constant \(\lambda\)" means minimising \(J(w) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \sum_{j \ge 1} w_j^2\), whose gradient-descent update is

\[ w_j \leftarrow w_j (1 - \eta\lambda) - \eta \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_j}, \]

the form used in the slides. "Lasso with constant \(\lambda\)" means minimising \(J(w) + \lambda \sum_{j \ge 1} \lvert w_j \rvert\), whose subgradient update for \(w_j \ne 0\) is

\[ w_j \leftarrow w_j - \eta \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_j} - \eta\lambda \operatorname{sign}(w_j). \]

P3.21 L1 · Foundation

Ridge and lasso, true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "Ridge regression with a large enough \(\lambda\) sets the least useful weights exactly to zero."

(b) "Lasso can be used as an automatic feature-selection method."

(c) "The lasso penalty \(\lambda \sum \lvert w_j \rvert\) is differentiable everywhere, so the ordinary gradient-descent update applies unchanged."

(d) "Elastic Net combines the L1 and L2 penalties, and is the usual recommendation when several features are highly correlated."

(e) "Regularisation should also be applied to the intercept \(w_0\), to keep the whole model small."

Hint

Think about the shape of each penalty right at \(w = 0\): a smooth bowl for ridge, a sharp V for lasso.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) False. Ridge shrinks every weight toward zero smoothly, but only a weight whose unregularised value is exactly zero ends up at zero. It produces small weights, not sparse ones.

(b) True. Lasso drives the weights of weak features exactly to 0, and the features it keeps are the selected set.

(c) False. \(\lvert w \rvert\) has a corner at \(w = 0\), where it has no derivative. The update needs a subgradient (any value in \([-1, 1]\) at 0), or a soft-thresholding step.

(d) True. Lasso tends to pick one feature from a correlated group arbitrarily. Elastic Net's L2 part spreads the weight across the group, while its L1 part still prunes irrelevant features.

(e) False. The intercept only sets the average level of the predictions. Penalising it would bias every prediction toward 0 and has nothing to do with model complexity.

Key insight: The difference between L1 and L2 comes down to the penalty's slope near zero. L2's slope \(\lambda w\) vanishes as \(w\) approaches 0, so its pull fades out. L1's slope stays at \(\pm\lambda\) all the way to 0, so it can push a weight all the way there.

P3.22 L2 · Computation

One regularised gradient-descent step: plain, ridge, lasso

A model \(h = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2\) is fitted to three examples:

\(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(y\)
1 2 3
2 0 2
3 1 4

The current weights are \(w = (w_0, w_1, w_2) = (1, 0.5, 0.2)\), with \(\eta = 0.1\) and regularisation constant \(\lambda = 0.5\). Use the conventions at the top of 5.E.

(a) Compute the predictions, the residuals and the three partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_j}\) of the unregularised cost.

(b) Perform one update in each of three ways: unregularised, ridge, and lasso.

(c) Which method shrank \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) most in this step, and why? For which values of \(\lvert w_j \rvert\) would the other method shrink more?

Hint

All three updates share the same data gradient. They differ only in the extra pull toward zero: \(\eta\lambda \cdot w_j\) for ridge, and \(\eta\lambda \cdot \operatorname{sign}(w_j)\) for lasso.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The predictions are \(1 + 0.5 + 0.4 = 1.9\), \(1 + 1 + 0 = 2.0\) and \(1 + 1.5 + 0.2 = 2.7\), so the residuals are \((-1.1, 0, -1.3)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0} &= (-1.1 + 0 - 1.3)/3 = \mathbf{-0.8}, \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1} &= (-1.1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 2 - 1.3 \cdot 3)/3 = \mathbf{-5/3 \approx -1.6667}, \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_2} &= (-1.1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 0 - 1.3 \cdot 1)/3 = \mathbf{-3.5/3 \approx -1.1667}. \end{aligned} \]

(b) The updated weights are:

Method \(w_0\) \(w_1\) \(w_2\)
Unregularised 1.08 0.6667 0.3167
Ridge (\(\times 0.95\), then the data step) 1.08 \(0.5 \cdot 0.95 + 0.1667 =\) 0.6417 \(0.2 \cdot 0.95 + 0.1167 =\) 0.3067
Lasso (data step, then \(-0.05 \cdot \operatorname{sign}\)) 1.08 \(0.6667 - 0.05 =\) 0.6167 \(0.3167 - 0.05 =\) 0.2667

\(w_0\) is identical in all three rows because it is not penalised.

(c) Lasso shrank more. Its pull is a constant \(\eta\lambda = 0.05\) per step, while ridge's pull is \(\eta\lambda \cdot \lvert w_j \rvert = 0.05 \cdot \lvert w_j \rvert\), which is only 0.025 for \(w_1 = 0.5\) and 0.01 for \(w_2 = 0.2\). Ridge shrinks more only when \(\lvert w_j \rvert > 1\). A correct lasso step must always move a weight toward 0 compared with the unregularised step; if your lasso weights come out larger than the unregularised ones, the sign of the penalty term is wrong.

Key insight: Ridge's pull toward zero is proportional to the weight, so it is strong on large weights and weak on small ones. Lasso's pull is the same size for every non-zero weight, which is why it is the one that finishes small weights off.

P3.23 L2 · Computation

Closed-form ridge against ordinary least squares

For centred data (no intercept needed), ridge regression minimises \(\lVert Xw - y \rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert^2\), and its closed-form solution is \(w = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y\). Use

\[ X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad y = (2, 1, 4). \]

(a) Compute the ordinary least-squares solution (\(\lambda = 0\)).

(b) Compute the ridge solution for \(\lambda = 1\) and for \(\lambda = 10\).

(c) Compare \(\lVert w \rVert^2\) across the three solutions. Does either weight ever reach exactly 0?

(d) Explain why \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) is invertible for every \(\lambda > 0\), even when \(X^\top X\) itself is singular.

Hint

Adding \(\lambda I\) adds \(\lambda\) to every eigenvalue of \(X^\top X\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(X^\top y = (6, 5)\). The inverse is \(\frac{1}{3} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\), so \(w_{\text{OLS}} = (7/3, 4/3) \approx (2.333, 1.333)\).

(b) For \(\lambda = 1\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{8} \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{so} \quad w = (13/8, 9/8) = \mathbf{(1.625, 1.125)}. \]

For \(\lambda = 10\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 1 \\ 1 & 12 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{143} \begin{pmatrix} 12 & -1 \\ -1 & 12 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{so} \quad w = (67/143, 54/143) \approx \mathbf{(0.4685, 0.3776)}. \]

A cross-check with sklearn's Ridge(alpha=λ, fit_intercept=False) gives the same values.

(c) \(\lVert w \rVert^2 \approx\) 7.22 (OLS), 3.91 (\(\lambda = 1\)) and 0.36 (\(\lambda = 10\)). Both weights shrink steadily as \(\lambda\) grows, but neither ever reaches exactly 0. In general,

\[ w_1 = \frac{7 + 6\lambda}{(\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 3)} \quad \text{and} \quad w_2 = \frac{4 + 5\lambda}{(\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 3)}. \]

Both numerators are positive for every \(\lambda \ge 0\), so the weights only tend to 0 as \(\lambda \to \infty\).

(d) \(X^\top X\) is positive semi-definite, so its eigenvalues are \(\ge 0\). Adding \(\lambda I\) raises every eigenvalue to at least \(\lambda > 0\), so the matrix is positive definite and therefore invertible. Ridge thus also fixes the singular-\(X^\top X\) problem from P3.4(b).

Key insight: Ridge makes the solution "smaller and more stable", not "sparser". It is the fix for wild coefficients and for nearly collinear features, but it does not select features.

P3.24 L3 · Application

Smooth shrinkage against soft thresholding

Assume the feature columns are orthonormal in the sense \(\frac{1}{n} X^\top X = I\), and let \(z_j = \frac{1}{n} x_j^\top y\) be the ordinary least-squares coefficients. With \(J = \frac{1}{2n} \lVert Xw - y \rVert^2\), the problem then splits into one-dimensional problems:

Ridge, minimising \(J + \frac{\lambda}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2\), gives \(w_j = z_j/(1 + \lambda)\).

Lasso, minimising \(J + \lambda \lVert w \rVert_1\), gives \(w_j = \operatorname{sign}(z_j) \cdot \max(\lvert z_j \rvert - \lambda, 0)\), which is called soft thresholding.

The OLS coefficients are \(z = (3.0, -1.2, 0.4, -0.1)\).

(a) Compute the ridge and lasso coefficients for \(\lambda = 0.5\).

(b) For which range of \(\lambda\) does lasso keep exactly two non-zero features? For which \(\lambda\) does it zero all four?

(c) Is there any finite \(\lambda\) for which ridge zeros a coefficient?

(d) Derive the lasso formula for a single coordinate, using the subgradient of \(\lvert w \rvert\).

Hint

For a single coordinate the lasso objective is \(\frac{1}{2}(w - z)^2 + \lambda \lvert w \rvert\). Treat \(w > 0\), \(w < 0\) and \(w = 0\) as separate cases.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) For \(\lambda = 0.5\):

Coefficient \(z\) Ridge \(z/1.5\) Lasso soft-threshold
\(w_1\) 3.0 2.0 2.5
\(w_2\) −1.2 −0.8 −0.7
\(w_3\) 0.4 0.2667 0
\(w_4\) −0.1 −0.0667 0

A numerical cross-check on a Hadamard design with sklearn (Lasso(alpha=0.5) and Ridge(alpha = \(n \cdot 0.5\))) gives the same values.

(b) Lasso zeros \(w_j\) exactly when \(\lambda \ge \lvert z_j \rvert\). Exactly two survive when \(0.4 \le \lambda < 1.2\), that is, \(\lambda \in [0.4, 1.2)\). All four are zero once \(\lambda \ge 3.0\).

(c) No. \(z_j/(1 + \lambda)\) is zero only if \(z_j = 0\), whatever \(\lambda\) is. Ridge rescales every coefficient by the same factor and never changes its sign or zeros it.

(d) The objective is \(f(w) = \frac{1}{2}(w - z)^2 + \lambda \lvert w \rvert\).

If \(w > 0\), then \(f' = w - z + \lambda = 0\) gives \(w = z - \lambda\), which is valid only if \(z > \lambda\).

If \(w < 0\), then \(w = z + \lambda\), which is valid only if \(z < -\lambda\).

At \(w = 0\), the subgradient is \(-z + \lambda \cdot [-1, 1]\), and 0 lies in this set exactly when \(\lvert z \rvert \le \lambda\).

Combining the three cases gives

\[ w = \operatorname{sign}(z) \cdot \max(\lvert z \rvert - \lambda, 0). \]

Key insight: Ridge divides each coefficient by the same factor, so a small coefficient stays small but non-zero. Lasso subtracts a fixed amount and clips at zero, so small coefficients are removed entirely while large ones are only shifted toward zero.

P3.25 L3 · Application

Checking a lasso solution with the subgradient at \(w = 0\)

Centred data with two features (no intercept):

\(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(y\)
1 1 2
2 1 3
−1 0 −1
−2 −2 −4

The lasso objective is \(L(w) = \frac{1}{2n} \lVert Xw - y \rVert^2 + \lambda (\lvert w_1 \rvert + \lvert w_2 \rvert)\), with \(n = 4\). Write \(A = \frac{1}{n} X^\top X\) and \(c = \frac{1}{n} X^\top y\), so that the gradient of the data term is \(Aw - c\).

(a) Compute \(A\) and \(c\), and the unregularised solution \(w = A^{-1} c\).

(b) A solver reports \(w = (1.3, 0)\) for \(\lambda = 1\). Verify the optimality conditions: for \(w_1 \ne 0\) the condition is \((Aw - c)_1 + \lambda \cdot \operatorname{sign}(w_1) = 0\), and for \(w_2 = 0\) the condition is \(\lvert (Aw - c)_2 \rvert \le \lambda\).

(c) A colleague claims that for \(\lambda = 0.5\) the solution still has \(w_2 = 0\). Assume \(w_2 = 0\), solve the \(w_1\) condition, and test the \(w_2\) condition. Is the claim right?

(d) Find the smallest \(\lambda\) for which \(w_2 = 0\) at the optimum.

(e) For contrast, the ridge solution at \(\lambda = 1\) (objective \(\frac{1}{2n} \lVert Xw - y \rVert^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2\)) is \((A + I)^{-1} c \approx (0.868, 0.692)\). Comment on the difference.

Hint

At \(w_2 = 0\) the subgradient of \(\lambda \lvert w_2 \rvert\) is the whole interval \([-\lambda, \lambda]\). So \(w_2 = 0\) is optimal exactly when the data gradient's pull on \(w_2\) is no stronger than \(\lambda\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 7 \\ 7 & 6 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(X^\top y = (17, 13)\), so

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 2.5 & 1.75 \\ 1.75 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad c = \begin{pmatrix} 4.25 \\ 3.25 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Solving gives \(w_{\text{OLS}} = (1, 1)\).

(b) At \(w = (1.3, 0)\),

\[ Aw - c = (2.5 \cdot 1.3 - 4.25,\ 1.75 \cdot 1.3 - 3.25) = (-1.0, -0.975). \]

For \(w_1\): \(-1.0 + 1 \cdot \operatorname{sign}(1.3) = 0\) ✓.

For \(w_2\): \(\lvert -0.975 \rvert = 0.975 \le 1\) ✓.

Both conditions hold, so (1.3, 0) is the lasso optimum. A cross-check with sklearn's Lasso(alpha=1, fit_intercept=False) returns (1.3, 0.0).

(c) With \(w_2 = 0\), the \(w_1\) condition is \(2.5 w_1 - 4.25 + 0.5 = 0\), so \(w_1 = 1.5\). Then \((Aw - c)_2 = 1.75 \cdot 1.5 - 3.25 = -0.625\), and \(\lvert -0.625 \rvert > 0.5\), so the condition fails. The data pulls on \(w_2\) harder than the penalty can resist, so \(w_2\) must become positive. The claim is wrong. The actual solution is about (1.182, 0.455).

(d) With \(w_2 = 0\) and \(w_1 > 0\), \(w_1(\lambda) = (4.25 - \lambda)/2.5\). Then

\[ (Aw - c)_2 = 0.7(4.25 - \lambda) - 3.25 = -0.275 - 0.7\lambda. \]

The condition \(0.275 + 0.7\lambda \le \lambda\) gives \(\lambda \ge 11/12 \approx 0.9167\). sklearn agrees: at \(\lambda = 0.91\) it gives \(w_2 \approx 0.007\), and at \(\lambda = 0.92\) it gives \(w_2 = 0\) exactly.

(e) Ridge keeps both weights clearly non-zero, and shrinks both. Lasso at the same \(\lambda\) has removed \(x_2\) entirely. The reason is that ridge's penalty gradient \(\lambda w_2\) vanishes at \(w_2 = 0\) and so cannot hold \(w_2\) there against any non-zero pull from the data. Lasso's subgradient at 0 can supply any counter-force up to \(\lambda\).

Key insight: "\(w = 0\) is optimal for lasso" means the data gradient at 0 has magnitude \(\le \lambda\). This gives an exact, checkable threshold for when a feature is dropped. Ridge has no such threshold.

P3.26 L3 · Application

Elastic Net: the mix, and correlated features

Define the Elastic Net objective as

\[ J(w) + \lambda \left[ r \lVert w \rVert_1 + \frac{1 - r}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2 \right], \]

where \(r\) is the L1 share. This matches sklearn's ElasticNet(alpha=λ, l1_ratio=r): \(r = 1\) gives Lasso and \(r = 0\) gives Ridge. (Some course material writes the mix with \(r\) and \(1 - r\) swapped, so always check which penalty \(r\) multiplies.)

(a) Evaluate the penalty term for \(w = (2, -1, 0)\) with \(\lambda = 0.4\) and \(r = 0.25\).

(b) Under the orthonormal setting of P3.24, the Elastic Net solution is \(w_j = \frac{\operatorname{sign}(z_j) \cdot \max(\lvert z_j \rvert - \lambda r, 0)}{1 + \lambda(1 - r)}\). For \(z = (3.0, -1.2, 0.4, -0.1)\), \(\lambda = 1\) and \(r = 0.5\), compute \(w\). Which properties of ridge and which of lasso does the result show?

(c) Two features are exact duplicates, \(x_1 = x_2 = x\), and the data supports a total effect \(w_1 + w_2 = 2\). Compare the L1 penalty \(\lvert w_1 \rvert + \lvert w_2 \rvert\) and the L2 penalty \(w_1^2 + w_2^2\) for the splits (2, 0), (1.5, 0.5) and (1, 1). Which split does each penalty prefer?

(d) Use (c) to explain why Elastic Net is preferred over Lasso when features come in highly correlated groups.

Hint

For (c), every same-sign split has the same L1 norm. Only the L2 term can tell the splits apart.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\lVert w \rVert_1 = 3\) and \(\lVert w \rVert^2 = 5\), so the penalty is

\[ 0.4 \cdot (0.25 \cdot 3 + 0.375 \cdot 5) = 0.4 \cdot (0.75 + 1.875) = \mathbf{1.05}. \]

(b) The threshold is \(\lambda r = 0.5\) and the divisor is \(1 + 0.5 = 1.5\), so

\[ w = (2.5/1.5, -0.7/1.5, 0, 0) \approx \mathbf{(1.667, -0.467, 0, 0)}. \]

sklearn's ElasticNet(alpha=1, l1_ratio=0.5) on an orthonormal design gives the same result.

From lasso it inherits exact zeros (\(w_3 = w_4 = 0\)). From ridge it inherits extra proportional shrinkage of the survivors (2.5 becomes 1.667).

(c) The penalties are:

Split \((w_1, w_2)\) L1 penalty L2 penalty
(2, 0) 2 4
(1.5, 0.5) 2 2.5
(1, 1) 2 2

L1 is indifferent: every split ties, so Lasso's answer is arbitrary and can jump between (2, 0) and (0, 2) when the data changes slightly. L2 strictly prefers the equal split (1, 1).

(d) With correlated groups, Lasso keeps one member of the group at random and drops the rest, so the choice is unstable and hard to interpret. Elastic Net's L2 part breaks the tie by sharing weight across the group (the grouping effect), while its L1 part still zeros features that are genuinely irrelevant. This combination is why Elastic Net is the recommendation for highly correlated features.

Key insight: Elastic Net is not just a compromise between Ridge and Lasso. Its L2 part fixes Lasso's specific failure on correlated features, while its L1 part keeps the sparsity that Ridge cannot provide.

P3.27 L4 · Analysis

Why lasso lands exactly on zero and ridge never does

Take a feature that is irrelevant to the target, so that the data gradient on its weight is \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = 0\), and start from \(w = 0.03\). Use \(\eta\lambda = 0.05\).

(a) Ridge: show that \(k\) steps of \(w_{k+1} = (1 - \eta\lambda) \cdot w_k\) give \(w_k = 0.03 \cdot 0.95^k\). What is \(w\) after 100 steps? Can it ever be exactly 0?

(b) Naive lasso subgradient: apply \(w_{k+1} = w_k - \eta\lambda \cdot \operatorname{sign}(w_k)\) for four steps. What goes wrong?

(c) Proximal (soft-threshold) lasso: apply \(w_{k+1} = \operatorname{sign}(u) \cdot \max(\lvert u \rvert - \eta\lambda, 0)\) with \(u = w_k - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial J}{\partial w}\). Where does \(w\) go, and in how many steps?

(d) Now allow a non-zero data gradient \(g\). Prove that the proximal lasso step lands exactly on 0 for a whole interval of values \(u = w - \eta g\), namely \(\lvert u \rvert \le \eta\lambda\), whereas the ridge step \((1 - \eta\lambda) w - \eta g = 0\) holds only on a single line in the \((w, g)\) plane, a measure-zero coincidence.

(e) Connect this to the closed forms of P3.24: which form of "zero" does each penalty produce at the optimum?

Hint

Ridge multiplies by a factor less than 1, and a non-zero number times a non-zero factor is never zero. Lasso subtracts a fixed amount, which can overshoot past 0 unless it is clipped.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Each step multiplies by 0.95, so \(w_k = 0.03 \cdot 0.95^k\). After 100 steps,

\[ w \approx 0.03 \times 0.00592 \approx \mathbf{1.78 \times 10^{-4}}, \]

which is small but positive. It is never exactly 0, because a product of non-zero numbers is non-zero. The weight decays geometrically forever.

(b) The steps are \(0.03 \to -0.02 \to 0.03 \to -0.02 \to 0.03\). The fixed-size step overshoots across 0 and oscillates, because \(\operatorname{sign}(w)\) flips each time and the subgradient method never "knows" to stop at 0. This is exactly the slides' warning that L1 is not differentiable and cannot be used efficiently with plain gradient-based methods.

(c) \(u = 0.03 - 0 = 0.03\) and \(\lvert u \rvert = 0.03 \le 0.05\), so \(w\) becomes exactly 0 in one step. It stays at 0 from then on, because \(u = 0\) at every later step.

(d) The soft-threshold output is 0 whenever \(\lvert u \rvert \le \eta\lambda\), that is, for every \((w, g)\) with

\[ \lvert w - \eta g \rvert \le \eta\lambda. \]

This is a band of positive width in the \((w, g)\) plane, so landing on 0 is a robust, typical outcome.

The ridge step is 0 only when \(w(1 - \eta\lambda) = \eta g\) exactly, which is a single line in the same plane. Iterates almost never hit it exactly, and even at the ridge optimum, \(w_j = 0\) requires the data's pull on that weight to be exactly zero.

(e) At the lasso optimum, \(w_j = 0\) whenever \(\lvert z_j \rvert \le \lambda\), a set of positive width (P3.24, P3.25). At the ridge optimum, \(w_j = z_j/(1 + \lambda) = 0\) only if \(z_j = 0\), so ridge's "zeros" are just coefficients that were already zero.

Key insight: Ridge shrinks by multiplying and lasso shrinks by subtracting and then clipping. Repeated multiplication by a factor below 1 approaches zero but never reaches it, while a subtraction that is clipped at zero reaches it in finitely many steps. This difference in the update rule is where lasso's sparsity comes from.

P3.28 L5 · Mastery

Choosing Ridge, Lasso or Elastic Net, and tuning \(\lambda\) honestly

Three teams each want a regularised linear model. In sklearn terms the options are Ridge, Lasso and ElasticNet (with l1_ratio the L1 share, as in P3.26).

Scenario A. A clinic has 80 patients and 500 gene-expression features. The goal is a model that names a short list of genes for follow-up.

Scenario B. An estate agent has 2,000 sales and 12 features, all of which are believed to matter. Floor area, number of rooms and number of bedrooms are strongly correlated with each other. The goal is accurate price prediction; nobody needs features removed.

Scenario C. A factory has 300 production runs and 150 sensor channels. The sensors come in groups of about ten near-duplicate channels on the same machine. The goal is a sparse model that names which machines matter, and that names the same machines when it is retrained next month.

(a) Recommend Ridge, Lasso or Elastic Net for each scenario, with a one-line reason.

(b) In Scenario A, could you fit ordinary least squares with the normal equation instead? Why or why not?

(c) For Scenario A, 60 patients are used for training and 20 are set aside as a test set. A Lasso is tuned by 5-fold cross-validation (CV) on the 60 training patients, giving:

\(\lambda\) Non-zero weights Training MSE CV MSE Test MSE
0.001 46 0.05 4.10 4.30
0.01 31 0.40 2.35 2.50
0.1 18 1.10 1.32 1.45
0.3 9 1.45 1.38 1.30
1 2 3.20 3.05 3.10

Which \(\lambda\) does the CV column select, and what test MSE should be reported for it?

(d) A colleague picks \(\lambda = 0.3\) "because it has the best test MSE, 1.30" and reports 1.30. What is wrong with this?

(e) The clinicians would much prefer 9 genes to 18. Is it legitimate to choose \(\lambda = 0.3\) anyway, and if so, how must that decision be made?

(f) Which rows show underfitting and overfitting? What does the table say about the claim "more regularisation can only help"?

(g) Why must the features be standardised before any of these models is fitted, and which statistics should be used to standardise the test patients?

Hint

Match each goal to the property it needs: exact zeros (L1), stable shared weights across correlated features (L2), or both. Then remember that any number used to choose something can no longer serve as an unbiased estimate of performance.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The recommendations are:

Scenario Choice Reason
A Lasso (or Elastic Net with a high l1_ratio) A short gene list needs exact zeros, which only an L1 term gives.
B Ridge Every feature should stay. The L2 penalty stabilises the weights of the correlated features by sharing the effect among them, without removing any.
C Elastic Net The L1 part gives sparsity. The L2 part keeps the near-duplicate sensors of one machine together (the grouping effect of P3.26), so the selection does not jump between duplicates from one retraining to the next.

(b) No. With an intercept, \(X^\top X\) is \(501 \times 501\) but has rank at most 60 (the number of training rows), so it is singular and \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) does not exist. Infinitely many weight vectors fit the training data exactly. Any \(\lambda > 0\) in the L2 part makes \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) invertible (P3.23), and the L1 part picks a sparse solution.

(c) The CV column is smallest at \(\lambda = 0.1\) (CV MSE 1.32), so the model is refitted with \(\lambda = 0.1\) on all 60 training patients and its test MSE, 1.45, is reported. The test column is read once, for the chosen model only.

(d) Choosing \(\lambda\) by the test column turns the test set into a second validation set. The value 1.30 is the minimum of five noisy estimates, so it is optimistically biased, and no untouched data is left to estimate the error honestly. With only 20 test patients, the difference between 1.30 and 1.45 is well within noise anyway.

(e) Yes, provided the decision uses only the CV column and is made before the test set is looked at. The CV MSE at \(\lambda = 0.3\) is 1.38, only 0.06 above the minimum, and it halves the number of genes. A rule such as "take the largest \(\lambda\) whose CV MSE is within a stated tolerance of the minimum" (the one-standard-error rule is the usual version) is a legitimate validation-based choice. The test MSE of whichever model is chosen is then reported, whatever it turns out to be.

(f) \(\lambda = 0.001\) and \(0.01\) overfit: training MSE is tiny while CV MSE is many times larger (gaps 4.05 and 1.95). \(\lambda = 1\) underfits: training and CV errors are both high and close (3.20 and 3.05), and only 2 genes survive. CV MSE is U-shaped in \(\lambda\), so too much regularisation hurts as much as too little. \(\lambda\) is a hyper-parameter that must be tuned, not a dial that only ever helps.

(g) The penalty \(\lambda \sum_j \lvert w_j \rvert\) or \(\lambda \sum_j w_j^2\) treats every weight alike, but the size of a weight depends on the units of its feature. Without standardisation, a feature measured on a large scale needs only a small weight, so it is barely penalised, and the selection depends on the choice of units. The test patients must be standardised with the training means and standard deviations: computing statistics on the test set would leak information about it, and would describe the test patients on a different scale from the one the model was trained on.

A further point for Scenario A: Lasso can select at most as many features as there are training rows (here at most 60, and 46 at the smallest \(\lambda\)). This is another reason to consider Elastic Net when \(p \gg n\).

Key insight: Pick the penalty from the goal (sparsity needs L1, correlated groups need L2, and both needs Elastic Net), and pick \(\lambda\) from validation data only. The test set is used once, at the end, to report the error of a model that has already been chosen.

5.F Evaluating a Regression Model (3.6)

Conventions for this subsection: with \(\bar{y}\) the mean of the observed \(y_i\) and \(\hat{y}_i\) the predictions, the total sum of squares is \(\text{SST} = \sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2\), the regression (explained) sum of squares is \(\text{SSR} = \sum_i (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\), and the error (residual) sum of squares is \(\text{SSE} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\), matching the slides. The coefficient of determination is \(R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}\). On a test set, \(\bar{y}\) is the test-set mean, as in sklearn's r2_score.

P3.29 L1 · Foundation

What \(R^2\) does and does not tell you

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "\(R^2 = 1\) on the training data means that every training residual is zero."

(b) "\(R^2 = 0.6\) means the model's predictions are correct 60% of the time."

(c) "For least squares with an intercept, adding a feature can never lower the training \(R^2\)."

(d) "\(R^2\) cannot be negative."

(e) "A model with training \(R^2 = 0.99\) cannot be overfitting."

(f) "A model that always predicts the training mean \(\bar{y}\) has training \(R^2 = 0\)."

Hint

Write \(R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}\) and ask, for each statement, what it says about SSE compared with SST.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(R^2 = 1\) means \(\text{SSE} = 0\), and a sum of squares is zero only if every term is zero.

(b) False. \(R^2\) is not an accuracy. It says that the model's squared error is 40% of the squared error of always predicting the mean, which is often described as the model explaining 60% of the variance in \(y\).

(c) True. The larger model can reproduce the smaller one by setting the new weight to 0, so its minimum SSE is at most as large. SST does not change, so \(R^2\) cannot fall.

(d) False. On new data, or for a model fitted without an intercept, SSE can exceed SST. Then \(R^2 < 0\), which means the model does worse than predicting the mean.

(e) False. Training \(R^2\) measures fit to the training data only. A degree-\((n-1)\) polynomial has training \(R^2 = 1\) and can be badly overfit. Only held-out error can detect overfitting.

(f) True. Then \(\hat{y}_i = \bar{y}\) for every \(i\), so \(\text{SSE} = \text{SST}\) and \(R^2 = 0\). This constant model is the baseline that \(R^2\) compares against.

Key insight: \(R^2\) compares a model's squared error with that of the "predict the mean" baseline. It is not an accuracy, it can be negative, and its training value says nothing about generalisation.

P3.30 L2 · Computation

\(R^2\) and \(\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\) by hand

Fit a least-squares line \(\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x\) to:

\(x\) 1 2 3 4 5
\(y\) 2 4 5 4 5

(a) Compute \(w_0\) and \(w_1\).

(b) Compute the fitted values, then SST, SSR and SSE. Check that \(\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\).

(c) Compute \(R^2\) both as \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST}\) and as \(1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}\). Also compute the square of the correlation coefficient between \(x\) and \(y\).

(d) Compute the training MSE and RMSE, and interpret \(R^2\) in one sentence.

Hint

Use \(w_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\) and \(w_0 = \bar{y} - w_1 \bar{x}\). All the sums are small integers or simple decimals.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\bar{x} = 3\) and \(\bar{y} = 4\). The deviations are \(x - \bar{x} = (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)\) and \(y - \bar{y} = (-2, 0, 1, 0, 1)\), so

\[ w_1 = \frac{4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2}{4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4} = \frac{6}{10} = 0.6, \qquad w_0 = 4 - 0.6 \cdot 3 = 2.2 . \]

The line is \(\hat{y} = 2.2 + 0.6x\).

(b) The fitted values are \(\hat{y} = (2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2)\) and the residuals are \((-0.8, 0.6, 1.0, -0.6, -0.2)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{SST} &= 4 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 = \mathbf{6}, \\ \text{SSR} &= 1.44 + 0.36 + 0 + 0.36 + 1.44 = \mathbf{3.6}, \\ \text{SSE} &= 0.64 + 0.36 + 1.00 + 0.36 + 0.04 = \mathbf{2.4}. \end{aligned} \]

\(\text{SSR} + \text{SSE} = 3.6 + 2.4 = 6 = \text{SST}\) ✓.

(c) \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST} = 3.6/6 = 0.6\) and \(1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST} = 1 - 2.4/6 = 0.6\), so \(R^2 = 0.6\). The correlation is \(r = 6/\sqrt{10 \cdot 6} \approx 0.7746\), and \(r^2 = 0.6\) as well. sklearn's LinearRegression and r2_score give the same line and \(R^2 = 0.6\).

(d) MSE = 2.4/5 = 0.48 and RMSE = \(\sqrt{0.48} \approx 0.693\). The line removes 60% of the squared error left by predicting \(\bar{y} = 4\) for everyone; a typical prediction is off by about 0.7.

Key insight: For least squares with an intercept, the total variation splits exactly into an explained part and a residual part, so the two formulas for \(R^2\) agree, and both equal the squared correlation between \(x\) and \(y\).

P3.31 L2 · Computation

Training error against test error, and a negative \(R^2\)

Two models are trained on the five points of P3.30, \((x, y) = (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5)\).

Model A is the line \(\hat{y} = 2.2 + 0.6x\).

Model B is the degree-4 polynomial through all five points, \(\hat{y} = (5x^4 - 54x^3 + 187x^2 - 210x + 120)/24\).

Five held-out test points are available, together with Model B's predictions (rounded to three decimals):

\(x\) 1.5 2.5 3.5 4.5 5.5
\(y\) 3.0 4.6 4.4 4.7 5.6
Model B prediction 2.867 4.805 4.617 3.805 8.867

(a) Give the training MSE of each model. (Model A's comes from P3.30.)

(b) Compute Model A's test predictions and the test MSE of both models.

(c) Compute the test \(R^2\) of both models, using the test-set mean.

(d) Interpret the sign of Model B's test \(R^2\). Which single test point contributes most to Model B's error, and why?

Hint

Model B has 5 parameters and there are 5 training points. For (c) you need the test SST, \(\sum (y_i - \bar{y}_{\text{test}})^2\), first.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Model A: 0.48 (P3.30). Model B: 0, because it passes through every training point.

(b) Model A predicts \((3.1, 3.7, 4.3, 4.9, 5.5)\). Its test errors are \((-0.1, 0.9, 0.1, -0.2, 0.1)\), so \(\text{SSE}_\text{test} = 0.88\) and the test MSE is 0.176.

Model B's test errors are about \((0.133, -0.205, -0.217, 0.895, -3.267)\), with squares \((0.018, 0.042, 0.047, 0.802, 10.675)\). So \(\text{SSE}_\text{test} \approx 11.583\) and the test MSE is about 2.317.

(c) The test mean is \(\bar{y}_\text{test} = 22.3/5 = 4.46\), and \(\text{SST}_\text{test} = 3.512\).

\[ R^2_A = 1 - \frac{0.88}{3.512} \approx \mathbf{0.749}, \qquad R^2_B = 1 - \frac{11.583}{3.512} \approx \mathbf{-2.298}. \]

sklearn's mean_squared_error and r2_score give the same values.

(d) A negative test \(R^2\) means Model B predicts the test points worse than the constant 4.46 would. The point \(x = 5.5\) contributes \(10.675/11.583 \approx 92\%\) of its test SSE: it lies outside the training range, where the interpolating polynomial swings up to 8.87. Model A is the better model, even though its training MSE is the larger of the two.

Key insight: Training error measures how well a model fits the data it has seen; only held-out error estimates how it will do on new data. A model with zero training error can still have a negative test \(R^2\).

P3.32 L3 · Application

Diagnosing a model from a \(\lambda\) sweep and from learning-curve descriptions

A degree-10 polynomial model (standardised features) is fitted with ridge regularisation on 40 training points and evaluated on 40 validation points. The noise in the data is known to give an MSE floor of about 0.75.

\(\lambda\) Training MSE Validation MSE
0 0.21 3.85
0.001 0.35 1.92
0.01 0.58 0.97
0.1 0.79 0.88
1 1.62 1.75
10 4.10 4.32

(a) Diagnose the model at \(\lambda = 0\) and at \(\lambda = 10\). Which \(\lambda\) would you choose?

(b) A colleague says: "The train–validation gap at \(\lambda = 10\) is only 0.22, so that model generalises well." What is wrong with this reasoning?

(c) The team reports "expected MSE on new data: 0.88" for the chosen model. Why is this slightly optimistic, and what should they do instead?

(d) Diagnose each of the following learning-curve descriptions (errors plotted against training-set size \(n\)) and recommend one action.

(i) Training error starts near 0 and rises slowly; validation error starts high and is still falling at the largest \(n\); a wide gap remains.

(ii) Both curves flatten out within a few hundred examples at almost the same level, about four times the noise floor.

(iii) The validation error is below the training error at every \(n\), by a wide margin.

Hint

A small gap is necessary for a good fit but not sufficient: the level of the errors, compared with the noise floor, matters too. For (iii), think about what could make data the model has never seen look easier than data it was trained on.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) At \(\lambda = 0\) the model overfits (high variance): training MSE 0.21 is below the noise floor, so the model is fitting noise, and validation MSE 3.85 is 18 times larger. At \(\lambda = 10\) it underfits (high bias): both errors are about 4, far above the floor of 0.75. Choose \(\lambda = 0.1\): validation MSE 0.88 is the lowest and close to the floor, and the gap is only 0.09.

(b) The gap measures variance, not quality. At \(\lambda = 10\) both errors are more than five times the noise floor, so the model is reliably bad: a small gap at a high error level is the signature of underfitting, not of good generalisation. The correct reading needs both the level of the errors and the gap.

(c) 0.88 is the minimum over six validation scores, and \(\lambda\) was chosen to make it small, so it is biased downward. The team should report the error on a separate test set that played no part in choosing \(\lambda\) (or use nested cross-validation).

(d) The diagnoses are:

(i) High variance (overfitting). The gap is still closing, so more training data will help. Increasing \(\lambda\) or reducing the degree would also help.

(ii) High bias (underfitting). The curves have met well above the floor, so more data will not help. Add capacity: lower \(\lambda\), raise the degree, or add features.

(iii) Suspicious; check the pipeline before trusting either number. Common causes are leakage or duplicate rows between the splits, a validation set drawn from an easier part of the data, or a "training error" that is not MSE at all (for example a logged training loss that includes the penalty \(\lambda \lVert w \rVert^2\)). A small validation set can produce this by chance at a few values of \(n\), but not consistently by a wide margin.

Key insight: Read every diagnosis from two numbers: the level of the errors relative to the noise floor, and the gap between training and validation error. High and close is bias, low and far apart is variance, and validation consistently better than training is a bug to find, not a result to report.

P3.33 L4 · Analysis

Why \(\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\) needs an intercept

Let \(X\) be an \(n \times p\) design matrix, \(w = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\) the least-squares weights, \(\hat{y} = Xw\), and \(e = y - \hat{y}\) the residuals. Write \(\mathbf{1}\) for the all-ones vector.

(a) Show from the normal equations that \(X^\top e = 0\), and deduce that \(\hat{y}^\top e = 0\).

(b) Now suppose the first column of \(X\) is \(\mathbf{1}\) (the model has an intercept). Show that \(\sum_i e_i = 0\), and prove that \(\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\).

(c) Deduce that, for least squares with an intercept, \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST} = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}\) and \(0 \le R^2 \le 1\).

(d) Fit the model \(\hat{y} = wx\) with no intercept to \((x, y) = (1, 5), (2, 5.5), (3, 6)\). Compute SST, SSR and SSE, and show that \(\text{SST} \ne \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\). Compute \(1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}\) and \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST}\).

(e) Which sum-of-squares identity does still hold without an intercept? Check it on the data of (d).

Hint

Write \(y - \bar{y}\mathbf{1} = (\hat{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}) + e\) and expand the squared norm. The cross term is the only thing to deal with, and it contains \(\hat{y}^\top e\) and \(\mathbf{1}^\top e\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The normal equations are \(X^\top X w = X^\top y\), so \(X^\top (y - Xw) = X^\top e = 0\): the residuals are orthogonal to every column of \(X\). Then

\[ \hat{y}^\top e = w^\top X^\top e = 0 . \]

(b) If the first column of \(X\) is \(\mathbf{1}\), the first row of \(X^\top e = 0\) reads \(\mathbf{1}^\top e = \sum_i e_i = 0\). Now expand:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{SST} = \lVert y - \bar{y}\mathbf{1} \rVert^2 &= \lVert (\hat{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}) + e \rVert^2 \\ &= \lVert \hat{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1} \rVert^2 + \lVert e \rVert^2 + 2\left(\hat{y}^\top e - \bar{y}\,\mathbf{1}^\top e\right) \\ &= \text{SSR} + \text{SSE} + 2(0 - 0) . \end{aligned} \]

So \(\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\). Both facts are needed: \(\hat{y}^\top e = 0\) holds for any least-squares fit, but \(\mathbf{1}^\top e = 0\) needs the intercept.

(c) Dividing the identity by SST gives \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST} + \text{SSE}/\text{SST} = 1\), so the two formulas for \(R^2\) agree. Both SSR and SSE are \(\ge 0\), so each ratio lies in \([0, 1]\), hence \(0 \le R^2 \le 1\).

(d) \(w = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2} = \frac{5 + 11 + 18}{14} = \frac{17}{7} \approx 2.429\), so \(\hat{y} \approx (2.429, 4.857, 7.286)\) and \(e \approx (2.571, 0.643, -1.286)\). Here \(\sum_i e_i = 27/14 \approx 1.929 \ne 0\). With \(\bar{y} = 5.5\):

\[ \text{SST} = \mathbf{0.5}, \qquad \text{SSE} = \tfrac{243}{28} \approx \mathbf{8.679}, \qquad \text{SSR} = \tfrac{365}{28} \approx \mathbf{13.036} . \]

\(\text{SSR} + \text{SSE} \approx 21.714\), which is not 0.5. The gap is the cross term \(-2\bar{y}\sum_i e_i = -2 \cdot 5.5 \cdot \tfrac{27}{14} \approx -21.214\).

The two "\(R^2\)" formulas now disagree wildly: \(1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST} \approx -16.36\) and \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST} \approx 26.07\). sklearn's LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False) gives \(w = 2.4286\) and r2_score \(= -16.36\). With an intercept, the fit is \(\hat{y} = 4.5 + 0.5x\), which is exact, and \(R^2 = 1\).

(e) \(\hat{y}^\top e = 0\) still holds, so the uncentred decomposition \(\lVert y \rVert^2 = \lVert \hat{y} \rVert^2 + \lVert e \rVert^2\) is true. Check: \(\lVert y \rVert^2 = 25 + 30.25 + 36 = 91.25\), and \(\lVert \hat{y} \rVert^2 + \lVert e \rVert^2 = \tfrac{289}{49} \cdot 14 + 8.679 \approx 82.571 + 8.679 = 91.25\) ✓.

Key insight: \(\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}\) is Pythagoras: the residual vector is orthogonal to the column space of \(X\). The decomposition measures variation about the mean, so the vector \(\mathbf{1}\) must lie in that column space, which is exactly what an intercept provides. Without it, \(R^2\) can fall outside \([0, 1]\) and its two formulas no longer agree.

5.G Module 3 Capstone

P3.34 L3 · Application

A small end-to-end pipeline: scale, solve, descend, regularise, evaluate

Training data (price in thousands):

Area \(x_1\) (\(\text{m}^2\)) Rooms \(x_2\) Price \(y\)
50 1 150
50 3 170
70 1 200
70 3 230

Held-out data: \((x_1, x_2, y) = (65, 2, 205)\) and \((55, 3, 185)\).

(a) Standardise both features as \(z = (x - \text{mean})/\text{SD}\), using the training mean and the population SD. Give the four training rows in \(z\) units, and the two held-out rows.

(b) With the design matrix \(A = [\mathbf{1}, z_1, z_2]\), solve the normal equation for \(w^* = (w_0, w_1, w_2)\). Compute the training SSE, SST and \(R^2\), and convert the model back to raw units.

(c) Run three steps of batch gradient descent on \(J(w) = \frac{1}{2n}\lVert Aw - y \rVert^2\), starting from \(w = 0\) with \(\eta = 0.5\). Explain the pattern, and say what \(\eta = 1\) would do.

(d) On the unscaled features, \(\frac{1}{n}A_{\text{raw}}^\top A_{\text{raw}}\) has eigenvalues of about \(3705\), \(1.11\) and \(0.0243\). What is the largest stable learning rate, and what happens with \(\eta = 0.5\)?

(e) Fit ridge regression, minimising \(\lVert Aw - y \rVert^2 + \lambda (w_1^2 + w_2^2)\) with \(\lambda = 1\) (intercept not penalised).

(f) For both the least-squares and the ridge model, compute the held-out predictions, the held-out MSE and the held-out \(R^2\).

(g) Why would "\(R^2\) on a single held-out point" be meaningless? Should \(\lambda\) be chosen using these two held-out points?

Hint

After standardisation the columns of \(A\) are mutually orthogonal and each has squared norm 4, so \(A^\top A = 4I\) and every system decouples. That also makes \(\nabla J = w - w^*\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Area has mean 60 and SD 10; rooms have mean 2 and SD 1. The training rows become \((z_1, z_2) = (-1, -1), (-1, 1), (1, -1), (1, 1)\). The held-out rows become \((0.5, 0)\) and \((-0.5, 1)\), using the training statistics.

(b) \(A^\top A = 4I\) and \(A^\top y = (750, 110, 50)\), so

\[ w^* = \tfrac{1}{4}(750, 110, 50) = \mathbf{(187.5,\ 27.5,\ 12.5)} . \]

The fitted values are \((147.5, 172.5, 202.5, 227.5)\) with residuals \((2.5, -2.5, -2.5, 2.5)\), so \(\text{SSE} = 25\). With \(\bar{y} = 187.5\), \(\text{SST} = 3675\), so \(R^2 = 1 - 25/3675 \approx 0.9932\). In raw units, \(w_1/10 = 2.75\) per \(\text{m}^2\), \(w_2/1 = 12.5\) per room, and the intercept is \(187.5 - 2.75 \cdot 60 - 12.5 \cdot 2 = -2.5\), giving \(\hat{y} = -2.5 + 2.75x_1 + 12.5x_2\).

(c) Because \(\frac{1}{n}A^\top A = I\), the gradient is \(\nabla J = \frac{1}{n}A^\top(Aw - y) = w - w^*\), and the update is \(w \leftarrow w - \eta(w - w^*)\). From \(w = 0\) this gives \(w_k = \left(1 - (1 - \eta)^k\right) w^*\):

Step \(w_0\) \(w_1\) \(w_2\) \(J(w)\)
1 93.75 13.75 6.25 4511.7
2 140.625 20.625 9.375 1130.3
3 164.0625 24.0625 10.9375 284.9

Each step halves the remaining distance to \(w^*\), in every coordinate at once. With \(\eta = 1\), gradient descent reaches \(w^*\) exactly in one step, because the cost contours are circles.

(d) Stability needs \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 2/3705 \approx \mathbf{5.4 \times 10^{-4}}\). The condition number is \(3705/0.0243 \approx 1.5 \times 10^5\), so even at a stable \(\eta\) the coordinate with eigenvalue 0.0243 would take on the order of \(10^5\) steps to converge. With \(\eta = 0.5\) the iteration diverges: after one step \(w \approx (93.75, 5762.5, 193.75)\), and the weights grow by a factor of roughly 1,850 per step after that. Scaling changes the path and the speed, not the minimiser.

(e) With \(A^\top A = 4I\), the penalised normal equations decouple: \(w_0 = 187.5\) (unpenalised) and \(w_j = (A^\top y)_j / (4 + \lambda)\). So \(w_{\text{ridge}} = (187.5,\ 22,\ 10)\), the same as sklearn's Ridge(alpha=1) on the standardised features.

(f) The held-out mean is 195 and the held-out SST is \(100 + 100 = 200\).

Model Predictions Held-out MSE Held-out \(R^2\)
Least squares 201.25, 186.25 \((3.75^2 + 1.25^2)/2 = \mathbf{7.8125}\) \(1 - 15.625/200 = \mathbf{0.9219}\)
Ridge, \(\lambda = 1\) 198.5, 186.5 \((6.5^2 + 1.5^2)/2 = \mathbf{22.25}\) \(1 - 44.5/200 = \mathbf{0.7775}\)

Here ridge does worse: the least-squares fit already has a training \(R^2\) of 0.993, so there is little variance for the penalty to remove, and the shrinkage only adds bias.

(g) For a single point, \(\text{SST} = (y - \bar{y})^2 = 0\), so \(R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/0\) is undefined. Report the squared error (or MSE over a set) instead. And no: two points are far too few to choose \(\lambda\) reliably, and if they are used to choose it they are no longer a test set. \(\lambda\) should be chosen by cross-validation on the training data.

Key insight: Each stage of the pipeline has its own rule: scale with training statistics only, prefer the closed form when \(p\) is small, use gradient descent with scaled features, choose \(\lambda\) by validation, and report the error on data that played no part in any of these choices.

P3.35 L4 · Analysis

A bias–variance study across polynomial degree

The true function is \(f(x) = 1 + 2x - 3x^2\). Training inputs are the \(n = 15\) equally spaced points \(x_1, \dots, x_{15}\) in \([-1, 1]\), and the targets are \(y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\) with independent noise \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(\sigma = 0.5\). A polynomial of degree \(d\) (with \(p = d + 1\) parameters) is fitted by least squares. "Test MSE" means the error on fresh noisy targets \(y_i' = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i'\) at the same 15 inputs. Over many simulated training sets, the averages are:

Degree \(d\) \(p\) Training MSE Test MSE \(\text{Bias}^2\) Variance
0 1 2.788 2.821 2.555 0.017
1 2 1.248 1.314 1.031 0.033
2 3 0.200 0.300 0.000 0.050
4 5 0.167 0.333 0.000 0.083
6 7 0.133 0.367 0.000 0.117
10 11 0.067 0.433 0.000 0.183
14 15 0.000 0.500 0.000 0.250

Here \(\text{Bias}^2\) and Variance are averaged over the 15 inputs: \(\text{Bias}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \left(E[\hat{f}(x_i)] - f(x_i)\right)^2\) and \(\text{Variance} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \operatorname{Var}(\hat{f}(x_i))\).

(a) Prove that at a fixed input \(x\), with \(y' = f(x) + \varepsilon'\) independent of the training data,

\[ E\left[(y' - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] = \sigma^2 + \left(E[\hat{f}(x)] - f(x)\right)^2 + \operatorname{Var}(\hat{f}(x)) . \]

(b) Check the decomposition on the rows \(d = 0\) and \(d = 10\).

(c) Classify each degree as underfitting, a good fit or overfitting, and choose a degree. Why is \(\text{Bias}^2\) exactly zero for every \(d \ge 2\)?

(d) Let \(H = A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\) be the hat matrix of the degree-\(d\) design \(A\), so that \(\hat{y} = Hy\). Show that the Variance column equals \(\sigma^2 p / n\).

(e) Show that the expected training MSE is \(\text{Bias}^2 + \sigma^2 (n - p)/n\) and the expected test MSE is \(\text{Bias}^2 + \sigma^2 (1 + p/n)\), so that the gap between them is \(2\sigma^2 p/n\). Check this on two rows.

Hint

For (a), add and subtract \(E[\hat{f}(x)]\) and use the independence of \(\varepsilon'\). For (d) and (e), \(H\) is symmetric and idempotent (\(H^2 = H\)), \(\operatorname{tr}(H) = p\), and \(E[\hat{y}] = Hf\), where \(f\) is the vector of true values.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Write \(\bar{f} = E[\hat{f}(x)]\). Since \(y' - \hat{f} = \varepsilon' + (f - \hat{f})\), and \(\varepsilon'\) has mean 0 and is independent of \(\hat{f}\),

\[ \begin{aligned} E\left[(y' - \hat{f})^2\right] &= E[\varepsilon'^2] + E\left[(f - \hat{f})^2\right] \\ &= \sigma^2 + E\left[\left((f - \bar{f}) + (\bar{f} - \hat{f})\right)^2\right] \\ &= \sigma^2 + (f - \bar{f})^2 + E\left[(\bar{f} - \hat{f})^2\right], \end{aligned} \]

because the cross term \(2(f - \bar{f})\,E[\bar{f} - \hat{f}]\) is 0. The last two terms are \(\text{Bias}^2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{f}(x))\).

(b) With \(\sigma^2 = 0.25\):

\(d = 0\): \(0.25 + 2.555 + 0.017 = 2.822\), against 2.821 in the table (the unrounded values, \(0.25 + 2.5547 + 0.0167 = 2.8214\), agree exactly).

\(d = 10\): \(0.25 + 0 + 0.183 = 0.433\) ✓.

(c) \(d = 0\) and \(d = 1\) underfit: \(\text{Bias}^2\) dominates and both errors are far above \(\sigma^2 = 0.25\). \(d = 2\) is the best fit, with the lowest test MSE (0.300). \(d \ge 4\) overfit progressively: training MSE keeps falling while test MSE rises, and \(d = 14\) interpolates the data (training MSE 0) with the worst test MSE among \(d \ge 2\). Choose \(d = 2\). \(\text{Bias}^2 = 0\) for \(d \ge 2\) because the true \(f\) is a quadratic, which every polynomial model of degree at least 2 contains, and least squares is unbiased when the model contains the truth. Beyond \(d = 2\), the extra degrees add only variance.

(d) \(\hat{y} = Hy = H(f + \varepsilon)\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{y}) = H(\sigma^2 I)H^\top = \sigma^2 H\). The average variance is

\[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \operatorname{Var}(\hat{y}_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(H) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}\left((A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top A\right) = \frac{\sigma^2 p}{n} . \]

For example, for \(d = 6\), \(0.25 \cdot 7/15 \approx 0.117\) ✓, and for \(d = 14\), \(0.25 \cdot 15/15 = 0.250\) ✓.

(e) The bias vector is \((I - H)f\), so \(n \cdot \text{Bias}^2 = \lVert (I - H)f \rVert^2\). For the training error, \(y - \hat{y} = (I - H)f + (I - H)\varepsilon\), and \(I - H\) is also symmetric and idempotent with trace \(n - p\):

\[ E\left[\lVert y - \hat{y} \rVert^2\right] = \lVert (I - H)f \rVert^2 + \sigma^2 \operatorname{tr}(I - H) = n\,\text{Bias}^2 + \sigma^2 (n - p) . \]

For the test error, \(y' - \hat{y} = (I - H)f + \varepsilon' - H\varepsilon\), and the three parts are uncorrelated:

\[ E\left[\lVert y' - \hat{y} \rVert^2\right] = n\,\text{Bias}^2 + n\sigma^2 + \sigma^2 \operatorname{tr}(H) = n\,\text{Bias}^2 + \sigma^2 (n + p) . \]

Dividing by \(n\) gives the two formulas, and the gap is \(2\sigma^2 p/n\).

Check \(d = 2\): training \(0.25 \cdot 12/15 = 0.200\) and test \(0.25 \cdot 18/15 = 0.300\), gap \(0.1 = 2 \cdot 0.25 \cdot 3/15\) ✓.

Check \(d = 14\): training 0, test \(0.25 \cdot 2 = 0.500\), gap 0.5 ✓.

A simulation with 40,000 training sets reproduces every entry of the table to within about 0.001.

Key insight: Test error is noise plus squared bias plus variance. Once the model is flexible enough to contain the truth, bias is zero and each extra parameter adds \(\sigma^2/n\) of variance, while the training error falls by the same amount. That is why the training error is optimistic by exactly \(2\sigma^2 p/n\) and cannot be used to choose the degree.

P3.36 L5 · Mastery

"\(R^2\) went up when I added a random feature, so the model is better"

An analyst fits house prices \(y\) against a single feature \(x\) on 8 training examples. A colleague then adds a column \(r\) produced by a random-number generator, independent of everything else, "to see what happens".

\(x\) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
\(r\) 0 2 −2 2 −2 −3 −2 3
\(y\) 3 5 6 6 9 11 12 16

Model 1 uses \(x\) only. Model 2 uses \(x\) and \(r\); its least-squares fit is \(\hat{y} \approx 0.7759 + 1.7241x + 0.1379r\), with training \(\text{SSE} = 170/29 \approx 5.862\).

A held-out set is also available:

\(x\) 2.5 4.5 6.5 9
\(r\) −3 −3 −2 −2
\(y\) 5 9 12 17

(a) Fit Model 1 by hand. Compute its training SSE and \(R^2\).

(b) Compute Model 2's training \(R^2\). In this sample the correlation between \(r\) and \(y\) is exactly 0, yet \(R^2\) rose. Prove that training \(R^2\) can never fall when a feature is added to a least-squares model, and explain how a feature with zero correlation with \(y\) can still raise it.

(c) Compute the adjusted \(R^2\), \(\bar{R}^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1}\) with \(p\) the number of features, for both models.

(d) Compute the held-out MSE of both models.

(e) Suppose six more random columns were added, so that Model 3 has 7 features plus an intercept. What would its training \(R^2\) be, and why?

(f) Write a short, correct rule for deciding whether to keep a new feature.

Hint

Model 2 can always set the weight on \(r\) to 0 and so reproduce Model 1 exactly. Least squares can only do at least as well as that.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\bar{x} = 4.5\), \(\bar{y} = 8.5\), \(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = 72\) and \(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 42\), so

\[ w_1 = \frac{72}{42} = \frac{12}{7} \approx 1.7143, \qquad w_0 = 8.5 - \frac{12}{7} \cdot 4.5 = \frac{11}{14} \approx 0.7857 . \]

Model 1 is \(\hat{y} \approx 0.7857 + 1.7143x\), with \(\text{SSE} = 46/7 \approx 6.571\). \(\text{SST} = 130\), so \(R^2 = 1 - 6.571/130 \approx 0.9495\).

(b) \(R^2_2 = 1 - 5.862/130 \approx 0.9549\), higher than Model 1's.

Proof that it cannot fall: Model 2 minimises SSE over all \((w_0, w_1, w_r)\), and the choice \(w_r = 0\) with Model 1's \((w_0, w_1)\) is one of the candidates, giving Model 1's SSE. So \(\text{SSE}_2 \le \text{SSE}_1\), and since SST is the same for both models, \(R^2_2 \ge R^2_1\). Equality needs the new column to be exactly uncorrelated with Model 1's residuals, which a random column almost never is.

Zero correlation with \(y\) is not the relevant condition. In this sample \(r\) happens to have a small correlation with \(x\) (about \(-0.08\)) and therefore a non-zero correlation with Model 1's residuals, so a non-zero \(w_r\) fits a little more of the noise. The increase is a property of these 8 points, not of any real relationship.

(c) With \(n = 8\):

\[ \bar{R}^2_1 = 1 - (0.0505)\cdot\frac{7}{6} \approx \mathbf{0.9410}, \qquad \bar{R}^2_2 = 1 - (0.0451)\cdot\frac{7}{5} \approx \mathbf{0.9369} . \]

The adjusted \(R^2\) falls: the gain in fit is too small to pay for the extra parameter.

(d) Model 1 predicts \((5.071, 8.500, 11.929, 16.214)\), with squared errors summing to 0.878, so its held-out MSE is about 0.219.

Model 2 predicts \((4.672, 8.121, 11.707, 16.017)\), with squared errors summing to 1.932, so its held-out MSE is about 0.483, more than twice as large. sklearn reproduces all of these numbers.

(e) \(R^2 = 1\), generically. With 8 parameters and 8 training points, the design matrix is square and (with probability 1 for random columns) invertible, so the model interpolates the data and \(\text{SSE} = 0\). A perfect training \(R^2\) built from pure noise is the clearest demonstration that training \(R^2\) measures fit, not merit.

(f) Keep a feature only if it lowers the error on data that was not used to fit the model: compare validation or cross-validation MSE (or \(R^2\)) with and without it. Adjusted \(R^2\) is a cheap in-sample correction that helps flag useless features, but it can still be fooled by chance on small samples. The test set is kept for the final report, not for this decision.

Key insight: Training \(R^2\) can only rise as features are added, so its rising is no evidence that a feature is useful. Whether a feature helps is decided by held-out error, which here doubles when the random column is added.

PART 6 — Module 4: Linear Models for Classification (Logistic Regression)

6.A From Linear to Logistic Regression (4.1)

P4.1 L1 · Foundation

Two complaints about least squares as a classifier

A classmate proposes: "For a yes/no target coded as 0/1, just fit ordinary least-squares regression and predict 1 whenever the fitted value is at least 0.5. Logistic regression is unnecessary." Give the two weaknesses of this proposal that the course highlights, each in one or two sentences.

Hint

One weakness is about the range of the fitted values; the other is about what happens to the 0.5 crossing point when you add a few extra, perfectly easy training points.

Answer & Key Insight

(1) The output is unbounded. A straight line

\[ h_\theta(x) = w_0 + w_1 x \]

happily produces values greater than 1 or less than 0, which cannot be read as probabilities of class 1.

(2) The boundary is very sensitive to outliers and new points. Every point pulls on the squared-error fit in proportion to its residual, so adding a few extreme but correctly labelled points (for example, very high-CGPA candidates who all got offers) tilts the line and drags the 0.5 crossing point sideways, which can misclassify points that were classified correctly before.

Key insight: Least squares measures how far a fitted value is from 0 or 1, not whether the class is right, so points that are "too correct" still pull the line; logistic regression fixes both problems by squashing the score through a sigmoid and using a loss that barely cares about confidently correct points.

P4.2 L1 · Foundation

Reading the sigmoid

Let \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\), with \(z = w^\top x + w_0\). True or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) \(\sigma(z)\) can equal exactly 0 or exactly 1 for a finite \(z\).

(b) \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\), so the decision boundary \(h(x) = 0.5\) is the set of points where \(w^\top x + w_0 = 0\).

(c) \(\sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z)\).

(d) Because \(\sigma\) is non-linear, the decision boundary of logistic regression on the raw features \(x\) is a curve, not a hyperplane.

Hint

For (d), ask which quantity is being compared with a threshold: \(\sigma(z)\) against 0.5, or \(z\) against 0?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) False. \(e^{-z}\) is strictly positive for every finite \(z\), so \(0 < \sigma(z) < 1\); the values 0 and 1 are only approached as \(z \to -\infty\) or \(z \to +\infty\).

(b) True.

\[ \sigma(0) = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = 0.5, \]

and \(\sigma\) is strictly increasing, so \(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\) exactly when \(z \ge 0\). The boundary is \(w^\top x + w_0 = 0\).

(c) True.

\[ \sigma(-z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{z}} = \frac{e^{-z}}{e^{-z} + 1} = 1 - \sigma(z). \]

(d) False. Since \(\sigma\) is monotone, "\(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\)" is the same condition as "\(z \ge 0\)", and \(z\) is linear in \(x\). The boundary \(w^\top x + w_0 = 0\) is therefore a hyperplane. A curved boundary appears only if you feed the model non-linear features such as \(x_1^2\) or \(x_1 x_2\).

Key insight: The sigmoid changes how confident the model is, not where it draws the line; the line is set entirely by the linear score \(z\).

P4.3 L2 · Computation

Three candidates through a fitted model

A fitted logistic model for "offer made" (1) versus "no offer" (0) is

\[ z = -5 + 0.6 \cdot x_1 + 0.2 \cdot x_2, \quad h(x) = \sigma(z), \]

where \(x_1\) is CGPA (0–10) and \(x_2\) is an aptitude score (0–10). Predict 1 when \(h(x) \ge 0.5\).

(a) Compute \(h(x)\) and the predicted class for candidates \(A = (8, 4)\), \(B = (6, 3)\) and \(C = (5, 10)\).

(b) Write the decision boundary as an equation in \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).

(c) A candidate has aptitude 7. What is the smallest CGPA at which the model predicts an offer?

Hint

Compute \(z\) first, then apply \(\sigma\). The boundary is where \(z = 0\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

  • A: \(z = -5 + 4.8 + 0.8 = 0.6\), \(h = \sigma(0.6) \approx\) 0.646, predict 1.
  • B: \(z = -5 + 3.6 + 0.6 = -0.8\), \(h = \sigma(-0.8) \approx\) 0.310, predict 0.
  • C: \(z = -5 + 3.0 + 2.0 = 0\), \(h =\) 0.5, which sits exactly on the boundary; under the "\(\ge 0.5\)" rule it is predicted 1.

(b) \(0.6x_1 + 0.2x_2 = 5\), which can be rewritten as \(x_2 = 25 - 3x_1\), a straight line in the \((x_1, x_2)\) plane.

(c) With \(x_2 = 7\):

\[ 0.6x_1 = 5 - 1.4 = 3.6, \]

so \(x_1 = 6.0\). Any CGPA of 6.0 or more gives an offer prediction.

Key insight: Classifying with logistic regression only needs the sign of \(z\); \(\sigma\) is needed when you want the probability itself, for example to rank candidates or to move the threshold away from 0.5.

P4.4 L3 · Application

Watching the least-squares boundary slide

One feature \(x\) and a 0/1 label:

\(x\) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
\(y\) 0 0 0 0 1 1 1 1

(a) Fit the least-squares line \(\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x\) and find the \(x\) at which \(\hat{y} = 0.5\). Which training points are misclassified by the rule "predict 1 if \(\hat{y} \ge 0.5\)"?

(b) Two more applicants arrive, \(x = 20\) and \(x = 25\), both with \(y = 1\). These are obviously positive. Refit the line on all ten points and find the new 0.5 crossing.

(c) Which original point is now misclassified? What are the fitted values at \(x = 20\) and \(x = 25\)?

(d) Explain in two sentences why logistic regression would not shift its boundary much when these two points are added.

Hint

For (a), the data are symmetric about \(x = 4.5\). For (b), use \(b_1 = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y})}{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}\) and \(b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\bar{x} = 4.5\), \(\bar{y} = 0.5\), \(\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y}) = 4\), \(\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 42\), so

\[ b_1 = \frac{4}{42} \approx 0.1905, \qquad b_0 = 0.5 - 0.1905 \cdot 4.5 \approx -0.3571. \]

The line is \(\hat{y} \approx -0.357 + 0.190x\), and \(\hat{y} = 0.5\) at \(x = 4.5\). No training point is misclassified. Note that the fit already leaves \([0, 1]\): \(\hat{y}(1) \approx -0.17\) and \(\hat{y}(8) \approx 1.17\).

(b) On all ten points, \(\hat{y} \approx 0.283 + 0.0391x\), so \(\hat{y} = 0.5\) at \(x \approx 5.54\).

(c) The point \(x = 5\) (\(y = 1\)) now gets \(\hat{y} \approx 0.479 < 0.5\) and is misclassified as 0. The new points get \(\hat{y}(20) \approx 1.07\) and \(\hat{y}(25) \approx 1.26\), both above 1.

(d) For logistic regression, a point's contribution to the gradient is \((h - y)x\). The far-right points are already given \(h \approx 1\) by any reasonable boundary near 4.5, so \(h - y \approx 0\) and they barely pull on the weights. The boundary is set by the points near the class overlap, not by easy points far away.

Key insight: Squared error punishes a correct prediction for being "too far" from 1, so easy points distort a least-squares classifier. The cross-entropy loss with a sigmoid gives such points almost no weight.

6.B Training: Cross-Entropy & Gradient Descent (4.2)

P4.5 L1 · Foundation

What the log-loss rewards and punishes

The per-example cross-entropy cost is

\[ \text{Cost}(h, y) = -\log h \ \text{ if } y = 1, \quad \text{and} \quad -\log(1 - h) \ \text{ if } y = 0. \]

True or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) If \(y = 1\) and the model outputs \(h = 1\), the cost is 0.

(b) If \(y = 1\) and the model outputs \(h \to 0\), the cost stays bounded, at most 1.

(c) For \(y = 0\) the cost is a decreasing function of \(h\).

(d) The combined form \(J = -\frac{1}{m} \sum [y \log h + (1 - y) \log(1 - h)]\) is just a compact way of writing the two cases, because exactly one of the two terms is switched on for each example.

Hint

Sketch \(-\log h\) on \((0, 1]\). What happens near \(h = 0\)?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(-\log 1 = 0\), so a fully confident correct prediction costs nothing.

(b) False. \(-\log h \to +\infty\) as \(h \to 0\). A confident wrong prediction is punished without limit; for example \(h = 0.01\) already costs

\[ -\ln 0.01 \approx 4.61. \]

(c) False. For \(y = 0\) the cost is \(-\log(1 - h)\), which increases as \(h\) rises towards 1. Predicting a high probability of class 1 for a true 0 is what gets punished.

(d) True. When \(y = 1\) the \((1 - y)\) term vanishes, and when \(y = 0\) the \(y\) term vanishes.

Key insight: Cross-entropy charges almost nothing for confident correct answers and an unbounded amount for confident wrong ones. That asymmetry is what pushes the model to fix its worst mistakes first.

P4.6 L2 · Computation

Log-loss on four predictions

A model gives these probabilities of class 1 (natural logs throughout):

Example \(y\) \(h\)
1 1 0.9
2 1 0.6
3 0 0.2
4 0 0.7

(a) Compute each example's cost and the mean cross-entropy \(J\).

(b) Which example contributes most, and is it classified correctly at threshold 0.5?

(c) Example 2's \(h\) drops to 0.01 and nothing else changes. What is example 2's new cost?

Hint

Use \(-\ln h\) for \(y = 1\) and \(-\ln(1 - h)\) for \(y = 0\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The costs are:

  • Example 1: \(-\ln 0.9 \approx 0.1054\)
  • Example 2: \(-\ln 0.6 \approx 0.5108\)
  • Example 3: \(-\ln 0.8 \approx 0.2231\)
  • Example 4: \(-\ln 0.3 \approx 1.2040\)

They sum to 2.0433, so

\[ J \approx \mathbf{0.511}. \]

(b) Example 4 contributes most (1.204). It is misclassified: \(h = 0.7 \ge 0.5\) predicts 1, but \(y = 0\).

(c) \(-\ln 0.01 \approx\) 4.61, more than twice the total of all four original costs.

Key insight: The mean log-loss is dominated by the examples the model gets confidently wrong, so a single badly mispredicted point can outweigh many good ones.

P4.7 L2 · Computation

One gradient-descent step by hand

Three training points with one feature (\(x_0 = 1\) is the bias input):

\(x\) \(y\)
1 0
2 1
4 1

The current weights are \(w_0 = -1\) and \(w_1 = 0.5\), and the learning rate is \(\eta = 0.5\). Use the batch update

\[ w_j \leftarrow w_j - \eta \cdot \frac{1}{m} \sum_i (h(x_i) - y_i)\, x_{ij}. \]

(a) Compute \(z\), \(h\) and \(h - y\) for each point.

(b) Compute both partial derivatives and the updated weights.

(c) Compute the mean cross-entropy before and after the update. Did the step help?

Hint

\(z = -1 + 0.5x\) gives \(-0.5\), 0 and 1. For the \(w_0\) derivative, use \(x_{i0} = 1\) for every point.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The three points give:

  • \(x = 1\): \(z = -0.5\), \(h \approx 0.3775\), \(h - y \approx +0.3775\)
  • \(x = 2\): \(z = 0\), \(h = 0.5\), \(h - y = -0.5\)
  • \(x = 4\): \(z = 1\), \(h \approx 0.7311\), \(h - y \approx -0.2689\)

(b) The partial derivatives are:

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0} &= \frac{0.3775 - 0.5 - 0.2689}{3} \approx -0.1305 \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1} &= \frac{0.3775 \cdot 1 - 0.5 \cdot 2 - 0.2689 \cdot 4}{3} \approx -0.5661 \end{aligned} \]

The updated weights are \(w_0 \approx -1 + 0.5 \cdot 0.1305 \approx -0.935\) and \(w_1 \approx 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot 0.5661 \approx 0.783\).

(c) \(J\) drops from \(\approx 0.4935\) to \(\approx 0.3840\), so yes, the step helped. The new probabilities are about 0.462, 0.653 and 0.900, and the point \(x = 1\) (\(y = 0\)) is now below 0.5, so all three points are classified correctly.

Key insight: The logistic update has the same form as the linear-regression update, error times input, except that the "prediction" is \(\sigma(w^\top x)\) instead of \(w^\top x\).

P4.8 L2 · Computation

Turning coefficients into odds statements

A credit model has log-odds of default

\[ z = -3 + 0.4 \cdot L - 0.02 \cdot I, \]

where \(L\) is the number of late payments in the last year and \(I\) is annual income in thousands.

(a) By what factor do the odds of default change for each extra late payment?

(b) By what factor do they change for each extra 10 thousand of income?

(c) A customer has \(L = 5\) and \(I = 50\). Compute the probability of default, then the odds, then the probability after one more late payment.

(d) Is it true that one more late payment multiplies the probability of default by the factor from (a)?

Hint
