(b) Compute \(P(\text{fraud} \mid A)\). Compare it with \(P(A \mid \text{fraud})\).

(c) A second, independent rule with the same error rates also fires. Using the answer to (b) as the new prior, compute \(P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{both alerts})\).

Hint

\(P(A) = P(A \mid \text{fraud}) P(\text{fraud}) + P(A \mid \text{legit}) P(\text{legit})\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ P(A) = 0.95 \times 0.002 + 0.03 \times 0.998 = 0.0019 + 0.02994 = \mathbf{0.03184}. \]

(b)

\[ P(\text{fraud} \mid A) = \frac{0.0019}{0.03184} = \mathbf{0.0597}. \]

Only about 6% of alerts are real fraud, although \(P(A \mid \text{fraud}) = 0.95\). The 3% false-alarm rate applied to 99.8% of transactions produces far more alerts than the 95% hit rate applied to 0.2%.

(c) With prior 0.0597:

\[ P(\text{fraud} \mid A_1, A_2) = \frac{0.95 \times 0.0597}{0.95 \times 0.0597 + 0.03 \times 0.9403} = \mathbf{0.668}. \]

Key insight: A posterior is pulled down by a small prior; one alert lifts fraud from 0.2% to 6%, and a second independent alert, with the old posterior as the new prior, lifts it to 67%.

P8.13 L3 · Application

Three kinds of coin: MLE, MAP and Bayes optimal

A mint makes three kinds of token. The probability of heads for each kind and the share of tokens of that kind are:

Kind \(h\) \(P(\text{H} \mid h)\) Prior \(P(h)\)
\(h_1\) 0.2 0.3
\(h_2\) 0.6 0.5
\(h_3\) 0.9 0.2

A token is drawn at random and tossed three times: \(D = \{\text{H}, \text{T}, \text{T}\}\).

(a) Compute \(P(D \mid h)\) for each kind. Which is \(h_{\text{MLE}}\)?

(b) Compute the posteriors \(P(h \mid D)\). Which is \(h_{\text{MAP}}\), and why does it differ from \(h_{\text{MLE}}\)?

(c) Predict the next toss using \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) alone, and using the Bayes optimal classifier. Do they agree?

(d) What are \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) and the Bayes optimal prediction if the prior is uniform?

(e) Suppose instead 30 tosses give 10 heads. The posteriors become about 0.914, 0.086 and 0.000. What happens to \(h_{\text{MAP}}\), and why?

Hint

\(P(D \mid h) = p (1 - p)^2\) for one head and two tails. For (c), \(P(\text{H} \mid D) = \sum_h P(\text{H} \mid h) P(h \mid D)\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(P(D \mid h_1) = 0.2 \times 0.8^2 = 0.128\), \(P(D \mid h_2) = 0.6 \times 0.4^2 = 0.096\), \(P(D \mid h_3) = 0.9 \times 0.1^2 = 0.009\). \(h_{\text{MLE}} = h_1\).

(b) Likelihood times prior: \(0.0384\), \(0.0480\), \(0.0018\), summing to \(P(D) = 0.0882\). So

\[ P(h_1 \mid D) = 0.435, \qquad P(h_2 \mid D) = 0.544, \qquad P(h_3 \mid D) = 0.020. \]

\(h_{\text{MAP}} = h_2\). \(h_1\) explains the data better (0.128 against 0.096), but \(h_2\) tokens are much more common (0.5 against 0.3), and with only three tosses the prior wins.

(c) \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) says \(P(\text{H}) = 0.6\), so it predicts heads. The Bayes optimal classifier computes

\[ P(\text{H} \mid D) = 0.2(0.435) + 0.6(0.544) + 0.9(0.020) = \mathbf{0.432}, \]

so it predicts tails. They disagree: \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) ignores the 44% of posterior mass on \(h_1\), which expects tails strongly.

(d) With a uniform prior the posterior is proportional to the likelihood: 0.549, 0.412, 0.039. \(h_{\text{MAP}} = h_1 = h_{\text{MLE}}\), and \(P(\text{H} \mid D) = 0.392\), so the Bayes optimal prediction is tails (now in agreement with \(h_{\text{MAP}}\)).

(e) \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) moves to \(h_1\) (posterior 0.914), agreeing with \(h_{\text{MLE}}\). The likelihood ratio grows with every toss (here \(1.18 \times 10^{-9}\) against \(6.6 \times 10^{-11}\), a factor of about 18) while the prior ratio stays at 0.6, so the data overwhelm the prior.

Key insight: MLE, MAP and Bayes optimal answer three different questions; they can give three different answers on scarce data, and they converge as data accumulate.

P8.14 L3 · Application

Four hypotheses, three instances

After training, four deterministic hypotheses have posteriors \(P(h_1 \mid D) = 0.4\), \(P(h_2 \mid D) = 0.3\), \(P(h_3 \mid D) = 0.2\), \(P(h_4 \mid D) = 0.1\). Their labels on three new instances are:

\(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(x_3\)
\(h_1\) + − −
\(h_2\) − + −
\(h_3\) − − +
\(h_4\) − + +

(a) Give the label predicted by \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) on each instance.

(b) Compute \(P(+ \mid x, D)\) on each instance and give the Bayes optimal labels. Is the Bayes optimal labelling one of the four hypotheses?

(c) Assume the true labelling is itself one of the four hypotheses, drawn according to the posterior. Compute the expected error of \(h_{\text{MAP}}\), of the Bayes optimal classifier and of the Gibbs classifier on each instance, and their averages over the three instances.

(d) Check the bound \(E[\text{error}_{\text{Gibbs}}] \le 2\, E[\text{error}_{\text{Bayes optimal}}]\).

Hint

Write \(q = P(+ \mid x, D)\). If the truth is + with probability \(q\), a fixed prediction of + is wrong with probability \(1 - q\). Gibbs predicts + with probability \(q\), independently of the truth.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(h_{\text{MAP}} = h_1\): (+, −, −).

(b) \(q(x_1) = 0.4\) (only \(h_1\)), \(q(x_2) = 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4\), \(q(x_3) = 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3\). All are below 0.5, so the Bayes optimal labels are (−, −, −), which is not any of the four hypotheses. It disagrees with \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) on \(x_1\).

(c) Expected errors:

\(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(x_3\) Average
\(h_{\text{MAP}}\) \(1 - 0.4 = 0.6\) 0.4 0.3 0.433
Bayes optimal, \(\min(q, 1 - q)\) 0.4 0.4 0.3 0.367
Gibbs, \(2q(1 - q)\) 0.48 0.48 0.42 0.460

(d) \(0.460 \le 2 \times 0.367 = 0.733\). The bound holds, with room to spare. Gibbs is worse than both deterministic rules here, but it only needs one hypothesis per prediction.

Key insight: The Bayes optimal classifier votes instance by instance, so it can beat every hypothesis in \(H\), including \(h_{\text{MAP}}\); Gibbs gives up some accuracy for speed, but never more than a factor of two in expectation.

P8.15 L4 · Analysis

Why Gibbs is at most twice as bad

Consider a binary label at a single instance \(x\), and let \(q = P(+ \mid x, D) = \sum_{h:\, h(x) = +} P(h \mid D)\). Assume, as in the Haussler et al. result, that the true labelling is drawn according to the same posterior, so the true label is + with probability \(q\).

(a) Show that the Bayes optimal classifier's error at \(x\) is \(\min(q, 1 - q)\) and the Gibbs classifier's error at \(x\) is \(2q(1 - q)\).

(b) Prove that \(2q(1 - q) \le 2\min(q, 1 - q)\), and extend the result to the expected error over instances.

(c) Fill in the table and describe when the ratio \(\frac{\text{error}_{\text{Gibbs}}}{\text{error}_{\text{Bayes optimal}}}\) is close to 1 and when it is close to 2.

\(q\) 0.05 0.20 0.35 0.50
Bayes optimal error
Gibbs error
Ratio

(d) With 10,000 hypotheses, how many hypothesis evaluations does each classifier need per prediction?

Hint

Gibbs errs if it samples + while the truth is −, or samples − while the truth is +; the two draws are independent. Then use \(\max(q, 1 - q) \le 1\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Bayes optimal predicts + exactly when \(q > 0.5\), so it is wrong with probability \(1 - q\) if \(q > 0.5\) and \(q\) otherwise: \(\min(q, 1 - q)\). Gibbs predicts + with probability \(q\), independently of the truth, so

\[ P(\text{Gibbs wrong}) = q(1 - q) + (1 - q)q = \mathbf{2q(1 - q)}. \]

(b) Write \(m = \min(q, 1 - q)\) and \(M = \max(q, 1 - q)\). Then \(q(1 - q) = mM\) and

\[ 2q(1 - q) = 2mM \le 2m \quad \text{because } M \le 1. \]

The inequality holds at every \(x\), so taking expectations over instances gives \(E[\text{error}_{\text{Gibbs}}] \le 2\, E[\text{error}_{\text{Bayes optimal}}]\).

(c)

\(q\) 0.05 0.20 0.35 0.50
Bayes optimal error 0.05 0.20 0.35 0.50
Gibbs error 0.095 0.32 0.455 0.50
Ratio 1.9 1.6 1.3 1.0

The ratio is \(2M\): close to 1 when the hypotheses are split evenly (\(q \approx 0.5\), both classifiers are near coin-flipping), and close to 2 when the posterior is nearly unanimous (\(q \to 0\) or 1), where both errors are tiny anyway.

(d) Bayes optimal: 10,000 evaluations (one per hypothesis, the slides' "linear in the number of candidate hypotheses"). Gibbs: 1 (plus one draw from the posterior).

Key insight: The factor 2 comes from Gibbs paying \(2mM\) instead of \(m\); it is worst exactly when the posterior is confident, which is also when the absolute errors are smallest.

10.C Naïve Bayes Classifier (8.3)

P8.16 L1 · Foundation

What is "naïve" about Naïve Bayes?

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "Naïve Bayes assumes that the features are independent of each other."

(b) "Naïve Bayes assumes that the features are independent of each other given the class, so \(P(X_1, \dots, X_n \mid Y) = \prod_i P(X_i \mid Y)\)."

(c) "Naïve Bayes is a generative model: it learns \(P(Y)\) and \(P(X \mid Y)\), and gets \(P(Y \mid X)\) from Bayes' theorem."

(d) "To classify, Naïve Bayes must compute \(P(X)\) for the new instance."

(e) "Training a discrete Naïve Bayes model is just counting; it needs no iterative optimisation."

(f) "If the independence assumption is violated, the predicted class is necessarily wrong."

Hint

Two features can be strongly related overall and still independent once the class is known (and vice versa).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) False. The assumption is conditional independence given \(Y\). The features may be strongly related overall, for example because both depend on the class.

(b) True. This is the Naïve Bayes assumption, and it is what makes the model feasible (P8.25).

(c) True. It models how the data are generated in each class, then reverses the conditioning with Bayes' theorem.

(d) False. \(P(X)\) is the same for every class, so the argmax of \(P(Y = c) \prod_i P(x_i \mid c)\) is enough. \(P(X)\) is needed only if you want normalised posteriors, and then it is just the sum of the scores.

(e) True. The MLE of each table entry is a relative frequency (P8.2), so training is a single pass of counting.

(f) False. The probabilities become miscalibrated, but the argmax is often still correct (P8.31).

Key insight: "Naïve" means one specific, strong assumption, conditional independence given the class; it buys a model that trains by counting, at the cost of probabilities that can be overconfident.

P8.17 L1 · Foundation

Which Naïve Bayes for which feature?

For each data set, name the Naïve Bayes variant that fits it (Gaussian, Multinomial, Bernoulli or Categorical, as in the slides' summary table with the scikit-learn classes GaussianNB, MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB, CategoricalNB) and say how \(P(x_i \mid y)\) is estimated.

(a) Customer records with Plan \(\in\) {Basic, Standard, Premium} and Region \(\in\) {North, South, East, West}.

(b) Iris-like measurements: petal length and sepal width in centimetres.

(c) Product reviews represented by how many times each vocabulary word occurs.

(d) Short SMS messages represented by a 0/1 flag per vocabulary word ("does the word occur?").

(e) A data set with blood pressure (mmHg) and smoker (yes/no) together.

Hint

Look at what one feature value is: a category, a real number, a count, or a presence flag.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Categorical NB. A look-up table of class-conditional frequencies per value, with Laplace smoothing \(\frac{N_{vc} + 1}{N_c + d}\).

(b) Gaussian NB. One \(N(\mu_{ik}, \sigma^2_{ik})\) per (feature, class), with the per-class mean and variance estimated from the data.

(c) Multinomial NB. \(P(w \mid c) = \frac{\text{count}(w, c) + 1}{\text{tokens in } c + \lvert V \rvert}\); every occurrence of a word contributes.

(d) Bernoulli NB. \(P(w \text{ present} \mid c) = \frac{\text{docs of } c \text{ with } w + 1}{N_c + 2}\); absent words also contribute a factor \(1 - p\).

(e) A mixed model: a Gaussian factor for blood pressure and a categorical (Bernoulli) factor for smoker, multiplied together under the same conditional-independence assumption (as in P8.23).

Key insight: Naïve Bayes is a family; the class prior and the product rule stay the same, and only the per-feature model \(P(x_i \mid y)\) changes with the type of the feature.

P8.18 L1 · Foundation

Bag of words and the two text models

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "In the bag-of-words representation, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' are the same document."

(b) "In the multinomial model, a word that appears five times in a test document contributes its probability \(P(w \mid c)\) five times."

(c) "In the Bernoulli model, words of the vocabulary that do not appear in the test document have no effect on the classification."

(d) "In the multinomial model, the Laplace denominator adds the vocabulary size \(\lvert V \rvert\) to the number of tokens in the class."

(e) "In the Bernoulli model, the Laplace denominator adds \(\lvert V \rvert\) to the number of documents in the class."

(f) "A word that occurs in a test document but never in the training data should be dropped from the computation."

Hint

The multinomial model is a model of token draws; the Bernoulli model is a model of one yes/no coin per vocabulary word.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. Only word counts are kept; word order is discarded.

(b) True. The likelihood is \(\prod_{\text{tokens}} P(u_j \mid c)\), so a repeated word appears repeatedly in the product, as \(P(w \mid c)^5\).

(c) False. Each absent word contributes \(1 - P(w \text{ present} \mid c)\). Absence is evidence; this is a main difference from the multinomial model.

(d) True. \(P(w \mid c) = \frac{\text{count}(w, c) + 1}{\text{tokens in } c + \lvert V \rvert}\), so the smoothed probabilities over the vocabulary sum to 1.

(e) False. Each word's Bernoulli variable has only two outcomes, so the denominator is \(N_c + 2\).

(f) True (the standard practice). The vocabulary \(V\) is fixed at training time. An unseen word has count 0 in every class, so it carries no information about the class; keeping it would only add a factor \(\frac{1}{\text{tokens in } c + \lvert V \rvert}\) that depends on the class's size, not on the content.

Key insight: The multinomial model counts how often each word is used; the Bernoulli model records which vocabulary words are used and which are not; that difference alone can flip a decision (P8.24).

P8.19 L2 · Computation

Discrete Naïve Bayes from a 12-row table

A gym records whether members renewed their membership:

# Age Visits Contract Renew
1 Young High Annual Yes
2 Young Low Monthly No
3 Middle High Monthly Yes
4 Senior Low Annual Yes
5 Middle Low Monthly No
6 Young High Monthly Yes
7 Senior Low Monthly No
8 Middle High Annual Yes
9 Young Low Annual No
10 Senior High Annual Yes
11 Middle Low Monthly Yes
12 Young Low Monthly No

A new member has Age = Middle, Visits = Low, Contract = Annual.

(a) Compute the class priors.

(b) Build the likelihood entries needed for this member, \(P(\text{Middle} \mid c)\), \(P(\text{Low} \mid c)\) and \(P(\text{Annual} \mid c)\), for both classes (no smoothing).

(c) Compute both scores, the predicted class and \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x)\).

Hint

Every likelihood is "count within the class divided by the class size": the denominators are 7 for Yes and 5 for No.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(P(\text{Yes}) = 7/12\), \(P(\text{No}) = 5/12\).

(b)

Yes (7 rows) No (5 rows)
\(P(\text{Middle} \mid c)\) 3/7 (rows 3, 8, 11) 1/5 (row 5)
\(P(\text{Low} \mid c)\) 2/7 (rows 4, 11) 5/5
\(P(\text{Annual} \mid c)\) 4/7 (rows 1, 4, 8, 10) 1/5 (row 9)

(c)

\[ \text{Score(Yes)} = \frac{7}{12} \cdot \frac{3}{7} \cdot \frac{2}{7} \cdot \frac{4}{7} = \mathbf{0.04082}, \qquad \text{Score(No)} = \frac{5}{12} \cdot \frac{1}{5} \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \mathbf{0.01667}. \]

Predict Renew = Yes, with

\[ P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = \frac{0.04082}{0.04082 + 0.01667} = \mathbf{0.710}. \]

(scikit-learn's CategoricalNB with a negligible \(\alpha\) gives the same 0.710.) Low visits point strongly to No (every non-renewer had low visits), but the annual contract and the middle age group point to Yes and outweigh it.

Key insight: Discrete Naïve Bayes is counting plus multiplication: prior times one table entry per attribute, then compare; each attribute casts a multiplicative vote.

P8.20 L2 · Computation

Laplace smoothing and the m-estimate

In class \(c\) there are \(N_c = 8\) training examples. The attribute Payment has \(d = 4\) values with these counts in class \(c\):

Card UPI Cash Cheque
5 3 0 0

The m-estimate is \(P(A_i \mid c) = \frac{N_{ic} + m\,p}{N_c + m}\), where \(p\) is a prior estimate of the probability and \(m\) the equivalent sample size.

(a) Give the MLE estimates. What happens to a test instance in class \(c\) that pays by cash?

(b) Give the Laplace (add-one) estimates and check that they sum to 1.

(c) Give the m-estimates with \(m = 2\) and \(p = 1/4\).

(d) Across all customers, the payment shares are Card 0.4, UPI 0.3, Cash 0.2, Cheque 0.1. Give the m-estimates with \(m = 5\) and these values as \(p\).

(e) Show that Laplace smoothing is the m-estimate with particular values of \(m\) and \(p\).

Hint

The m-estimate adds \(m\) imaginary examples, distributed over the values in proportions \(p\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) 5/8, 3/8, 0, 0. A cash payer gets \(P(\text{Cash} \mid c) = 0\), so the whole score for class \(c\) is 0, whatever the other attributes say: the zero-frequency problem.

(b) \(\frac{N_{ic} + 1}{8 + 4}\): 6/12 = 0.500, 4/12 = 0.333, 1/12 = 0.083, 1/12 = 0.083, which sum to \(12/12 = 1\).

(c) \(\frac{N_{ic} + 0.5}{10}\): 0.55, 0.35, 0.05, 0.05.

(d) \(\frac{N_{ic} + 5p}{13}\):

\[ \frac{5 + 2}{13} = \mathbf{0.538}, \quad \frac{3 + 1.5}{13} = \mathbf{0.346}, \quad \frac{0 + 1}{13} = \mathbf{0.077}, \quad \frac{0 + 0.5}{13} = \mathbf{0.038}. \]

Unseen values now get probabilities in proportion to how common they are in the population, instead of equal shares.

(e) With \(m = d\) and \(p = 1/d\), \(m p = 1\) and \(\frac{N_{ic} + 1}{N_c + d}\) is exactly the Laplace estimate (here \(m = 4\), \(p = 1/4\)).

Key insight: Smoothing is MAP estimation with imaginary examples (P8.7): Laplace spreads \(d\) pseudo-counts evenly, the m-estimate lets you choose how many (\(m\)) and how to spread them (\(p\)).

P8.21 L2 · Computation

Gaussian Naïve Bayes with two sensors

A pump is monitored by its temperature (°C) and vibration (mm/s). Past readings:

Class Temperature Vibration
Normal 60, 62, 65, 63, 60 2.0, 2.4, 1.8, 2.2, 2.1
Faulty 70, 74, 69 3.5, 2.9, 3.2

(Within each class, the \(j\)-th temperature and the \(j\)-th vibration come from the same reading.) A new reading is Temperature = 66, Vibration = 2.6.

(a) Compute the priors and, for each (feature, class) pair, the mean and the sample variance.

(b) Evaluate the four Gaussian densities \(N(x; \mu, s^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi s^2}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 s^2}\right)\) at the new reading.

(c) Compute both scores, the predicted class and \(P(\text{Normal} \mid x)\).

(d) A density value of 0.146 is not a probability. Why may it still be used inside Naïve Bayes?

Hint

Four separate one-dimensional Gaussians are needed: one per feature per class. The two features of a class are never combined into one covariance.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(P(\text{Normal}) = 5/8\), \(P(\text{Faulty}) = 3/8\).

Temperature \(\mu\), \(s^2\) Vibration \(\mu\), \(s^2\)
Normal 62, 4.5 (deviations −2, 0, 3, 1, −2; sum of squares 18) 2.1, 0.05 (sum of squares 0.20)
Faulty 71, 7 (deviations −1, 3, −2; sum of squares 14) 3.2, 0.09 (sum of squares 0.18)

(b)

\[ \begin{aligned} N(66; 62, 4.5) &= \mathbf{0.0318}, & N(2.6; 2.1, 0.05) &= \mathbf{0.1464}, \\ N(66; 71, 7) &= \mathbf{0.0253}, & N(2.6; 3.2, 0.09) &= \mathbf{0.1800}. \end{aligned} \]

(c)

\[ \text{Score(Normal)} = \frac{5}{8} (0.0318)(0.1464) = \mathbf{0.00291}, \qquad \text{Score(Faulty)} = \frac{3}{8} (0.0253)(0.1800) = \mathbf{0.00171}. \]

Predict Normal, with \(P(\text{Normal} \mid x) = \frac{0.00291}{0.00291 + 0.00171} = \mathbf{0.630}\). Both features are about two standard deviations from each class mean, so the larger prior of Normal decides.

(d) The density is \(P(x \le X \le x + dx \mid c) / dx\) for a tiny \(dx\). The same \(dx\) appears in every class's score and cancels in the comparison and in the normalisation, so densities can stand in for probabilities. (A density can even exceed 1 when \(s^2\) is small.)

Key insight: Gaussian NB replaces each count table by a per-class mean and variance; the rest (prior times product, then argmax) is unchanged.

P8.22 L3 · Application

Churn prediction with a zero count

A telecom operator records 14 customers:

# Plan Usage Support calls Contract Churn
1 Basic Low 3+ Monthly Yes
2 Basic Low 3+ Monthly Yes
3 Standard Low 1–2 Monthly Yes
4 Basic High 3+ Monthly Yes
5 Standard Low 3+ Annual Yes
6 Basic Low 1–2 Monthly Yes
7 Premium High 0 Annual No
8 Premium High 1–2 Annual No
9 Standard High 0 Monthly No
10 Premium Low 0 Annual No
11 Basic High 0 Annual No
12 Standard High 1–2 Annual No
13 Premium High 3+ Monthly No
14 Basic Low 0 Annual No

Classify the customer {Plan = Premium, Usage = Low, Support calls = 3+, Contract = Monthly}.

(a) Using MLE (unsmoothed) estimates, compute both scores. What is predicted, and why is that prediction untrustworthy?

(b) Apply Laplace smoothing to the conditional probabilities (Plan and Support calls have 3 values, Usage and Contract have 2). Compute both scores, the predicted class and \(P(\text{Churn} = \text{Yes} \mid x)\).

(c) As a diagnostic, drop the Plan attribute and recompute the unsmoothed scores. What does this show about the effect of one zero?

Hint

No churner in the training data was on the Premium plan, so one factor of the Yes score is \(0/6\).

Answer & Key Insight

Priors: \(P(\text{Yes}) = 6/14\), \(P(\text{No}) = 8/14\).

(a) Unsmoothed:

\[ \text{Yes}: \frac{6}{14} \cdot \frac{0}{6} \cdot \frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{4}{6} \cdot \frac{5}{6} = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \text{No}: \frac{8}{14} \cdot \frac{4}{8} \cdot \frac{2}{8} \cdot \frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{2}{8} = \mathbf{0.00223}. \]

The model predicts No with \(P(\text{No} \mid x) = 1\). It is untrustworthy because a single unseen combination (Premium among six churners) vetoes three attributes that all point strongly to Yes (low usage, many support calls, monthly contract).

(b) Laplace, \(\frac{N_{vc} + 1}{N_c + d}\):

Premium Low 3+ Monthly
Yes (\(N_c = 6\)) \(1/9\) \(6/8\) \(5/9\) \(6/8\)
No (\(N_c = 8\)) \(5/11\) \(3/10\) \(2/11\) \(3/10\)

\[ \text{Yes}: \frac{6}{14} \cdot \frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{6}{8} \cdot \frac{5}{9} \cdot \frac{6}{8} = \mathbf{0.01488}, \qquad \text{No}: \frac{8}{14} \cdot \frac{5}{11} \cdot \frac{3}{10} \cdot \frac{2}{11} \cdot \frac{3}{10} = \mathbf{0.00425}. \]

Predict Churn = Yes, with \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = \frac{0.01488}{0.01488 + 0.00425} = \mathbf{0.778}\) (scikit-learn's CategoricalNB(alpha=1) agrees). Smoothing reverses the decision.

(c) Without Plan: Yes \(= \frac{6}{14} \cdot \frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{4}{6} \cdot \frac{5}{6} = 0.198\) and No \(= \frac{8}{14} \cdot \frac{2}{8} \cdot \frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{2}{8} = 0.00446\), so \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = 0.978\). Together with the priors, the other three attributes favour Yes by a factor of about 44; the unsmoothed zero alone turned that into a certain No.

Key insight: Because Naïve Bayes multiplies, one zero count is a veto; Laplace smoothing turns "never seen in 6 examples" into "rare" (1/9), which lets the remaining evidence speak.

P8.23 L3 · Application

Mixed features: income and employment type

A lender's records of 10 applicants (income in thousand dollars per month):

Approved Income Employment
Yes 5.2 Salaried
Yes 6.8 Salaried
Yes 4.5 Self-employed
Yes 7.5 Salaried
Yes 6.0 Self-employed
Yes 6.0 Salaried
No 3.0 Self-employed
No 4.8 Salaried
No 2.6 Self-employed
No 3.6 Self-employed

Use a Gaussian factor for Income (sample variance) and a count table for Employment (no smoothing needed).

(a) Compute the priors, the per-class mean and sample variance of Income, and \(P(\text{Self-employed} \mid c)\).

(b) Classify a self-employed applicant with Income = 4.6, and give \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x)\).

(c) Classify a salaried applicant with the same income.

(d) For a self-employed applicant, the posterior of Yes crosses 0.5 at an income of about 4.89 (between the two class means). For a salaried applicant it crosses at about 4.14. Explain in words why the threshold moves.

(e) Would the answer to (b) change if the population variance (divide by \(N_k\)) were used? (With it, \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = 0.329\).)

Hint

The Employment factor multiplies the Gaussian factor; a factor that favours one class has to be overcome by the income evidence.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(P(\text{Yes}) = 0.6\), \(P(\text{No}) = 0.4\).

Yes: \(\mu = 36.0/6 = \mathbf{6.0}\), sum of squared deviations 5.78, \(s^2 = \mathbf{1.156}\); \(P(\text{Self} \mid \text{Yes}) = \mathbf{2/6}\).

No: \(\mu = 14.0/4 = \mathbf{3.5}\), sum of squared deviations 2.76, \(s^2 = \mathbf{0.92}\); \(P(\text{Self} \mid \text{No}) = \mathbf{3/4}\).

(b) \(N(4.6; 6.0, 1.156) = 0.1589\) and \(N(4.6; 3.5, 0.92) = 0.2155\).

\[ \text{Score(Yes)} = 0.6 \cdot \frac{2}{6} \cdot 0.1589 = \mathbf{0.0318}, \qquad \text{Score(No)} = 0.4 \cdot \frac{3}{4} \cdot 0.2155 = \mathbf{0.0646}. \]

Predict No, \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = \mathbf{0.330}\).

(c) \(P(\text{Salaried} \mid \text{Yes}) = 4/6\), \(P(\text{Salaried} \mid \text{No}) = 1/4\):

\[ \text{Score(Yes)} = 0.6 \cdot \frac{4}{6} \cdot 0.1589 = 0.0636, \qquad \text{Score(No)} = 0.4 \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot 0.2155 = 0.0215. \]

Predict Yes, \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = \mathbf{0.747}\).

(d) Being self-employed multiplies the odds of Yes by \(\frac{2/6}{3/4} = 0.44\); being salaried multiplies them by \(\frac{4/6}{1/4} = 2.67\). A self-employed applicant needs stronger income evidence (a higher income) to reach even odds, so the threshold moves up for self-employed and down for salaried applicants.

(e) No. The posterior barely moves (0.330 to 0.329); with these class sizes the two variance conventions give almost the same densities.

Key insight: In a mixed Naïve Bayes model each feature contributes one multiplicative factor of its own type; a categorical factor shifts the decision threshold on the continuous feature.

P8.24 L3 · Application

Multinomial against Bernoulli on a tiny corpus

Vocabulary \(V = \{\text{goal}, \text{match}, \text{team}, \text{vote}, \text{party}\}\). Training documents:

Doc Text Class
d1 goal match goal team Sports
d2 match team team Sports
d3 goal match Sports
d4 vote party vote team Politics
d5 party vote Politics

Classify the test document "team team team vote" with Laplace smoothing under:

(a) the multinomial model;

(b) the Bernoulli model.

(c) Explain why the two models disagree.

(d) Under the multinomial model, classify "team vote" (each word once). What does this show?

Hint

Multinomial: count tokens per class (Sports has 9, Politics has 6). Bernoulli: count documents containing each word (Sports has 3 documents, Politics 2), and remember the absent words.

Answer & Key Insight

Priors: \(P(S) = 3/5\), \(P(P) = 2/5\).

(a) Sports tokens: goal 3, match 3, team 3 (9 in all). Politics tokens: vote 3, party 2, team 1 (6 in all). With \(\lvert V \rvert = 5\):

\[ P(\text{team} \mid S) = \frac{3 + 1}{9 + 5} = \frac{4}{14}, \quad P(\text{vote} \mid S) = \frac{1}{14}, \quad P(\text{team} \mid P) = \frac{1 + 1}{6 + 5} = \frac{2}{11}, \quad P(\text{vote} \mid P) = \frac{4}{11}. \]

\[ \text{Sports}: \frac{3}{5} \left(\frac{4}{14}\right)^3 \frac{1}{14} = \mathbf{0.00100}, \qquad \text{Politics}: \frac{2}{5} \left(\frac{2}{11}\right)^3 \frac{4}{11} = \mathbf{0.00087}. \]

Multinomial predicts Sports, \(P(S \mid d) = 0.533\).

(b) Document frequencies, smoothed by \(\frac{n + 1}{N_c + 2}\):

goal match team vote party
Sports (3 docs) 3/5 4/5 3/5 1/5 1/5
Politics (2 docs) 1/4 1/4 2/4 3/4 3/4

The test document has team and vote present, and goal, match and party absent:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Sports}: &\ \tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(1 - \tfrac{4}{5}\right) \cdot \tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{1}{5} \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}\right) = \mathbf{0.00461}, \\ \text{Politics}: &\ \tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{4}\right)\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{4}\right) \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} \cdot \tfrac{3}{4} \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{3}{4}\right) = \mathbf{0.02109}. \end{aligned} \]

Bernoulli predicts Politics, \(P(P \mid d) = 0.821\). (scikit-learn's MultinomialNB(alpha=1) and BernoulliNB(alpha=1) give 0.533 and 0.821.)

(c) The multinomial model counts "team" three times, and team is more frequent among Sports tokens, so the repetition outweighs "vote". The Bernoulli model ignores repetition (team is just "present", in 2 of the 3 Sports documents and 1 of the 2 Politics documents, so it is weak evidence) but uses absences: goal and match are absent, which is typical of Politics and unusual for Sports.

(d) \(\frac{3}{5} \cdot \frac{4}{14} \cdot \frac{1}{14} = 0.0122\) against \(\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{2}{11} \cdot \frac{4}{11} = 0.0264\): Politics, \(P(P \mid d) = 0.684\). The multinomial verdict in (a) rests entirely on the word count.

Key insight: Multinomial NB listens to how often words are used, Bernoulli NB to which words are used and which are missing; on short or repetitive texts this design choice can decide the class.

P8.25 L4 · Analysis

Why the independence assumption is needed: counting parameters

(a) A classifier has a binary class \(Y\) and \(n\) binary features. How many free parameters are needed to store \(P(Y)\) and the full joint \(P(X_1, \dots, X_n \mid Y)\)? How many does Naïve Bayes need?

(b) Evaluate both for \(n = 10\), \(n = 30\), and for the slides' digit task (5 against 6) with \(28 \times 28 = 784\) binary pixels.

(c) With 1,000 training examples and \(n = 30\), how many examples fall, on average, into each cell of one class's joint table? What does that mean for estimating the joint directly?

(d) Generalise to \(K\) classes and \(n\) features with \(v\) values each.

(e) For \(K = 3\) classes and \(n = 20\) continuous features, compare Gaussian NB with a model that uses one full-covariance Gaussian per class.

Hint

A distribution over \(m\) outcomes has \(m - 1\) free parameters, because the probabilities must sum to 1.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The joint over \(n\) binary features has \(2^n\) outcomes, so \(2^n - 1\) free parameters per class. In total:

\[ \text{Full joint: } 2(2^n - 1) + 1, \qquad \text{Naïve Bayes: } 2n + 1, \]

(one Bernoulli parameter \(P(X_i = 1 \mid Y = y)\) per feature per class, plus the prior).

(b)

\(n\) Full joint Naïve Bayes
10 2,047 21
30 2,147,483,647 61
784 about \(2^{785} \approx 10^{236}\) 1,569

(c) Each class has \(2^{30} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{9}\) cells, so even if all 1,000 examples were in one class there would be about \(9.3 \times 10^{-7}\) examples per cell. Almost every cell is empty, so almost every test instance has an MLE likelihood of 0 (or, with smoothing, the uniform pseudo-count only): the joint cannot be learned. Naïve Bayes estimates each \(P(X_i \mid Y)\) from all examples of the class.

(d) Full joint: \(K(v^n - 1) + (K - 1)\). Naïve Bayes: \(K n (v - 1) + (K - 1)\). Exponential in \(n\) against linear in \(n\).

(e) Gaussian NB: a mean and a variance per (feature, class), \(2nK + (K - 1) = 120 + 2 = \mathbf{122}\). Full covariance: \(K\left(n + \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\right) + (K - 1) = 3(20 + 210) + 2 = \mathbf{692}\). The independence assumption makes each covariance matrix diagonal.

Key insight: The full class-conditional joint grows exponentially with the number of features, so it can never be estimated from realistic data; conditional independence replaces it with \(n\) one-dimensional problems, trading some bias for an enormous reduction in variance.

10.D Naïve Bayes vs Logistic Regression (8.4)

P8.26 L1 · Foundation

Generative or discriminative?

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "Logistic regression models \(P(Y \mid X)\) directly; Naïve Bayes models \(P(Y)\) and \(P(X \mid Y)\) and uses Bayes' theorem."

(b) "A trained Naïve Bayes model can generate synthetic feature vectors for a class; a trained logistic-regression model cannot."

(c) "Every Gaussian Naïve Bayes classifier has exactly the logistic (linear-in-\(x\)) form \(P(Y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i)\)."

(d) "Trained on the same data, Gaussian NB with a shared variance and logistic regression always give the same weights."

(e) "Logistic regression assumes that the features are conditionally independent given the class."

(f) "If a feature is missing for a test instance, Naïve Bayes can simply leave out that feature's factor."

Hint

Ask which distribution each model writes down, and which likelihood each one maximises when it is trained.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. That is the definition of discriminative against generative.

(b) True. Sample \(y\) from \(P(Y)\), then each \(x_i\) from \(P(X_i \mid y)\). Logistic regression has no model of \(X\) at all.

(c) False. Only when each feature's variance is shared by the classes (P8.29). With class-specific variances the log-odds contain \(x_i^2\) terms and the boundary is quadratic.

(d) False. GNB maximises the joint likelihood \(\prod P(x, y)\) by plug-in means and variances; logistic regression maximises the conditional likelihood \(\prod P(y \mid x)\). They agree only in the limit, and only if the GNB assumptions are true (P8.28 shows how they can differ).

(e) False. It makes no assumption about \(P(X \mid Y)\); it only assumes the log-odds are linear in \(x\).

(f) True. Summing \(P(x \mid y)\) over the missing feature's values gives 1 under conditional independence, so its factor drops out. Logistic regression needs imputation.

Key insight: Naïve Bayes tells a story of how the data are generated and reverses it; logistic regression fits the decision directly; with shared Gaussian variances the two stories meet in the same functional form.

P8.27 L2 · Computation

A Gaussian NB posterior, evaluated three ways

A one-feature Gaussian NB model has \(P(Y = 1) = \pi = 0.25\), \(X \mid Y = 0 \sim N(2, 4)\) and \(X \mid Y = 1 \sim N(6, 4)\) (the same variance for both classes).

(a) Using Bayes' theorem directly, compute \(P(Y = 1 \mid x)\) at \(x = 2\), \(x = 4\) and \(x = 6\).

(b) Show that the log-odds \(\log \frac{P(Y = 1 \mid x)}{P(Y = 0 \mid x)}\) are a linear function \(w_0 + w_1 x\), and find \(w_0\) and \(w_1\). Check your three answers from (a) with \(\sigma(w_0 + w_1 x)\).

(c) Where is the decision boundary \(P(Y = 1 \mid x) = 0.5\)? Why is it not at the midpoint \(x = 4\) of the two means?

Hint

In the ratio of the two densities, the normalising constants \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\) cancel because the variance is shared.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Scores \(\pi N(x; 6, 4)\) and \((1 - \pi) N(x; 2, 4)\):

\(x\) Score(1) Score(0) \(P(Y = 1 \mid x)\)
2 0.00675 0.14960 0.043
4 0.03025 0.09074 0.250
6 0.04987 0.02025 0.711

(b)

\[ \log \frac{P(Y = 1 \mid x)}{P(Y = 0 \mid x)} = \log \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} + \frac{(x - 2)^2 - (x - 6)^2}{2 \cdot 4} = \log \frac{1}{3} + \frac{8x - 32}{8} = -1.0986 + x - 4. \]

So \(w_1 = 1\) and \(w_0 = -5.099\). Then \(\sigma(-3.099) = 0.043\), \(\sigma(-1.099) = 0.250\) and \(\sigma(0.901) = 0.711\), matching (a).

(c) \(x = 5.099\). At the midpoint the two densities are equal, so the posterior equals the prior, 0.25 (see the row \(x = 4\)). Because class 1 is rarer, \(x\) must move \(\log 3 / w_1 = 1.099\) further towards class 1's mean before the odds are even.

Key insight: A Gaussian NB with shared variance is a logistic regression in disguise: the prior sets the intercept shift, and the separation of the means relative to the variance sets the slope.

P8.28 L3 · Application

Same form, different fit

One feature, two classes, equal class sizes:

\[ \text{Class 0}: 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5 \qquad \text{Class 1}: 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8 \]

For a shared-variance Gaussian NB, \(P(Y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(w_0 + w_1 x)\) with

\[ w_1 = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{\sigma^2}, \qquad w_0 = \log \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} + \frac{\mu_0^2 - \mu_1^2}{2\sigma^2} \]

(derived in P8.29). Unregularised logistic regression, fitted numerically by maximising the conditional log-likelihood, gives \(w_0 = -7.815\), \(w_1 = 1.748\).

(a) Estimate \(\mu_0\), \(\mu_1\) and the pooled MLE variance \(\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_k \sum_{i \in k} (x_i - \mu_k)^2\). Compute the GNB weights and decision boundary, and compare them with logistic regression's.

(b) A new class-1 example with \(x = 30\) is added (a correct but extreme case). Recompute the GNB weights and boundary. (Logistic regression's refit gives the same weights, \(-7.815\) and \(1.748\), to three decimals.)

(c) Compare \(P(Y = 1 \mid x = 7)\) under GNB before and after the new point, and under logistic regression.

(d) Explain the difference in behaviour in terms of generative against discriminative fitting.

Hint

The new point drags class 1's mean up and inflates the pooled variance. Logistic regression's gradient contribution from a point is \((y_i - \sigma_i) x_i\); what is \(y_i - \sigma_i\) for a point classified correctly with probability almost 1?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\mu_0 = 17/6 = 2.833\) and \(\mu_1 = 6\). The within-class sums of squares are 10.833 and 10, so \(\sigma^2 = 20.833 / 12 = 1.736\). With \(\pi = 0.5\):

\[ w_1 = \frac{6 - 2.833}{1.736} = \mathbf{1.824}, \qquad w_0 = 0 + \frac{2.833^2 - 36}{2 \times 1.736} = \mathbf{-8.056}. \]

The GNB boundary is \(-w_0 / w_1 = \mathbf{4.417}\) (the midpoint of the means); logistic regression's is \(7.815 / 1.748 = \mathbf{4.470}\). Same form, similar but not identical weights.

(b) Now \(N = 13\), \(\pi = 7/13\), \(\mu_1 = 66/7 = 9.429\), and the pooled sum of squares is 514.5, so \(\sigma^2 = 39.58\):

\[ w_1 = \frac{9.429 - 2.833}{39.58} = \mathbf{0.167}, \qquad w_0 = \log \frac{7}{6} + \frac{2.833^2 - 9.429^2}{2 \times 39.58} = \mathbf{-0.867}. \]

The boundary moves to 5.21, and the slope collapses by a factor of 11.

(c) \(P(Y = 1 \mid x = 7)\): GNB before 0.991, GNB after 0.574, logistic regression 0.988 (unchanged).

(d) GNB fits the class-conditional densities: the extreme point is "evidence" that class 1 is wide and far away, so it changes \(\mu_1\) and \(\sigma^2\) and therefore the posterior everywhere. Logistic regression fits only \(P(y \mid x)\): the point is already classified correctly with \(\sigma_i \approx 1\), so \(y_i - \sigma_i \approx 0\) and it barely affects the gradient. When the Gaussian assumption is wrong (as with this outlier), the discriminative fit is more robust; when it is right, GNB uses the data more efficiently.

Key insight: Generative and discriminative models can share the same functional form yet fit different parameters, because they maximise different likelihoods: GNB the joint \(P(x, y)\), logistic regression the conditional \(P(y \mid x)\).

P8.29 L4 · Analysis

Deriving the sigmoid from Gaussian Naïve Bayes

Assume (as in the slides' self-read derivation) that \(Y \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\), that \(X_i \mid Y = k \sim N(\mu_{ik}, \sigma_i^2)\) with a variance that does not depend on \(k\), and that the \(X_i\) are conditionally independent given \(Y\).

(a) Starting from Bayes' theorem, show that

\[ P(Y = 1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left( \log \frac{1 - \pi}{\pi} + \sum_i \log \frac{P(X_i \mid Y = 0)}{P(X_i \mid Y = 1)} \right)}. \]

(b) Substitute the Gaussian densities and show that \(P(Y = 1 \mid X) = \sigma\!\left(w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i\right)\), giving \(w_i\) and \(w_0\) in terms of \(\pi\), \(\mu_{i0}\), \(\mu_{i1}\) and \(\sigma_i\).

(c) What changes if the variances are class-specific, \(\sigma_{ik}^2\)? Give the extra term and describe the decision boundary.

(d) Count the parameters of shared-variance GNB and of logistic regression for \(n\) features. What does that say about which model makes more assumptions?

(e) The slides write \(P(Y = 1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i)}\). How are those weights related to yours?

Hint

Divide the numerator and denominator of Bayes' theorem by \(P(Y = 1) P(X \mid Y = 1)\), and use \(a = \exp(\log a)\). In the Gaussian log-ratio, the \(X_i^2\) terms cancel only if the two variances are equal.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ P(Y = 1 \mid X) = \frac{P(Y = 1) P(X \mid Y = 1)}{P(Y = 1) P(X \mid Y = 1) + P(Y = 0) P(X \mid Y = 0)} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{P(Y = 0) P(X \mid Y = 0)}{P(Y = 1) P(X \mid Y = 1)}}. \]

Conditional independence turns the ratio of joints into a product of per-feature ratios, and writing the ratio as \(\exp(\log(\cdot))\) gives the stated form.

(b) For one feature with shared \(\sigma_i\),

\[ \log \frac{N(X_i; \mu_{i0}, \sigma_i^2)}{N(X_i; \mu_{i1}, \sigma_i^2)} = \frac{(X_i - \mu_{i1})^2 - (X_i - \mu_{i0})^2}{2\sigma_i^2} = \frac{\mu_{i0} - \mu_{i1}}{\sigma_i^2} X_i + \frac{\mu_{i1}^2 - \mu_{i0}^2}{2\sigma_i^2}. \]

The \(X_i^2\) terms cancel. The exponent is linear in \(X\), so \(P(Y = 1 \mid X) = \sigma(w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i)\) with

\[ w_i = \frac{\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i0}}{\sigma_i^2}, \qquad w_0 = \log \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} + \sum_i \frac{\mu_{i0}^2 - \mu_{i1}^2}{2\sigma_i^2}. \]

(P8.27: \(w_1 = (6 - 2)/4 = 1\), \(w_0 = \log \frac{1}{3} + \frac{4 - 36}{8} = -5.099\).)

(c) With \(\sigma_{i0} \ne \sigma_{i1}\) the log-ratio gains the term

\[ X_i^2 \left( \frac{1}{2\sigma_{i1}^2} - \frac{1}{2\sigma_{i0}^2} \right) + \log \frac{\sigma_{i1}}{\sigma_{i0}}, \]

so the log-odds are quadratic in \(X\) and the decision boundary is a quadric (in one dimension, up to two thresholds). The posterior is no longer exactly logistic in \(X\) (P8.23 is such a case).

(d) GNB: \(2n\) means, \(n\) variances and \(\pi\): \(3n + 1\). Logistic regression: \(n + 1\). GNB's extra parameters describe \(P(X \mid Y)\), which logistic regression never assumes. Logistic regression is the weaker set of assumptions (any model whose log-odds are linear), so it is right more often in the limit; GNB, when its assumptions hold, needs fewer examples to reach its (equal) limit.

(e) The slides' weights are the negatives of these, \(w^{\text{slides}} = -w\), since \(\frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} = \sigma(z)\).

Key insight: The logistic sigmoid is exactly what Bayes' theorem produces from class-conditional Gaussians that share their variance; logistic regression keeps that form and drops the Gaussian story.

10.E Module 8 Capstone

P8.30 L5 · Mastery

Long documents and floating-point underflow

A multinomial NB news classifier works well on headlines, but on full articles it suddenly predicts the same class for everything, and printing the scores shows 0.0 for both classes.

(a) Double-precision numbers have a smallest normal value of about \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\) and a smallest subnormal value of about \(4.9 \times 10^{-324}\). If a typical smoothed word probability is \(10^{-4}\), after how many tokens does the product of word probabilities leave the normal range, and after how many does it become exactly 0?

(b) Explain why the classifier then predicts one fixed class.

(c) For a 1,200-token article, the sums of log word probabilities are \(\sum_j \log P(u_j \mid A) = -10{,}250.4\) and \(\sum_j \log P(u_j \mid B) = -10{,}262.9\), with priors \(P(A) = 0.3\) and \(P(B) = 0.7\). Compute the two log-scores and the predicted class.

(d) Compute \(P(A \mid d)\) without leaving log space (the log-sum-exp trick).

(e) Does working with logs ever change the predicted class? What changes for Gaussian NB?

Hint

\(\log \prod = \sum \log\), and \(\log\) is increasing. For normalising, subtract the largest log-score before exponentiating.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(10^{-4k} < 2.2 \times 10^{-308}\) once \(4k > 307.7\): after about 77 tokens the product leaves the normal range, and at 81 tokens (\(10^{-324}\)) it is rounded to exactly 0. In Python, 0.0001**81 is 0.0. A full article has hundreds or thousands of tokens.

(b) Both scores become 0.0, so the comparison is a tie, and argmax returns the first class every time. The model's evidence has been destroyed by the arithmetic, not by the data.

(c)

\[ \begin{aligned} \log \text{Score}(A) &= \log 0.3 - 10{,}250.4 = \mathbf{-10{,}251.604}, \\ \log \text{Score}(B) &= \log 0.7 - 10{,}262.9 = \mathbf{-10{,}263.257}. \end{aligned} \]

Predict \(A\), by a log-odds margin of 11.653.

(d) With \(m = \max = -10{,}251.604\),

\[ \log \sum_c \text{Score}(c) = m + \log\!\left(e^{0} + e^{-11.653}\right), \qquad P(A \mid d) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-11.653}} = \mathbf{0.999991}. \]

Every exponent stays near 0, so nothing underflows. (Exponentiating the raw log-scores, \(e^{-10251.6}\), gives 0.0 in floating point.)

(e) Never: \(\log\) is strictly increasing, so the argmax is the same, and only the arithmetic becomes stable. For Gaussian NB, use \(\log N(x; \mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\) directly instead of computing a tiny density (the slides' humidity example has a density of \(1.28 \times 10^{-97}\) from a single feature). The slides make the same point: "in practice compare sums of logs".

Key insight: Naïve Bayes multiplies one factor per token or feature, so on realistic inputs the product underflows; summing log-probabilities gives the same decision and keeps it computable.

P8.31 L5 · Mastery

Correlated features count the same evidence twice

The slides' telecom example notes that Plan and Usage are probably correlated given churn. To see what correlated features do, take the extreme case: a feature that is an exact copy of another.

(a) In P8.22 (Laplace smoothing), a data engineer adds a column "Data tier" that is an exact copy of Usage. For the same customer (Usage = Low, so Data tier = Low), what happens to the posterior odds and to \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x)\)? Does the predicted class change?

(b) In P8.19 (no smoothing), the column "Visits" is duplicated in the same way. For the same member (Visits = Low), recompute the odds and \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x)\). Does the predicted class change?

(c) State a rule for when double-counted evidence flips the decision.

(d) Correlation here was perfect. Why do the slides nevertheless say that Naïve Bayes often classifies well even though the assumption is "doubtful"?

(e) Suggest two practical remedies.

Hint

A duplicated feature multiplies the posterior odds by its likelihood ratio \(\frac{P(x_i \mid \text{Yes})}{P(x_i \mid \text{No})}\) a second time.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The Usage = Low likelihood ratio is \(\frac{6/8}{3/10} = 2.5\). The odds were \(\frac{0.01488}{0.00425} = 3.50\); the copy multiplies them by 2.5 again, to 8.75, so \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x)\) rises from 0.778 to 0.897 (confirmed with CategoricalNB(alpha=1) on the duplicated table). The class (Yes) does not change; only the confidence is inflated.

(b) The Visits = Low ratio is \(\frac{2/7}{5/5} = 0.286\). The odds were \(\frac{0.04082}{0.01667} = 2.449\); after duplication they are \(2.449 \times 0.286 = \mathbf{0.700}\), so \(P(\text{Yes} \mid x)\) falls from 0.710 to 0.412. The prediction flips from Yes to No, although the copy adds no new information.

(c) Duplicating feature \(i\) adds \(\log \frac{P(x_i \mid \text{Yes})}{P(x_i \mid \text{No})}\) to the log-odds a second time. The decision flips when this extra term has the opposite sign to the original log-odds and is larger in magnitude. In (a) the extra term (\(\log 2.5 = 0.92\)) agreed with the decision; in (b) it (\(\log 0.286 = -1.25\)) opposed a margin of only \(\log 2.449 = 0.90\).

(d) Real correlations are partial, so the over-counting is usually much smaller than a full copy. And the classifier only needs the ranking of the class scores to be right, not their values; over-counting often pushes probabilities further in the direction they were already going (as in (a)). The probabilities become overconfident, but the argmax often survives.

(e) For example: drop or merge redundant features (keep one of Usage and Data tier, or combine Plan and Usage into one joint feature "Plan × Usage" so their dependence is modelled); select features by cross-validation; or use logistic regression, which can lower the weight of correlated features because it fits \(P(y \mid x)\) jointly.

Key insight: Correlated features make Naïve Bayes count the same evidence more than once; the result is always overconfidence, and it becomes a wrong decision only when the double-counted evidence is against a narrow margin.

P8.32 L5 · Mastery

Naïve Bayes as the first model for a small text data set

A support team has 300 labelled tickets in 4 equally common categories (billing, login, delivery, refund). Tickets are about 40 tokens long; after cleaning, the vocabulary has 5,000 words. A colleague proposes to start with a fine-tuned deep network.

(a) Make the case for multinomial NB as the first baseline: how many parameters does it have, and how are they estimated?

(b) How many training tokens does each class have? At least how many vocabulary words must have a zero count in each class? What smoothed probabilities do an unseen word and a word seen once receive?

(c) Why does Naïve Bayes tend to do well relative to discriminative models when data are this scarce?

(d) Describe an evaluation protocol that gives an honest estimate of NB's accuracy and also tunes the smoothing constant \(\alpha\).

(e) Name two signs that it is time to move beyond Naïve Bayes.

Hint

Compare the number of tokens per class with the size of the vocabulary. For (c), think about how many parameters each model must estimate and how.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(P(c)\) for 4 classes (3 free parameters) and \(P(w \mid c)\) for 5,000 words per class: about \(4 \times 5{,}000 = 20{,}000\) probabilities, each a smoothed relative frequency. Training is one pass of counting, has no learning rate or iterations, takes milliseconds, and is easy to inspect (the top words per class).

(b) \(75 \times 40 = \mathbf{3{,}000}\) tokens per class. At most 3,000 distinct words can occur in a class, so at least 2,000 of the 5,000 words have a zero count in every class. With Laplace smoothing the denominator is \(3{,}000 + 5{,}000 = 8{,}000\): an unseen word gets \(\frac{1}{8000} = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\), a word seen once \(\frac{2}{8000} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\). Smoothing is not optional here.

(c) Each NB parameter is estimated separately from all the class's data (P8.25), so the model has low variance; its strong independence assumption is a bias that matters less when data are scarce. A discriminative model fits all its weights jointly by optimisation and needs more data (or strong regularisation) before its weaker assumptions pay off; Mitchell's chapter, cited in the slides, describes GNB approaching its asymptotic error with fewer examples than logistic regression.

(d) Hold out a stratified test set (for example 60 tickets) and do not touch it. On the remaining 240, run stratified 5-fold cross-validation over a grid such as \(\alpha \in \{0.1, 0.3, 1, 3\}\) (fitting the vocabulary inside each fold), choose \(\alpha\), refit on all 240 and report accuracy and per-class F1 on the test set once. Use log-probabilities throughout (P8.30).

(e) For example: learning curves show NB's validation accuracy has stopped improving while a regularised logistic regression keeps improving as data grow; the errors come from word order or negation ("not charged twice"), which a bag of words cannot represent; strongly correlated n-gram features make the probabilities badly overconfident (P8.31).

Key insight: On small text data sets, Naïve Bayes is cheap, hard to overfit and surprisingly accurate, which makes it the baseline every more complex model has to beat.

P8.33 L5 · Mastery

The trap: \(P(\text{class} \mid \text{evidence})\) is not \(P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{class})\)

1% of a company's incoming e-mail is phishing. The word invoice appears in 30% of phishing e-mails and in 3% of legitimate ones.

(a) An analyst says: "invoice appears in 30% of phishing mail, so a mail containing invoice is phishing with probability 0.3." A second analyst says: "invoice is 10 times more common in phishing, so a mail containing it is about 91% (10/11) likely to be phishing." What is each one computing, and what is the correct \(P(\text{phishing} \mid \textit{invoice})\)?

(b) A junior engineer's Naïve Bayes code ranks classes by \(\prod_i P(x_i \mid c)\), omitting \(P(c)\). Using only the word invoice, what does the code predict for a mail that contains it, and what does the full MAP rule predict?

(c) Out of 10,000 e-mails, how many contain invoice, how many of those are phishing, and how many false alarms does the engineer's rule raise?

(d) When is it actually correct to rank by \(P(x \mid c)\) alone?

Hint

Multiply the likelihood ratio by the prior odds: posterior odds = \(\frac{P(e \mid c_1)}{P(e \mid c_2)} \cdot \frac{P(c_1)}{P(c_2)}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The first analyst reports \(P(\textit{invoice} \mid \text{phishing}) = 0.3\), the likelihood. The second uses the likelihood ratio, 10, but implicitly assumes equal priors. Correctly:

\[ P(\text{phishing} \mid \textit{invoice}) = \frac{0.30 \times 0.01}{0.30 \times 0.01 + 0.03 \times 0.99} = \frac{0.003}{0.0327} = \mathbf{0.092}. \]

Equivalently, posterior odds \(= 10 \times \frac{1}{99} = 0.101\). Both analysts are wrong; the mail is still about 91% likely to be legitimate.

(b) The likelihood-only code compares 0.30 with 0.03 and predicts phishing. The MAP rule compares \(0.003\) with \(0.0297\) and predicts legitimate. Ignoring the prior is the "MAP = MLE" shortcut, which is only valid for a uniform prior.

(c) Phishing: \(100 \times 0.30 = \mathbf{30}\) contain invoice; legitimate: \(9{,}900 \times 0.03 = \mathbf{297}\) do. The engineer's rule flags all 327, of which 297 are false alarms (91%), consistent with (a).

(d) Only when the classes have equal priors (or when, by design, we want to ignore them, for example on a deliberately balanced evaluation set, accepting that the deployed error rate will differ). In general \(P(c \mid e) = P(e \mid c)\) only if \(P(c) = P(e)\).

Key insight: Likelihoods are counted inside a class; decisions need posteriors; the prior is the bridge, and leaving it out is the base-rate error in its Naïve Bayes form.

P8.34 L5 · Mastery

Six tempting statements about Bayesian learning

Each statement is wrong or misleading. Explain why, with a number or an example where possible.

(a) "My Gaussian NB printed \(P(x \mid c) = 3.99\) for a part diameter. Probabilities cannot exceed 1, so there is a bug." (The diameters of class \(c\) have \(\sigma = 0.1\) cm, and \(x\) equals the class mean.)

(b) "MAP is always better than MLE, because it uses more information."

(c) "Naïve Bayes gave \(P(\text{spam} \mid x) = 0.9999\), so we can be almost certain."

(d) "Naïve Bayes is the Bayes optimal classifier, since both use Bayes' theorem."

(e) "\(h_{\text{MAP}}\) has posterior 0.4, so its prediction on any new instance is correct with probability 0.4."

(f) "Since logistic regression and Gaussian NB have the same sigmoid form, it does not matter which one we train."

Hint

For each statement, ask which assumption it silently adds: a density as a probability, a correct prior, independence, a single hypothesis, or a shared training objective.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Not a bug. It is a density: at the mean, \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \times 0.1} = \mathbf{3.99}\) per cm. A density can exceed 1 when \(\sigma\) is small; only its integral must be 1. It is valid inside the NB score (P8.21).

(b) Only if the prior is right. A wrong prior biases the estimate: in P8.7 a strong \(\text{Beta}(31, 31)\) prior gave 0.529 after 7 heads in 10 tosses of a coin whose heads rate was 0.7. With plenty of data the two coincide anyway; MAP helps mainly with scarce data and zero counts.

(c) Overconfident. Correlated features are counted repeatedly (P8.31), and on long documents hundreds of factors push the posterior towards 0 or 1 (P8.30). NB's ranking is often good; its probabilities need calibration before they are trusted as probabilities.

(d) No. Naïve Bayes is one model with a strong conditional-independence assumption, whose parameters are point estimates. The Bayes optimal classifier averages the predictions of all hypotheses weighted by their posteriors; it is optimal for its hypothesis space and prior, and Naïve Bayes is generally not.

(e) No. The probability that the label at \(x\) is \(v\) is \(\sum_{h:\, h(x) = v} P(h \mid D)\). In P8.14, \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) (posterior 0.4) had a 0.4 chance of being right at \(x_1\) but 0.6 at \(x_2\) and 0.7 at \(x_3\), because other hypotheses agreed with it there.

(f) It matters. They maximise different likelihoods (joint against conditional), so on the same data they fit different weights, and an outlier can change GNB's slope by a factor of 11 while leaving logistic regression untouched (P8.28). They coincide only in the limit, and only when the GNB assumptions hold.

Key insight: Most mistakes in Bayesian learning come from forgetting an assumption: densities are not probabilities, priors can be wrong, independence inflates confidence, and \(h_{\text{MAP}}\) is not the whole posterior.

PART 11 — Module 9: Ensemble Learning

Conventions used throughout this module: \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. In AdaBoost the labels are \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), the \(n\) training weights start at \(w_i = 1/n\), and in round \(t\) the weak learner \(h_t\) has weighted error \(\varepsilon_t = \sum_{i:\, h_t(x_i) \ne y_i} w_i\) (the weights always sum to 1). Then

\[ \alpha_t = \frac12 \ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon_t}{\varepsilon_t}, \qquad w_i \leftarrow \frac{w_i \, e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i)}}{Z_t}, \qquad H(x) = \operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_t \alpha_t h_t(x)\Big), \]

where \(Z_t\) is the sum of the unnormalised new weights, so a misclassified example is multiplied by \(e^{\alpha_t}\) and a correct one by \(e^{-\alpha_t}\) before renormalisation. Gradient boosting for regression uses squared loss, starts from the mean \(F_0 = \bar{y}\), fits a regression stump to the residuals \(r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)\) (each leaf predicts the mean residual of its records, and the split minimises the total squared error of the residuals), and updates \(F_m = F_{m-1} + \eta \, h_m\) with learning rate \(\eta\). A bootstrap sample of a training set of size \(n\) is \(n\) draws with replacement. Intermediate values are kept exact; only final answers are rounded.

11.A Ensemble Foundations (9.1)

P9.1 L1 · Foundation

Weak learners and kinds of ensemble

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "A weak learner is a model whose accuracy is only slightly better than random guessing."

(b) "A Random Forest is a heterogeneous ensemble, because every tree in it is different."

(c) "An ensemble of a logistic regression, an SVM and a k-NN classifier, combined by a meta-model, is a homogeneous ensemble."

(d) "Combining weak learners can only help if each of them is better than chance and they do not all make the same mistakes."

(e) "An ensemble always has a lower training error than its best member."

(f) "A decision stump (a tree of depth 1) is the classic weak learner used in AdaBoost."

Hint

"Homogeneous" and "heterogeneous" refer to the type of base algorithm, not to whether the fitted models happen to differ.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. For binary classification that means an error rate a little below 0.5; boosting turns many such learners into a strong learner.

(b) False. All its members are decision trees, so it is homogeneous. The trees differ because each sees a different bootstrap sample and different random feature subsets, not because the algorithm changes.

(c) False. Three different algorithms make it heterogeneous; combining them with a meta-model is stacking.

(d) True. Learners worse than chance pull a vote the wrong way, and learners that err on the same examples cannot outvote each other's mistakes (see P9.5).

(e) False. Nothing guarantees it. A bagged ensemble of fully grown trees can have a higher training error than a single fully grown tree (which has zero), and a majority vote can be wrong on a point that one member gets right.

(f) True. A stump has high bias and low variance, and AdaBoost reduces the bias by adding many of them, each focused on different examples.

Key insight: An ensemble is homogeneous or heterogeneous according to its base algorithm, and it works only when the members are individually better than chance and make errors that are not all the same.

P9.2 L1 · Foundation

Bagging, boosting and stacking side by side

For each statement, say whether it describes bagging, boosting, stacking, or more than one of them.

(a) The base learners can be trained in parallel, independently of each other.

(b) Each new learner is trained with more emphasis on the examples the previous learners got wrong.

(c) The main effect is to reduce the variance of a low-bias, high-variance base learner such as a deep tree.

(d) The main effect is to reduce the bias of a high-bias, low-variance base learner such as a stump.

(e) A second-level model learns how to combine the predictions of several different first-level models.

(f) The final prediction is a weighted vote, where better learners get larger weights computed from their error.

(g) Each learner is fitted on a bootstrap sample of the training data.

(h) The combination of members is a fixed rule (average or majority vote) that is not itself learned.

Hint

Ask two questions for each statement: are the members trained one after another or independently, and is the combining rule fixed, computed from errors, or learned?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Bagging (and the first level of stacking, whose base models are also independent).

(b) Boosting.

(c) Bagging.

(d) Boosting.

(e) Stacking.

(f) Boosting (AdaBoost's \(\alpha_t\)).

(g) Bagging (including Random Forest).

(h) Bagging.

Key insight: Bagging is parallel and fixes variance, boosting is sequential and fixes bias, and stacking learns the combination itself from heterogeneous models.

P9.3 L2 · Computation

Majority vote of independent classifiers

Several binary classifiers make errors independently of each other, and each one is correct with probability \(p\) on a new case. The ensemble predicts by majority vote.

(a) Compute the probability that a majority of 3 classifiers with \(p = 0.7\) is correct.

(b) Repeat for 5 classifiers with \(p = 0.7\).

(c) Repeat for 5 classifiers with \(p = 0.45\). What has happened?

(d) The 3 classifiers in (a) turn out to be three copies of the same model. What is the majority-vote accuracy now?

Hint

The number of correct classifiers is \(\text{Bin}(n, p)\). A majority of 3 needs at least 2 correct; a majority of 5 needs at least 3.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) At least 2 of 3 correct:

\[ P = \binom{3}{2}(0.7)^2(0.3) + (0.7)^3 = 0.441 + 0.343 = \mathbf{0.784}. \]

(b) At least 3 of 5 correct:

\[ P = \binom{5}{3}(0.7)^3(0.3)^2 + \binom{5}{4}(0.7)^4(0.3) + (0.7)^5 = 0.3087 + 0.36015 + 0.16807 = \mathbf{0.837}. \]

(c) With \(p = 0.45\) the same sum gives \(P = 0.407\), which is worse than one classifier alone. Voting amplifies whichever side of 0.5 the members are on.

(d) Identical copies always agree, so the vote is just the single model: \(P = 0.7\).

Key insight: Majority voting helps only when the members are better than chance and their errors are independent; it hurts below 0.5 and does nothing for copies.

P9.4 L3 · Application

Which ensemble for which base learner?

A team has a classification problem where the best achievable error (the noise level) is about 10%. They tried four base learners and recorded the training error and the 5-fold cross-validation error.

Base learner Training error CV error
A. Fully grown decision tree 0% 24%
B. Decision stump (depth 1) 31% 32%
C. Logistic regression on the raw features 18% 19%
D. Decision tree of depth 3 14% 16%

(a) For each learner, say whether its main problem is high bias, high variance or neither.

(b) For A and B, choose bagging (or Random Forest) or boosting, and justify the choice.

(c) A team member proposes "boost the logistic regression with AdaBoost to fix its bias". Explain why this helps far less than boosting stumps, and suggest something better.

(d) Which of the four is the usual base learner in gradient boosting libraries, and why?

Hint

A large gap between training and CV error signals variance; both errors far above the noise level signals bias. For (c), think about what a weighted sum of linear decision functions is.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) A: high variance (zero training error, 14 points worse on CV). B: high bias (both errors far above 10%, almost no gap). C: high bias (both errors about 18–19%). D: moderate bias, low variance (small gap, errors still above 10%).

(b) A → bagging / Random Forest. Averaging many deep trees trained on bootstrap samples keeps their low bias and cancels much of their variance. B → boosting. Each stump is stable but too simple; boosting adds stumps sequentially, each concentrating on the current mistakes, so the sum can represent a much more complex boundary and the bias falls.

(c) AdaBoost outputs \(\operatorname{sign}\left(\sum_t \alpha_t (w_t^\top x + b_t)\right)\), and a weighted sum of linear functions is again linear, so the ensemble can still only draw a hyperplane. Its bias barely moves. Better options are to add non-linear features (interactions, polynomials), to switch to boosted trees, or to use the logistic regression as one input to a stacked ensemble with tree models.

(d) D. Shallow trees (depth 3 to 6) are the standard base learner in gradient boosting: they have low variance, so the sequence of trees can lower the bias without the variance exploding, and depth above 1 lets each tree capture feature interactions.

Key insight: Diagnose the base learner first: bag a high-variance learner, boost a high-bias one, and remember that boosting cannot add capacity that the sum of base learners does not have.

P9.5 L4 · Analysis

Why voting works, and when it fails

Let \(n\) (odd) binary classifiers each be correct with probability \(p > 0.5\), independently.

(a) Write the majority-vote accuracy \(A_n\) as a binomial sum, and evaluate it for \(p = 0.6\) and \(n = 1, 5, 11, 21, 101\).

(b) Explain why \(A_n \to 1\) as \(n \to \infty\) whenever \(p > 0.5\).

(c) Now drop independence. Three classifiers are tested on the same 10 cases, and each is correct on exactly 7 of them. Construct a pattern of correct and incorrect predictions for which the majority vote is correct on only 6 cases, and another for which it is correct on all 10.

(d) Prove that 6 is the minimum in (c).

(e) Explain why ensembles trained on the same data tend to behave more like the bad case than like the independent case, and what bagging and Random Forest do about it.

Hint

For (b), think about the fraction of classifiers that are correct. For (d), a case where the majority is wrong uses at most one "correct" prediction, and a case where it is right uses at most three.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The vote is correct when more than half of the members are correct:

\[ A_n = \sum_{k = (n+1)/2}^{n} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n-k}. \]

For \(p = 0.6\):

\(n\) 1 5 11 21 101
\(A_n\) 0.600 0.683 0.754 0.826 0.979

(b) The fraction of correct members \(K/n\) has mean \(p\) and variance \(p(1-p)/n \to 0\). By the law of large numbers \(K/n \to p > 0.5\), so the probability that \(K/n > 0.5\) tends to 1.

(c) Write 1 for correct. The bad pattern (6 of 10):

Case 1–6 7 8 9 10
Classifier 1 1 1 0 0 0
Classifier 2 1 0 1 0 0
Classifier 3 1 0 0 1 0
Majority right wrong wrong wrong wrong

The classifiers "waste" their correct votes by all being right on the same easy cases. The good pattern (10 of 10) spreads the errors so that no two classifiers are wrong on the same case: classifier 1 is wrong on cases 1–3, classifier 2 on cases 4–6, classifier 3 on cases 8–10, and every case has at least two correct votes.

(d) Let \(m\) be the number of cases the majority gets right. Those cases use at most 3 correct predictions each, and the other \(10 - m\) cases use at most 1 each. The three classifiers make \(3 \times 7 = 21\) correct predictions in total, so

\[ 3m + (10 - m) \ge 21 \;\Rightarrow\; m \ge 5.5 \;\Rightarrow\; m \ge \mathbf{6}. \]

So the majority can be less accurate (60%) than every member (70%), even though each member beats chance.

(e) Models fitted to the same data with the same algorithm make positively correlated errors: they all fail on the same hard or noisy cases, as in the bad pattern. The binomial gain in (a) assumes independence and disappears as the correlation grows. Bagging decorrelates members by giving each a different bootstrap sample; Random Forest decorrelates them further by restricting every split to a random subset of features, so the trees cannot all reuse the same dominant split.

Key insight: The binomial "wisdom of crowds" result needs independent errors; correlated errors can make the vote no better, or even worse, than one member, which is why ensembles work so hard to make their members different.

11.B Bagging & Random Forest (9.2)

P9.6 L1 · Foundation

Bootstrapping and Random Forest facts

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "A bootstrap sample of 1,000 records contains 1,000 distinct records."

(b) "Bagging trains its base models one after another, each on the errors of the previous one."

(c) "For a regression target, a bagged ensemble predicts the average of its members' predictions; for a class label, it predicts the majority vote."

(d) "A Random Forest is bagging of decision trees plus a random subset of features considered at every split."

(e) "In a Random Forest, each tree is given one random subset of features at the start and uses only those features everywhere in the tree."

(f) "If a Random Forest considers all \(p\) features at every split, it is exactly bagged decision trees."

(g) "Adding more trees to a Random Forest makes it overfit more, so the number of trees must be tuned carefully."

Hint

Sampling with replacement lets the same record be drawn several times. For (g), think about what happens to an average as you add more terms.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) False. Drawing with replacement repeats some records and misses others; on average only about 63.2% of the records are distinct (P9.7).

(b) False. That is boosting. Bagging trains its models independently, so they can be trained in parallel.

(c) True. That is the aggregation step of bagging, as in the slides' Random Forest rating example.

(d) True.

(e) False. The random subset is redrawn at every node, so a tree can still use every feature somewhere, just not always the best one at each split.

(f) True. With \(m = p\) the feature subsampling does nothing, and only the bootstrap randomness is left.

(g) False. More trees average more terms, so the variance of the forest falls towards a floor and the test error levels off; it does not rise. The number of trees is limited by computing cost, not by overfitting. (Tree depth and \(m\) are the knobs that control fit.)

Key insight: Bagging is parallel resampling plus averaging, and Random Forest adds fresh feature subsampling at every split; more trees never hurt, they only stop helping.

P9.7 L2 · Computation

How much of the data does a bootstrap sample miss?

A bootstrap sample of size \(n\) is drawn from a training set of size \(n\).

(a) Show that the probability that a particular record is not in the sample is \((1 - 1/n)^n\), and evaluate it for \(n = 5, 10, 100, 1000\).

(b) Find the limit as \(n \to \infty\).

(c) For \(n = 1000\), what is the expected number of distinct records in a bootstrap sample, and the expected number of out-of-bag (OOB) records?

(d) A bagged ensemble has 50 trees and \(n = 1000\). For how many trees, on average, is a given record out of bag? What is the probability that it is out of bag for no tree?

Hint

Each of the \(n\) draws misses a particular record with probability \(1 - 1/n\), and the draws are independent. Use \(\lim_{n \to \infty} (1 - 1/n)^n = e^{-1}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) One draw misses the record with probability \(1 - 1/n\), and all \(n\) independent draws miss it with probability \((1 - 1/n)^n\):

\(n\) 5 10 100 1000
\((1 - 1/n)^n\) 0.3277 0.3487 0.3660 0.3677

(b) \(e^{-1} \approx 0.3679\). About 36.8% of the records are left out of each bootstrap sample and about 63.2% appear at least once.

(c) Distinct records: \(1000 \times (1 - 0.999^{1000}) = 1000 \times 0.63230 = \mathbf{632.3}\). OOB records: \(1000 \times 0.36770 = \mathbf{367.7}\).

(d) The expected number of trees for which the record is OOB is \(50 \times 0.36770 = \mathbf{18.4}\). The probability that it is in bag for all 50 trees is

\[ (1 - 0.36770)^{50} = \mathbf{1.1 \times 10^{-10}}, \]

so in practice every record gets an OOB prediction.

Key insight: Each bootstrap sample leaves out roughly one record in three, which makes every bagged model different and leaves a built-in validation set for each tree.

P9.8 L2 · Computation

Averaging, hard votes and soft votes

(a) A Random Forest of 5 regression trees predicts the price of a flat (in lakh rupees) as 212, 198, 205, 220 and 190. What does the forest predict?

(b) A Random Forest of 5 classification trees is asked whether an e-mail is spam. The trees' estimated probabilities of spam are 0.55, 0.60, 0.52, 0.10 and 0.15, and each tree's hard label is spam when its probability exceeds 0.5. Find the prediction by majority (hard) vote.

(c) Find the prediction by averaging the probabilities (soft vote) with a 0.5 threshold.

(d) Explain why the two rules disagree, and which one uses more information.

Hint

Count the trees above 0.5 for the hard vote; average all five numbers for the soft vote.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The forest averages:

\[ \hat{y} = \frac{212 + 198 + 205 + 220 + 190}{5} = \frac{1025}{5} = \mathbf{205}. \]

(b) Three trees (0.55, 0.60, 0.52) vote spam and two vote not spam, so the hard vote is spam (3 to 2).

(c) The mean probability is \(1.92/5 = 0.384 < 0.5\), so the soft vote is not spam.

(d) The three "spam" trees are barely above 0.5, while the two "not spam" trees are very confident. A hard vote throws the confidence away and counts each tree once; a soft vote keeps it. Soft voting uses more information and is what scikit-learn's RandomForestClassifier does, but it relies on the members' probabilities being reasonably calibrated.

Key insight: Bagging aggregates by averaging; for classification, averaging labels (hard vote) and averaging probabilities (soft vote) can give different answers when the members differ in confidence.

P9.9 L2 · Computation

Counting features in a Random Forest

A Random Forest classifier is trained on a data set with \(p = 25\) features. At each split it considers a fresh random subset of \(m = \lfloor \sqrt{p} \rfloor\) features.

(a) Compute \(m\). What would the common default \(m = \lfloor p/3 \rfloor\) for regression forests give?

(b) What is the probability that a particular feature is among the candidates at a given split?

(c) Feature \(X_1\) is by far the strongest predictor, and any split that may use it does use it. Out of 200 trees, how many root nodes are expected not to split on \(X_1\)? How many would not split on it in plain bagging?

(d) There are three strong features. What is the probability that at least one of them is among the candidates at a split?

(e) Explain in one or two sentences why (c) makes the trees of a forest less correlated than bagged trees.

Hint

The candidate subset is a random choice of \(m\) features out of \(p\), without replacement. For (d), compute the probability that none of the three strong features is chosen.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(m = \lfloor \sqrt{25} \rfloor = 5\). For regression, \(\lfloor 25/3 \rfloor = \mathbf{8}\).

(b) By symmetry each feature is equally likely to be in the subset, so

\[ P = \frac{m}{p} = \frac{5}{25} = \mathbf{0.2}. \]

(c) Each root misses \(X_1\) with probability 0.8, so about \(200 \times 0.8 = \mathbf{160}\) roots split on some other feature. In plain bagging every split sees all features, so (apart from rare bootstrap samples where another feature happens to win) essentially all 200 roots split on \(X_1\).

(d) The probability that all 5 candidates come from the 22 other features is

\[ \frac{\binom{22}{5}}{\binom{25}{5}} = \frac{26334}{53130} = 0.4957, \]

so the probability that at least one strong feature is available is \(0.504\).

(e) With bagging, the same dominant feature sits at the top of almost every tree, so the trees have similar structure and make similar errors. Feature subsampling forces many trees to start from other features, so their errors are less correlated and averaging cancels more of them (P9.11).

Key insight: Random Forest's per-split feature subsampling takes the dominant feature away from most splits, which makes the trees more different from each other at a small cost in individual tree accuracy.

P9.10 L3 · Application

Out-of-bag error by hand

A bagged ensemble of 5 fully grown trees is trained on 6 records with labels

Record 1 2 3 4 5 6
True label Y N Y Y N N

The bootstrap samples (record numbers drawn) were:

Tree Bootstrap sample
T1 2, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5
T2 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 6
T3 1, 1, 4, 4, 5, 5
T4 2, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6
T5 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 5

Each tree's predictions on all six records are:

Tree 1 2 3 4 5 6
T1 Y N N Y N N
T2 N N Y Y N N
T3 Y Y N Y N Y
T4 Y N Y Y N N
T5 Y N Y Y N N

(a) List the out-of-bag records of each tree.

(b) For each record, take the majority vote of only the trees for which it is out of bag, and compute the OOB error of the ensemble.

(c) Compute the ensemble's training (resubstitution) error, using all 5 trees on every record.

(d) Which of the two numbers is the honest estimate of test error, and why?

Hint

A record is out of bag for a tree if its number does not appear in that tree's bootstrap sample. Notice that each tree is right on every record it was trained on.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The OOB sets are T1: {1, 3, 6}, T2: {1, 5}, T3: {2, 3, 6}, T4: {1, 4}, T5: {3, 6}.

(b) OOB votes per record:

Record True OOB trees OOB votes OOB prediction Correct?
1 Y T1, T2, T4 Y, N, Y Y yes
2 N T3 Y Y no
3 Y T1, T3, T5 N, N, Y N no
4 Y T4 Y Y yes
5 N T2 N N yes
6 N T1, T3, T5 N, Y, N N yes

The OOB error is \(2/6 = 0.333\).

(c) With all five trees, record 2 gets N, N, Y, N, N (N) and record 3 gets N, Y, N, Y, Y (Y); every record is classified correctly, so the training error is 0.

(d) The OOB error. Each OOB vote comes only from trees that never saw the record, so it behaves like a validation prediction. The training error is optimistic because fully grown trees reproduce the labels of the records they were trained on.

Key insight: Out-of-bag evaluation gives bagging and Random Forest a free validation estimate: each record is judged only by the trees that did not train on it.

P9.11 L4 · Analysis

Averaging correlated learners

Let \(f_1, \dots, f_B\) be the predictions of \(B\) base learners at a fixed input. They are identically distributed with variance \(\sigma^2\), and every pair has correlation \(\rho \ge 0\). The ensemble predicts \(\bar{f} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} f_b\).

(a) Show that

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\bar{f}) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2. \]

(b) Take \(\sigma^2 = 4\) and \(\rho = 0.6\) (bagged deep trees). Compute \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{f})\) for \(B = 1, 10, 100\) and as \(B \to \infty\).

(c) How large must \(B\) be for the second term to be at most 1% of the first?

(d) A Random Forest with feature subsampling gives \(\rho = 0.2\), but each tree is slightly worse, with \(\sigma^2 = 4.5\). Compute \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{f})\) for \(B = 100\) and compare with (b).
