MAPE prefers B by a wide margin, because A's 2-unit error on a product that sells 2 units is a 100% error, while B's 10-unit miss on 100 units is only 10%.

(c) \(\bar{y} = 32.4\) and \(SST = 6155.2\).

\[ R^2_A = 1 - \frac{20}{6155.2} = \mathbf{0.9968}, \qquad R^2_B = 1 - \frac{100}{6155.2} = \mathbf{0.9838}. \]

Both look excellent, because the spread of \(y\) is dominated by product 5; \(R^2\) hides the 100% error on product 1 completely.

(d) Model C has \(SSE = 48^2 + 40^2 + 30^2 + 20^2 + 50^2 = 7704 > SST\):

\[ R^2_C = 1 - \frac{7704}{6155.2} = \mathbf{-0.252}. \]

A negative \(R^2\) means the model is worse than predicting the actual mean, 32.4, for every product. On test data nothing stops this from happening.

(e) "Relative error is what matters" is MAPE (or another percentage error). "Every unit costs the same" is MAE. If large misses are disproportionately costly (stock-outs on the bestseller), RMSE/MSE is the right choice.

Key insight: There is no neutral regression metric: choosing MAE, RMSE or MAPE is choosing how to weigh small errors against large ones and absolute errors against relative ones, so the metric must come from the cost of errors in the application.

P11.6 L3 · Application

The 98%-accurate fraud model that catches nothing

A test set of 2000 card transactions contains 40 frauds. Two models are evaluated:

  • Model Z predicts "legitimate" for every transaction.
  • Model M flags 120 transactions, of which 30 are frauds.

(a) Write both confusion matrices (fraud = positive).

(b) Compute accuracy, precision, recall and \(F_1\) for both models. Which model wins on accuracy?

(c) What is the ROC-AUC of Model Z, whose score is the same constant for every transaction?

(d) A missed fraud costs the bank Rs 500 and a false alarm (a call to the customer) costs Rs 5. Compute the total cost of each model on this test set.

(e) Compute the balanced accuracy, \(\frac{TPR + TNR}{2}\), for both models. Which metric would you put on the dashboard, and why?

Hint

For Model M, the 90 flagged legitimate transactions are false positives and the 10 frauds it did not flag are false negatives.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

Model TP FP FN TN
Z 0 0 40 1960
M 30 90 10 1870

(b)

Metric Model Z Model M
Accuracy \(\frac{1960}{2000} = \mathbf{0.98}\) \(\frac{30 + 1870}{2000} = \mathbf{0.95}\)
Precision undefined (no positive predictions) \(\frac{30}{120} = \mathbf{0.25}\)
Recall \(\mathbf{0}\) \(\frac{30}{40} = \mathbf{0.75}\)
\(F_1\) \(\mathbf{0}\) \(\frac{2(0.25)(0.75)}{1.0} = \mathbf{0.375}\)

Model Z wins on accuracy although it never catches a fraud. This is the accuracy paradox of slide 259: with 98% legitimate transactions, the trivial rule already scores 98%.

(c) AUC = 0.5. A constant score cannot rank any fraud above any legitimate transaction (every pair is a tie, counted as one half).

(d)

\[ \text{Cost}_Z = 40 \times 500 = \textbf{Rs 20,000}, \qquad \text{Cost}_M = 10 \times 500 + 90 \times 5 = \textbf{Rs 5,450}. \]

(e) Model Z: \(\frac{0 + 1}{2} = \mathbf{0.50}\). Model M: \(TNR = \frac{1870}{1960} = 0.954\), so \(\frac{0.75 + 0.954}{2} = \mathbf{0.852}\). For a rare positive class, report recall and precision (or \(F_1\)), AUC, and above all the expected cost; accuracy should not be the headline metric.

Key insight: When one class is rare, accuracy mostly measures the class balance, not the model; the right metric is the one that tracks the real cost of each kind of mistake.

P11.7 L4 · Analysis

Cross-validation variance and the once-only test set

A classifier is evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation on 500 labelled examples (100 per fold). The fold accuracies are

\[ 0.82,\ 0.78,\ 0.85,\ 0.80,\ 0.75. \]

(a) Compute the CV estimate of accuracy, the sample standard deviation of the fold scores, and the naive standard error \(s/\sqrt{5}\).

(b) If each fold were an independent sample of 100 cases from a model with true accuracy 0.80, what standard deviation would binomial sampling alone produce for a fold score? Compare with (a).

(c) Why is \(s/\sqrt{k}\) only a rough guide, and usually an underestimate, for the uncertainty of a CV estimate?

(d) A team skips cross-validation and instead evaluates 20 hyper-parameter settings directly on a test set of 200 cases, then reports the best score. Suppose all 20 settings really have accuracy 0.80. Use the fact that the expected maximum of 20 independent standard normal variables is about 1.867 to estimate the expected reported accuracy.

(e) State the rule this illustrates and the correct procedure.

Hint

For (d), each test accuracy is approximately \(N(0.80, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma = \sqrt{0.8 \times 0.2/200}\); the reported number is the largest of 20 such draws.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The mean is \(\bar{a} = \mathbf{0.80}\). The deviations are \(0.02, -0.02, 0.05, 0, -0.05\), so

\[ s = \sqrt{\frac{0.0004 + 0.0004 + 0.0025 + 0 + 0.0025}{4}} = \sqrt{0.00145} = \mathbf{0.0381}, \qquad \frac{s}{\sqrt{5}} = \mathbf{0.0170}. \]

(b)

\[ \sqrt{\frac{0.8 \times 0.2}{100}} = \mathbf{0.040}, \]

which is about the observed spread of 0.038. The fold-to-fold differences are what pure test-sample noise on 100 cases looks like; they are not evidence that the folds are "different".

(c) The five scores are not independent: any two training sets share 300 of their 400 examples, and every example is tested once, so the estimate pools all 500 test predictions. The variance of a CV estimate has no unbiased estimator in general, and \(s/\sqrt{k}\) tends to understate it because it ignores the correlation between folds. As a rough cross-check, treating all 500 predictions as one test set gives \(\sqrt{0.16/500} = \mathbf{0.0179}\).

(d) Each test score has \(\sigma = \sqrt{0.16/200} = 0.0283\), so

\[ E[\text{best reported}] \approx 0.80 + 1.867 \times 0.0283 = \mathbf{0.853}. \]

(A simulation with exact binomial counts gives 0.851.) The team will typically report about 85% for a model whose true accuracy is 80%, an optimistic bias of about 5 points that comes purely from selection.

(e) The test set must be used once, for the final chosen model. Select hyper-parameters by cross-validation (or a validation split) on the training data, refit the chosen setting on all training data, and only then score it on the untouched test set. If the test set has been used for selection, its score is no longer an estimate of generalisation error.

Key insight: Every evaluation score is a noisy draw; choosing the best of many draws turns noise into apparent skill, which is why selection and final assessment need separate data.

13.B Statistically Comparing Two Models (11.2)

P11.8 L1 · Foundation

Reading confidence intervals and tests correctly

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "Slide 734's two-step process for comparing models is: estimate a confidence interval for each model's accuracy, then test whether the observed difference is statistically significant."

(b) "Doubling the size of the test set halves the width of the confidence interval for accuracy."

(c) "If two models are scored on the same test set, their two accuracy estimates are independent random variables."

(d) "McNemar's test uses only the test cases on which the two models disagree."

(e) "If the difference between two models is not statistically significant, we have shown that the two models are equally accurate."

(f) "A model that reaches 86% on a test set of 50 cases and one that reaches 86% on a test set of 5000 cases are equally trustworthy estimates."

Hint

The half-width of the interval is \(z\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}\): look at how it depends on \(n\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. Slide 734: "estimating the confidence interval of a given model accuracy" and "testing the statistical significance of the observed deviation".

(b) False. The width is proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\); doubling \(n\) shrinks it by a factor \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\). Halving it needs four times as many cases.

(c) False. Both models face the same easy and hard cases, so their correctness indicators are positively correlated. Treating them as independent wastes this pairing (P11.11, P11.12).

(d) True. Cases that both models get right, or both get wrong, carry no information about which model is better; the statistic depends only on the discordant counts \(b\) and \(c\).

(e) False. "Not significant" means the data are consistent with no difference, not that the difference is zero. With a small test set, even a real 3-point gap is usually not significant.

(f) False. The 95% half-width is \(1.96\sqrt{0.86 \times 0.14/50} = 0.096\) for 50 cases but only 0.0096 for 5000 cases.

Key insight: An accuracy without its sample size is half a number; the interval width, which shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{n}\), tells you how much the point estimate can be trusted.

P11.9 L2 · Computation

A confidence interval for test accuracy

A spam filter classifies 850 of 1000 test emails correctly.

(a) Compute the 95% confidence interval for its true accuracy.

(b) Compute the 99% interval.

(c) Another team reports the same accuracy, 85%, from a test set of only 100 emails. Compute their 95% interval.

(d) How many test emails would be needed for a 95% interval of half-width at most 0.01, if accuracy stays near 0.85?

(e) Write the 95% interval for the error rate of the filter in (a).

Hint

\(\hat{p} = 0.85\); compute \(SE = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}\) once and multiply by the right \(z\). For (d), solve \(z \cdot SE \le 0.01\) for \(n\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ SE = \sqrt{\frac{0.85 \times 0.15}{1000}} = 0.01129, \qquad 0.85 \pm 1.96 \times 0.01129 = 0.85 \pm 0.0221 \Rightarrow \mathbf{[0.828,\ 0.872]}. \]

(b) \(0.85 \pm 2.576 \times 0.01129 = 0.85 \pm 0.0291 \Rightarrow\) [0.821, 0.879]. More confidence costs a wider interval.

(c)

\[ SE = \sqrt{\frac{0.85 \times 0.15}{100}} = 0.0357, \qquad 0.85 \pm 0.0700 \Rightarrow \mathbf{[0.780,\ 0.920]}. \]

The same point estimate is three times less precise: \(\sqrt{1000/100} = 3.16\).

(d)

\[ n \ge \frac{1.96^2 \times 0.85 \times 0.15}{0.01^2} = 4898.04 \Rightarrow n = \mathbf{4899}. \]

(e) The error rate is \(1 - \text{accuracy}\), so its interval is [0.128, 0.172]: the same half-width, 0.0221, around 0.15.

Key insight: A test set is a sample, and its accuracy is a sample proportion; the binomial standard error tells you how many test cases you need before a one-point difference means anything.

P11.10 L2 · Computation

Two models on two independent test sets

Model A was evaluated on a test set of 600 cases and got 504 right. Model B, built by another team, was evaluated on a separate, independently drawn test set of 500 cases and got 400 right.

(a) Compute both accuracies and the observed difference.

(b) Test \(H_0: p_A = p_B\) against \(H_1: p_A \ne p_B\) with the pooled two-proportion \(z\) test. Report \(z\), the two-sided p-value and your conclusion at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

(c) Compute a 95% confidence interval for \(p_A - p_B\) using the unpooled standard error. Is it consistent with (b)?

(d) Suggest one change to the evaluation design that would make the comparison more powerful.

Hint

The pooled proportion is \(\hat{p} = \frac{504 + 400}{600 + 500}\); the pooled standard error is \(\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_A} + \frac{1}{n_B}\right)}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\hat{p}_A = \frac{504}{600} = \mathbf{0.84}\), \(\hat{p}_B = \frac{400}{500} = \mathbf{0.80}\), difference 0.04.

(b) \(\hat{p} = \frac{904}{1100} = 0.8218\).

\[ SE = \sqrt{0.8218 \times 0.1782 \left(\frac{1}{600} + \frac{1}{500}\right)} = 0.02317, \qquad z = \frac{0.04}{0.02317} = \mathbf{1.73}. \]

The two-sided p-value is \(2P(Z > 1.73) = \mathbf{0.084} > 0.05\). Do not reject \(H_0\): a 4-point gap on test sets of this size could plausibly be sampling noise.

(c)

\[ SE_u = \sqrt{\frac{0.84 \times 0.16}{600} + \frac{0.80 \times 0.20}{500}} = 0.02332, \qquad 0.04 \pm 1.96 \times 0.02332 \Rightarrow \mathbf{[-0.006,\ 0.086]}. \]

The interval contains 0, which agrees with the test in (b).

(d) Score both models on the same test set and use McNemar's test (P11.11). Pairing removes the variation caused by the two test sets having different difficulty, and usually gives much more power for the same number of cases. A larger test set also helps.

Key insight: A difference between two accuracies has a standard error larger than either accuracy alone, so a gap that looks large in a leaderboard can easily be within noise.

P11.11 L3 · Application

McNemar's test on a shared test set

Two churn classifiers, A and B, are scored on the same 1000 test customers. The paired outcomes are:

B correct B wrong
A correct 800 70
A wrong 40 90

(a) Compute each model's accuracy.

(b) Carry out McNemar's test. Report \(\chi^2\), the p-value and the conclusion at \(\alpha = 0.05\). Quote the continuity-corrected statistic as a check.

(c) A colleague ignores the pairing and runs a pooled two-proportion \(z\) test on 870/1000 versus 840/1000. Compute their \(z\) and p-value. Why do the two analyses disagree, and which is right?

(d) Suppose instead the table had been: both correct 720, A correct and B wrong 150, A wrong and B correct 120, both wrong 10. Show that the accuracies are the same as before, and redo McNemar's test.

(e) What does the comparison of (b) and (d) teach about the information an accuracy gap carries?

Hint

Only the off-diagonal cells enter McNemar's test: \(b = 70\) (A right, B wrong) and \(c = 40\) (A wrong, B right).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\text{acc}_A = \frac{800 + 70}{1000} = \mathbf{0.87}\), \(\text{acc}_B = \frac{800 + 40}{1000} = \mathbf{0.84}\).

(b)

\[ \chi^2 = \frac{(70 - 40)^2}{70 + 40} = \frac{900}{110} = \mathbf{8.18}, \qquad p = P(\chi^2_1 > 8.18) = \mathbf{0.0042}. \]

The corrected statistic is \(\frac{29^2}{110} = 7.65\) with \(p = 0.0057\). Either way reject \(H_0\): A is significantly more accurate than B on this population.

(c) The pooled proportion is 0.855, so

\[ SE = \sqrt{0.855 \times 0.145 \times \frac{2}{1000}} = 0.01575, \qquad z = \frac{0.03}{0.01575} = \mathbf{1.91}, \qquad p = \mathbf{0.057}. \]

This test is not significant at 5% and is the wrong test. It assumes the two accuracies come from independent samples, but both models were scored on the same customers; 890 of the 1000 cases (both right or both wrong) contribute nothing to the difference yet inflate its assumed variance. McNemar's test uses the pairing correctly.

(d) \(\text{acc}_A = \frac{720 + 150}{1000} = 0.87\) and \(\text{acc}_B = \frac{720 + 120}{1000} = 0.84\), the same as before.

\[ \chi^2 = \frac{(150 - 120)^2}{270} = \frac{900}{270} = \mathbf{3.33}, \qquad p = \mathbf{0.068}. \]

Now the gap is not significant.

(e) The same 3-point gap is convincing when the models rarely disagree (110 discordant cases, split 70 to 40) and unconvincing when they disagree often (270 cases, split 150 to 120). The accuracies alone cannot tell you whether a gap is significant; you need the paired disagreement counts.

Key insight: When two models share a test set, the evidence for "A beats B" lives entirely in the cases where they disagree; McNemar's test reads exactly that evidence and ignores the rest.

P11.12 L4 · Analysis

Deriving the standard error of an accuracy estimate

Let \(X_i = 1\) if the model classifies test case \(i\) correctly and 0 otherwise, for \(n\) test cases drawn independently from the deployment population. Let \(p\) be the model's true accuracy and \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i\).

(a) Show that \(E[\hat{p}] = p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{p}) = \frac{p(1 - p)}{n}\). Explain where independence is used.

(b) Justify the interval \(\hat{p} \pm z\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}\).

(c) At which \(p\) is the standard error largest? Use this to find the smallest test set that guarantees a 95% half-width of at most 0.02 whatever the accuracy turns out to be.

(d) Now two models A and B are scored on the same \(n\) cases, with correctness indicators \(X_{Ai}\) and \(X_{Bi}\). Show that

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_A) + \operatorname{Var}(X_B) - 2\operatorname{Cov}(X_A, X_B)}{n}, \]

and explain why pairing helps when the models tend to be right on the same cases.

(e) Let \(D_i = X_{Ai} - X_{Bi} \in \{-1, 0, 1\}\). With \(b\) cases where only A is right and \(c\) where only B is right, estimate \(\operatorname{Var}(D)\) and compute the paired \(z = \frac{\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B}{SE}\) for the data of P11.11(b), \(b = 70\), \(c = 40\), \(n = 1000\). Compare \(z^2\) with McNemar's \(\chi^2 = 8.18\).

Hint

Each \(X_i\) is Bernoulli: \(E[X_i] = p\), \(E[X_i^2] = p\). For (e), \(D_i\) is \(+1\) with probability \(b/n\), \(-1\) with probability \(c/n\), and 0 otherwise.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Linearity of expectation gives \(E[\hat{p}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum E[X_i] = \frac{1}{n} \cdot np = p\), so \(\hat{p}\) is unbiased. For one case, \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = E[X_i^2] - p^2 = p - p^2 = p(1 - p)\). Independence makes all covariances zero, so the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat{p}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \frac{np(1 - p)}{n^2} = \mathbf{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}. \]

Equivalently, \(n\hat{p} \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)\).

(b) By the central limit theorem \(\hat{p}\) is approximately \(N\!\left(p, \frac{p(1 - p)}{n}\right)\) for large \(n\), so \(P\left(\lvert \hat{p} - p \rvert \le z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}\right) \approx 1 - \alpha\). The unknown \(p\) inside the square root is replaced by \(\hat{p}\), which gives the Wald interval. It is reliable when \(n\hat{p}\) and \(n(1 - \hat{p})\) are both reasonably large (say at least 10).

(c) \(p(1 - p)\) has derivative \(1 - 2p\), which is zero at \(p = 0.5\), where \(p(1 - p) = 0.25\) is largest. Then

\[ 1.96 \times \frac{0.5}{\sqrt{n}} \le 0.02 \;\Rightarrow\; n \ge \left(\frac{1.96 \times 0.5}{0.02}\right)^2 = \mathbf{2401}. \]

(d) \(\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B = \frac{1}{n}\sum (X_{Ai} - X_{Bi})\) is a mean of \(n\) independent copies of \(D = X_A - X_B\), so its variance is \(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(D)}{n}\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(D) = \operatorname{Var}(X_A) + \operatorname{Var}(X_B) - 2\operatorname{Cov}(X_A, X_B)\). Models usually find the same cases easy or hard, so the covariance is positive and the variance of the difference is smaller than the independent-samples value \(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_A) + \operatorname{Var}(X_B)}{n}\). In P11.11 the correlation between \(X_A\) and \(X_B\) is about 0.56.

(e) \(E[D] = \frac{b - c}{n}\) and \(E[D^2] = \frac{b + c}{n}\), so

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(D) = \frac{b + c}{n} - \left(\frac{b - c}{n}\right)^2 = 0.110 - 0.0009 = 0.1091. \]

\[ SE = \sqrt{\frac{0.1091}{1000}} = 0.01045, \qquad z = \frac{0.03}{0.01045} = \mathbf{2.87}, \qquad z^2 = \mathbf{8.25}. \]

This is almost exactly McNemar's 8.18. (McNemar's statistic is \(\frac{(b - c)^2}{b + c}\), which is the same calculation with the small term \(\left(\frac{b - c}{n}\right)^2\) dropped, as it is under \(H_0\).) The paired standard error, 0.0104, is much smaller than the unpaired 0.0157 of P11.11(c).

Key insight: The standard error of an accuracy is the standard error of a Bernoulli mean; pairing two models on one test set subtracts their covariance, and McNemar's test is simply that paired \(z\) test written in terms of the discordant counts.

13.C Fairness, Accountability, Transparency (11.3)

P11.13 L1 · Foundation

FAccT vocabulary

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "An ML model only follows the instructions in its code, so it cannot discriminate."

(b) "Negative legacy is bias that enters a model through historical data and labels that record past discrimination."

(c) "A model achieves fairness through unawareness if none of the sensitive features (such as race or gender) are used as inputs."

(d) "Fairness through unawareness guarantees that the model's decisions are statistically independent of the sensitive attribute."

(e) "Accountability is the question of who takes responsibility when an ML model fails or causes harm."

(f) "COMPAS predicts a defendant's risk of reoffending from 137 features; if race is not one of them, the tool cannot produce racially different error rates."

(g) "Fairness, in the sense of slide 740, is the absence of bias towards an individual or a group."

Hint

Slide 740 asks "Aren't machines just following human instructions?" and answers that models approximate patterns in data. Ask where the patterns come from.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) False. A trained model's behaviour comes from the data, not from hand-written rules. It approximates the patterns in its training data and can learn, and even amplify, the biases in them (slide 740).

(b) True. If past hiring, lending or policing decisions were biased, labels such as "hired", "repaid" or "re-arrested" encode that bias, and a model trained to reproduce them inherits it (slide 739).

(c) True. That is the definition on slide 741.

(d) False. Other features can encode the sensitive attribute (postcode, shopping habits, first name). The model can rebuild the attribute from these proxies, and its decisions remain correlated with it (slide 742; P11.15, P11.16).

(e) True. Slide 735 frames accountability as "Who takes the responsibilities for failed ML models?"

(f) False. Features such as prior arrests, neighbourhood or age at first arrest can be correlated with race, and arrest records themselves can reflect unequal policing. Excluding race does not stop the error rates from differing by race.

(g) True. This is the definition the slides quote from Mehrabi et al. (2019).

Key insight: A model is a mirror of its data: removing a column does not remove the information in it, and labels produced by a biased process teach the model that bias.

P11.14 L2 · Computation

Three fairness metrics from two confusion matrices

A loan model is audited on 1000 past applicants, split into two groups. "Positive" means the applicant actually repaid; the model approves (predicts positive) or rejects.

Group TP FP FN TN Total
A 240 40 60 160 500
B 140 30 60 270 500

(a) Compute each group's base rate and accuracy.

(b) Compute the selection (approval) rates and the demographic parity difference. Compute the disparate-impact ratio (lower selection rate divided by higher) and compare it with the common "four-fifths" threshold of 0.8.

(c) Compute the TPRs and the equal-opportunity difference. Also compute the FPRs: does the model satisfy equalized odds (equal TPR and equal FPR)?

(d) Compute the precisions and the predictive-parity difference.

(e) Which group is disadvantaged by each criterion, and in what sense?

Hint

Selection rate \(= \frac{TP + FP}{n}\), \(TPR = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\), precision \(= \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\). Compute each one per group, then subtract.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Base rates: A \(= \frac{300}{500} = \mathbf{0.60}\), B \(= \frac{200}{500} = \mathbf{0.40}\). Accuracies: A \(= \frac{400}{500} = \mathbf{0.80}\), B \(= \frac{410}{500} = \mathbf{0.82}\). By accuracy the model looks slightly better for B.

(b)

\[ \text{SR}_A = \frac{280}{500} = 0.56, \qquad \text{SR}_B = \frac{170}{500} = 0.34, \qquad \Delta_{DP} = \mathbf{0.22}. \]

The ratio is \(\frac{0.34}{0.56} = \mathbf{0.607} < 0.8\), so by the four-fifths rule of thumb this would be flagged as disparate impact against B.

(c) \(TPR_A = \frac{240}{300} = 0.80\) and \(TPR_B = \frac{140}{200} = 0.70\), so the equal-opportunity difference is 0.10: a B applicant who would repay is approved 70% of the time, against 80% for A. \(FPR_A = \frac{40}{200} = 0.20\) and \(FPR_B = \frac{30}{300} = 0.10\). Equalized odds fails on both components.

(d) \(\text{prec}_A = \frac{240}{280} = 0.857\) and \(\text{prec}_B = \frac{140}{170} = 0.824\), so the predictive-parity difference is 0.034, small. An approval means nearly the same thing in both groups.

(e) Demographic parity and equal opportunity both say B is disadvantaged (fewer approvals overall, and fewer approvals among people who would repay). Predictive parity is nearly satisfied. The FPRs show that A's non-repayers are approved twice as often as B's, which benefits A applicants but costs the lender. Part of the selection gap is explained by the different base rates (0.60 versus 0.40), which is why demographic parity alone is not a full verdict.

Key insight: "Is the model fair?" has no single answer: each fairness metric conditions on a different set of people (everyone, the truly positive, the predicted positive), and the same model can pass one and fail another.

P11.15 L2 · Computation

Measuring how strongly a proxy encodes a protected attribute

In a hiring data set of 20 applicants, \(G = 1\) marks membership of a protected group and \(Z = 1\) marks "often shops at market M" (compare slide 742). Race is not given to the model, but \(Z\) is.

\(Z = 1\) \(Z = 0\) Total
\(G = 1\) 8 2 10
\(G = 0\) 2 8 10

(a) Compute \(P(Z = 1 \mid G = 1)\), \(P(Z = 1 \mid G = 0)\) and \(P(G = 1 \mid Z = 1)\).

(b) Compute the correlation between \(Z\) and \(G\) (the phi coefficient of the 2-by-2 table).

(c) How accurately can \(G\) be guessed from \(Z\) alone, using the rule "guess \(G = 1\) iff \(Z = 1\)"?

(d) A "blind" screening model learned from historical decisions rejects everyone with \(Z = 1\). Compute the selection rate in each group and the demographic parity difference.

Hint

For a 2-by-2 table with cells \(a, b\) (first row) and \(c, d\) (second row), \(\phi = \frac{ad - bc}{\sqrt{(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)}}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(P(Z = 1 \mid G = 1) = \frac{8}{10} = \mathbf{0.8}\), \(P(Z = 1 \mid G = 0) = \frac{2}{10} = \mathbf{0.2}\), \(P(G = 1 \mid Z = 1) = \frac{8}{10} = \mathbf{0.8}\).

(b)

\[ \phi = \frac{8 \times 8 - 2 \times 2}{\sqrt{10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10}} = \frac{60}{100} = \mathbf{0.60}. \]

(c) The rule is right for the 8 + 8 diagonal cases: accuracy 16/20 = 0.80, against 0.50 for guessing.

(d) Applicants with \(Z = 0\) are selected: \(\frac{2}{10} = \mathbf{0.2}\) in group \(G = 1\) and \(\frac{8}{10} = \mathbf{0.8}\) in group \(G = 0\). The demographic parity difference is 0.6, although \(G\) was never an input.

Key insight: A feature that predicts the protected attribute 80% of the time is the protected attribute with some noise added; "not using race" means nothing if the model can recover race from what it does use.

P11.16 L3 · Application

A "blind" hiring tree that rediscovers ethnicity

A firm trains a hiring model on 40 past applicants. Ethnicity (Hispanic or White) is removed before training, so the model sees only \(Q\) (meets the skills requirement: yes/no) and \(M\) (often shops at market M: yes/no). The label is the past recruiters' decision, "Hired".

\(M\) \(Q\) Hispanic White Total Hired
yes yes 8 1 9 2
yes no 8 1 9 0
no yes 2 9 11 10
no no 2 9 11 2

(a) Show that both ethnic groups have the same qualification rate. Compute the correlation (phi) between \(M = \text{yes}\) and being Hispanic.

(b) Count the training errors (against "Hired") of the one-feature rules "hire iff \(Q = \text{yes}\)" and "hire iff \(M = \text{no}\)".

(c) A depth-2 decision tree predicts the majority label in each of the four cells. Write its rule and count its training errors.

(d) For the tree of (c), compute the selection rate of each ethnic group and, among qualified applicants only, the hiring rate of each group.

(e) The firm's data scientist argues that the tree is "fair through unawareness" and also more accurate than the \(Q\)-only rule. Rebut both claims.

Hint

The tree that best fits biased labels will use any feature that helps it reproduce those labels, including one that mostly encodes ethnicity.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Hispanic qualified: \(8 + 2 = 10\) of 20; White qualified: \(1 + 9 = 10\) of 20. Both 50%. For \(M\): Hispanic 16 yes and 4 no; White 2 yes and 18 no.

\[ \phi = \frac{16 \times 18 - 4 \times 2}{\sqrt{20 \times 20 \times 18 \times 22}} = \frac{280}{398.0} = \mathbf{0.70}. \]

(b) "Hire iff \(Q = \text{yes}\)": of the 20 qualified, 12 were hired, so 8 errors; of the 20 unqualified, 2 were hired, so 2 errors. 10 errors (accuracy 0.75). "Hire iff \(M = \text{no}\)": of 22 with \(M = \text{no}\), 12 hired, so 10 errors; of 18 with \(M = \text{yes}\), 2 hired. 12 errors (accuracy 0.70).

(c) The cell majorities are: (yes, yes) 2 of 9 hired, so reject; (yes, no) reject; (no, yes) 10 of 11, so hire; (no, no) 2 of 11, so reject. The rule is hire iff \(Q = \text{yes}\) and \(M = \text{no}\), with \(2 + 0 + 1 + 2 = \mathbf{5}\) errors (accuracy 0.875).

(d) Only the (no, yes) cell is hired: 2 Hispanic and 9 White applicants.

\[ \text{SR}_{\text{Hispanic}} = \frac{2}{20} = \mathbf{0.10}, \qquad \text{SR}_{\text{White}} = \frac{9}{20} = \mathbf{0.45}. \]

Among qualified applicants, \(\frac{2}{10} = \mathbf{0.20}\) of Hispanic and \(\frac{9}{10} = \mathbf{0.90}\) of White applicants are hired. The equal-opportunity gap is 0.70.

(e) Unawareness: the tree never sees ethnicity, but \(M\) is a strong proxy (\(\phi = 0.70\)), and splitting on it rebuilds the ethnic gap: equally qualified Hispanic applicants are hired at less than a quarter of the White rate. Accuracy: the tree is "more accurate" only against labels that record past recruiters' bias. Qualified applicants who shop at market M (8 of those 9 are Hispanic) were hired 2 times in 9, while qualified applicants who do not (9 of 11 White) were hired 10 times in 11: the labels record the recruiters' bias, not merit. A model that reproduces those labels reproduces the bias, so the \(Q\)-only rule (equal selection rate 0.5 for both groups) is penalised for refusing to discriminate. Fixes start with auditing outcomes by group, questioning the labels, and testing every input for proxy strength, not just deleting the sensitive column.

Key insight: Fairness through unawareness fails twice over: proxies let the model recover the hidden attribute, and biased labels reward it for doing so, so higher accuracy against history can mean more faithful discrimination.

P11.17 L3 · Application

Negative legacy: when the label itself is biased

A risk tool is trained to predict "re-arrested within two years". Two districts each have 1000 released defendants, and in both districts exactly 300 actually reoffend. District B is policed much more heavily: a reoffence in B leads to a recorded re-arrest with probability 0.9, in district A with probability 0.5. Assume no one is arrested who did not reoffend.

(a) Compute the recorded re-arrest rate in each district.

(b) Model P is a perfect predictor of true reoffending: it flags exactly the 300 real reoffenders in each district. Evaluate it against the recorded labels: compute precision, FPR and accuracy in each district.

(c) Model R is trained on the records and reproduces them exactly: it flags the 150 recorded re-arrests in A and the 270 in B. Evaluate it against the recorded labels, then against the true outcomes (TPR, FPR, selection rate per district).

(d) An auditor with access only to arrest records compares P and R. Which model will they call more accurate, and which fairer? What is actually true?

Hint

Under recorded labels, a real reoffender who was never re-arrested counts as a negative, so flagging that person counts as a false positive.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) A: \(0.5 \times 300 = 150\), rate 0.15. B: \(0.9 \times 300 = 270\), rate 0.27. The true rate is 0.30 in both.

(b) In A, P flags 300; 150 are recorded (TP) and 150 are unrecorded reoffenders (FP against the records), and 700 non-reoffenders are TN.

\[ \text{prec}_A = \frac{150}{300} = \mathbf{0.50}, \qquad FPR_A = \frac{150}{850} = \mathbf{0.176}, \qquad \text{acc}_A = \frac{850}{1000} = \mathbf{0.85}. \]

In B, TP = 270, FP = 30, TN = 700:

\[ \text{prec}_B = \frac{270}{300} = \mathbf{0.90}, \qquad FPR_B = \frac{30}{730} = \mathbf{0.041}, \qquad \text{acc}_B = \mathbf{0.97}. \]

On paper the perfect model looks worse and "unfair" to district A.

(c) Against the records, R is perfect in both districts (accuracy 1, no errors). Against the truth, \(TPR_A = \frac{150}{300} = \mathbf{0.50}\) and \(TPR_B = \frac{270}{300} = \mathbf{0.90}\), \(FPR = 0\) in both, and the selection rates are 0.15 versus 0.27, a demographic parity gap of 0.12 between two populations with identical true risk.

(d) The records-only auditor calls R both more accurate and fairer. In truth, P treats the two districts identically, while R flags B residents 1.8 times as often as A residents for the same behaviour, because it learned the policing pattern rather than the offending pattern. Every metric computed against biased labels inherits the bias.

Key insight: Negative legacy is not cured by a better model or a better metric: if the label measures "was caught" rather than "did it", the model, its accuracy and its fairness audit all measure the policing.

P11.18 L4 · Analysis

Equal error rates cannot give equal precision when base rates differ

A classifier has \(TPR = 0.8\) and \(FPR = 0.1\) in both of two groups, so it satisfies equalized odds. Group A has base rate \(\pi_A = 0.5\) and group B has \(\pi_B = 0.2\).

(a) For 1000 people in each group, write the confusion matrices.

(b) Compute precision (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV) and selection rate in each group.

(c) Show in general that

\[ \text{PPV} = \frac{TPR \cdot \pi}{TPR \cdot \pi + FPR \cdot (1 - \pi)}, \]

and prove that, for fixed \(TPR > 0\) and \(FPR > 0\), PPV is strictly increasing in \(\pi\).

(d) Keeping \(TPR_B = 0.8\), what would \(FPR_B\) have to be for group B to reach group A's precision? What does that do to equalized odds?

(e) Conclude: under what conditions can a classifier satisfy equalized odds, predictive parity and demographic parity at once?

Hint

Write PPV as \(\frac{1}{1 + \frac{FPR}{TPR} \cdot \frac{1 - \pi}{\pi}}\) and look at what happens to \(\frac{1 - \pi}{\pi}\) as \(\pi\) grows.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

Group TP FN FP TN
A (500 positive, 500 negative) 400 100 50 450
B (200 positive, 800 negative) 160 40 80 720

(b)

\[ \text{PPV}_A = \frac{400}{450} = \mathbf{0.889}, \qquad \text{PPV}_B = \frac{160}{240} = \mathbf{0.667}. \]

\(\text{NPV}_A = \frac{450}{550} = \mathbf{0.818}\) and \(\text{NPV}_B = \frac{720}{760} = \mathbf{0.947}\). Selection rates are \(\frac{450}{1000} = \mathbf{0.45}\) and \(\frac{240}{1000} = \mathbf{0.24}\). Equal error rates give a 22-point precision gap and a 21-point selection gap.

(c) Per person, \(P(\text{flag}, \text{positive}) = TPR \cdot \pi\) and \(P(\text{flag}, \text{negative}) = FPR \cdot (1 - \pi)\), and PPV is the first divided by their sum. Dividing through by \(TPR \cdot \pi\),

\[ \text{PPV}(\pi) = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{FPR}{TPR} \cdot \frac{1 - \pi}{\pi}}. \]

The factor \(\frac{1 - \pi}{\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi} - 1\) is strictly decreasing in \(\pi\), and \(\frac{FPR}{TPR} > 0\), so the denominator decreases and PPV strictly increases with \(\pi\). Two groups with the same TPR and FPR therefore have equal PPV only if \(\pi_A = \pi_B\) (or \(FPR = 0\), which makes \(\text{PPV} = 1\) in both).

(d)

\[ \frac{0.16}{0.16 + 0.8 \, FPR_B} = \frac{0.4}{0.45} \;\Rightarrow\; 0.16 + 0.8 \, FPR_B = 0.18 \;\Rightarrow\; FPR_B = \mathbf{0.025}. \]

Group B's FPR would have to be a quarter of A's 0.1, so equalized odds breaks: the classifier must hold the lower-base-rate group to a stricter standard to make its flags equally reliable.

(e) Selection rate is \(TPR \cdot \pi + FPR(1 - \pi)\), which also varies with \(\pi\) whenever \(TPR \ne FPR\). Equal TPR and FPR plus equal selection rates require \((TPR - FPR)(\pi_A - \pi_B) = 0\), so with different base rates \(TPR = FPR\); but then \(\text{PPV} = \pi\), which differs between the groups unless \(TPR = FPR = 0\). All three criteria hold together only for the useless classifier that flags nobody. Even a perfect classifier (\(TPR = 1\), \(FPR = 0\)) gets equalized odds and predictive parity but selects 50% versus 20%, failing demographic parity. With equal base rates, there is no conflict.

Key insight: When groups differ in base rate, "equally accurate errors" and "equally reliable flags" are mathematically incompatible; choosing a fairness criterion is a value judgement about which kind of error matters most, not a technical detail.

13.D Interpretability (11.4)

P11.19 L1 · Foundation

Interpretable models and who needs them

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "A shallow decision tree is interpretable because every prediction can be read as a path of if-then conditions from the root to a leaf."

(b) "A k-NN prediction can be explained by showing the \(k\) training examples that voted for it."

(c) "In a linear regression, the feature with the largest absolute coefficient is always the most important one."

(d) "Interpretability matters only to model designers who want to debug their models."

(e) "Because high-performing models tend to be less interpretable (slide 748), a more interpretable model is always less accurate."

(f) "On MNIST digit recognition, a deep convolutional network is typically far more accurate, and far less interpretable, than a linear classifier."

(g) "A logistic regression coefficient \(w_j\) means that a one-unit increase in \(x_j\), with the other features held fixed, multiplies the odds of the positive class by \(e^{w_j}\)."

Hint

Slide 743 lists three groups who benefit from interpretability. For (c), ask what happens to a coefficient if you measure the feature in grams instead of kilograms.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. The contact-lens tree of slide 744 is an example: each leaf is a conjunction of readable conditions.

(b) True. "These five past cases are most similar to you, and four of them were approved" is an explanation by example (slide 747).

(c) False. A coefficient's size depends on the feature's units. Measuring area in square metres instead of square feet multiplies its coefficient by about 10.8 without changing the model. Compare coefficients only after standardising the features (P11.22).

(d) False. Slide 743 names end users (trust, understanding consequences), regulators (compliance, audits, accountability) and model designers (diagnosis).

(e) False. It is a tendency, not a law. On many tabular problems a well-tuned logistic regression or small tree is within noise of a black box (P11.21); the trade-off has to be measured, not assumed.

(f) True. Linear classifiers reach roughly 92% on MNIST and convolutional networks over 99%; the network's millions of weights have no individual meaning.

(g) True. This is the odds-ratio reading of slide 253: the log-odds rise by \(w_j\), so the odds are multiplied by \(e^{w_j}\).

Key insight: Interpretable models explain themselves through their structure (paths, coefficients, neighbours); the price of a black box must be justified by a measured, significant gain in performance.

P11.20 L2 · Computation

Explaining one decision of a logistic regression

A lender's logistic regression gives the log-odds of repayment as

\[ z = -1.5 + 0.30\,x_1 - 0.05\,x_2 + 0.20\,x_3, \]

where \(x_1\) is annual income in lakh rupees, \(x_2\) is the debt-to-income ratio in percent, and \(x_3\) is years in current employment. An applicant has \(x_1 = 6\), \(x_2 = 40\), \(x_3 = 2\).

(a) Compute \(z\), the predicted probability of repayment and the decision at threshold 0.5.

(b) Write each feature's contribution \(w_j x_j\) to \(z\). Which feature drives the rejection?

(c) Compute and interpret the odds ratio \(e^{w_j}\) for each feature. By what factor do the odds change if the debt ratio falls by 10 points?

(d) The applicant asks what would change the decision. Holding the other features fixed, find the change in each single feature that brings \(z\) to 0.

Hint

\(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\), and the decision flips exactly where \(z = 0\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ z = -1.5 + 1.8 - 2.0 + 0.4 = \mathbf{-1.3}, \qquad P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{1.3}} = \mathbf{0.214}. \]

Rejected.

(b) Income contributes +1.8, debt ratio −2.0, employment +0.4, and the intercept −1.5. The debt-to-income ratio is the largest negative contribution.

(c) \(e^{0.30} = \mathbf{1.35}\): each extra lakh of income multiplies the odds of repayment by 1.35. \(e^{-0.05} = \mathbf{0.951}\): each extra point of debt ratio cuts the odds by about 4.9%. \(e^{0.20} = \mathbf{1.22}\) per year of employment. A 10-point fall in debt ratio multiplies the odds by \(e^{0.5} = \mathbf{1.65}\).

(d) The model needs \(\Delta z = +1.3\).

\[ \Delta x_2 = \frac{1.3}{-0.05} = -26, \qquad \Delta x_1 = \frac{1.3}{0.30} = 4.33, \qquad \Delta x_3 = \frac{1.3}{0.20} = 6.5. \]

So: debt ratio down from 40% to 14%, or income up by 4.33 lakh (to 10.33), or 6.5 more years of employment.

Key insight: A linear model's explanation is exact arithmetic: each feature's contribution to the score can be listed, and the counterfactual "what would change the decision" is a one-line division, something a black box cannot give directly.

P11.21 L3 · Application

Reading a tree and a k-NN vote, and weighing a black box

A bank compares an interpretable decision tree with a gradient-boosted ensemble (GB) for loan approval. The tree is:

  • If debt ratio \(> 45\%\): reject.
  • Else, if years employed \(< 1\):
    • if income \(< 4\) lakh: reject;
    • else: approve.
  • Else: approve.

(a) Explain, as you would to the applicant, the tree's decision for P (debt ratio 30%, 0.5 years employed, income 3.5 lakh) and for Q (debt ratio 50%, 10 years employed, income 20 lakh).

(b) A 5-NN model is also tried. For applicant P, the 5 nearest past applicants (after scaling) had outcomes: repaid, repaid, defaulted, repaid, defaulted. What does 5-NN predict, and what is its explanation? Give one weakness of this explanation.

(c) On the same 2000 test applicants, the tree is correct on 1720 and GB on 1750. The tree is right where GB is wrong on 135 cases, and GB is right where the tree is wrong on 165 cases. Compute both accuracies with 95% confidence intervals, then run McNemar's test.

(d) The regulator requires that every rejected applicant receives the main reasons for the rejection. Which model would you deploy, and why?

Hint

For McNemar, \(b = 135\) and \(c = 165\). Ask whether 1.5 points of accuracy are clearly real before paying for them with interpretability.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) P: debt ratio 30% is not above 45%; employed less than 1 year; income 3.5 lakh is below 4 lakh, so rejected: "short employment history combined with low income". Q: debt ratio 50% exceeds 45%, so rejected at the first question, regardless of the high income and long employment: "debt ratio above 45%". The path is the explanation.

(b) 3 of 5 neighbours repaid, so 5-NN predicts repay (approve). Explanation: "the most similar past applicants mostly repaid". Weaknesses: the explanation depends on the distance metric and on feature scaling (which features made these people "similar" is hidden), and a 3-to-2 vote shows the decision is fragile. Note that the tree and the 5-NN model disagree about P.

(c)

\[ \text{Tree: } 0.860 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.86 \times 0.14}{2000}} = 0.860 \pm 0.015 \Rightarrow \mathbf{[0.845,\ 0.875]}, \]

\[ \text{GB: } 0.875 \pm 0.0145 \Rightarrow \mathbf{[0.861,\ 0.889]}. \]

The intervals overlap heavily. McNemar:

\[ \chi^2 = \frac{(135 - 165)^2}{135 + 165} = \frac{900}{300} = \mathbf{3.00}, \qquad p = \mathbf{0.083} \]

(corrected: 2.80, \(p = 0.094\)). The 1.5-point gap is not significant at 5%.

(d) Deploy the tree (or a comparably accurate logistic regression). The accuracy gain from GB is not statistically established, while the tree gives an exact, auditable reason for every rejection and makes proxy or fairness problems visible in its splits. GB would need post-hoc explanation tools whose output approximates, rather than equals, the model's logic. If a larger test set later showed a real and material gain, the decision could be revisited.

Key insight: The interpretability–performance trade-off is only a trade-off if the performance gap is real; test it first, and when it is small or uncertain, the transparent model wins.

P11.22 L4 · Analysis

Linear coefficients versus forest feature importances

A linear regression predicts a flat's price (in lakh rupees) from area (square feet), number of bedrooms and distance to the city centre (km):

Feature Coefficient Standard deviation of feature
Area 0.05 400
Bedrooms 2.0 0.9
Distance −0.8 5

(a) Rank the features by \(\lvert \text{coefficient} \rvert\), then by the effect of a one-standard-deviation change. Which ranking reflects importance, and why?

(b) Suppose a second feature, area in square metres, is added (almost an exact copy of area in square feet). Show that the linear coefficients are no longer identifiable, and explain what ridge regression does with two identical features. What happens to a random forest's impurity-based importances in the same situation?

(c) A random forest on the same task has test \(R^2 = 0.86\). Permuting each feature's column in the test set gives \(R^2 = 0.52\) for area, 0.83 for bedrooms and 0.74 for distance. Compute the permutation importances and rank the features.

(d) List three things the linear model's coefficients tell a user that the forest's importances do not.

(e) Give one situation in which you would still prefer the forest.

Hint

The standardised effect of feature \(j\) is \(w_j \times \operatorname{sd}(x_j)\). For (b), if \(x_2 = x_1\) then \(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 = (w_1 + w_2) x_1\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) By \(\lvert w \rvert\): bedrooms (2.0), distance (0.8), area (0.05). By one-standard-deviation effect:

\[ \text{area: } 0.05 \times 400 = \mathbf{20}, \qquad \text{distance: } -0.8 \times 5 = \mathbf{-4}, \qquad \text{bedrooms: } 2.0 \times 0.9 = \mathbf{1.8}. \]

The second ranking (area, distance, bedrooms) reflects importance. A raw coefficient is "per unit", and the units differ: one square foot is tiny, one bedroom is large. Standardising puts every feature on the scale of its typical variation.

(b) With \(x_2 \approx c\,x_1\), the model depends (almost) only on \(w_1 + c\,w_2\), so infinitely many coefficient pairs fit equally well; ordinary least squares returns unstable values, possibly huge and of opposite sign (one simulated run gave 14.4 and −11.4 for a true effect of 3). Ridge picks the minimum-norm split and, for exact copies, divides the effect equally (1.5 and 1.5 for a true 3). A random forest uses the two columns interchangeably at its splits, so its impurity importance is also shared between them and each copy looks about half as important as the single feature did. Either way, "importance" of correlated features must be read as a group.

(c) Importance is the drop in \(R^2\): area \(0.86 - 0.52 = \mathbf{0.34}\), distance \(0.86 - 0.74 = \mathbf{0.12}\), bedrooms \(0.86 - 0.83 = \mathbf{0.03}\). The ranking agrees with the standardised linear effects.

(d) The linear model gives: the direction of each effect (distance lowers price); its size in real units (each extra km costs 0.8 lakh); and an exact per-prediction decomposition (P11.20). It also states that the effect is the same for every flat. Forest importances are global, unsigned and only relative; impurity-based importance is also biased towards features with many distinct values (as information gain is biased towards attributes like Customer ID in Module 5).

(e) When the relationship is strongly non-linear or full of interactions (for example, distance matters much more for small flats), the forest is clearly and significantly more accurate on held-out data, and the use (say, an internal price estimate reviewed by a human) does not require a legally binding explanation of each prediction.

Key insight: A linear coefficient is a signed, per-unit, per-prediction explanation but must be standardised before comparison; a forest's importance is only a global ranking and is easily distorted by correlated or high-cardinality features.

13.E Module 11 Capstone

P11.23 L5 · Mastery

Designing the evaluation protocol for a loan model

A bank has five years of past loan applications (60,000 loans with known repayment outcomes, 8% defaults) and wants to replace its scorecard with a new model. Applicants come from two regions; region R2 is a small minority. You are asked to write the evaluation protocol that must be passed before deployment.

(a) How should the data be split, and why might a random split be the wrong choice here?

(b) Which performance metrics will you report, and which one is the headline? Justify using the 8% default rate and the different costs of a bad loan and a wrongly rejected good applicant.

(c) Describe the subgroup analysis. In the test set, region R2 has 300 applicants with accuracy 0.80, and only 60 R2 applicants who would repay; their TPR is 0.70. Compute the 95% half-widths for these two estimates. The majority region has a TPR of 0.80 on 600 repayers. Is the TPR gap of 0.10 significant? What does this imply for the audit?

(d) Which fairness metrics will you compute, and what will you do about proxy features?

(e) What interpretability and accountability requirements will you add?

(f) What happens after deployment?

Hint

Every number in the protocol, including each fairness metric, is an estimate from a sample; small subgroups need intervals and tests just as overall accuracy does.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Use an out-of-time split: train and tune (by stratified \(k\)-fold CV) on the first years, validate on the next period, and keep the most recent year as the test set, touched once. A random split mixes future and past loans, so it overstates performance when economic conditions drift. Stratify by default status and region so that rare cells appear in every fold.

(b) Accuracy is useless as a headline: rejecting nobody already scores 92%. Report ROC-AUC (ranking quality), precision and recall for defaults at the operating threshold, a calibration check (predicted default probabilities match observed rates, since they feed pricing), and the headline: expected cost (or profit) at the chosen threshold, with the threshold set on the validation data from the cost of a bad loan versus a lost good customer. Give a confidence interval for every number.

(c) Compute the full confusion matrix and all metrics per region (and per other protected attribute available for audit, such as gender and age band).

\[ \text{acc}_{R2}: \; 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.8 \times 0.2}{300}} = \pm\mathbf{0.045}, \qquad TPR_{R2}: \; 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.70 \times 0.30}{60}} = \pm\mathbf{0.116}. \]

For the TPR gap (repayers approved: 480 of 600 versus 42 of 60), the pooled proportion is \(\frac{522}{660} = 0.791\) and

\[ SE = \sqrt{0.791 \times 0.209 \times \left(\frac{1}{600} + \frac{1}{60}\right)} = 0.0551, \qquad z = \frac{0.10}{0.0551} = \mathbf{1.82}, \qquad p \approx \mathbf{0.069}. \]

Not significant at 5%, but far too uncertain to call the model fair: the R2 TPR could plausibly be anywhere from 0.58 to 0.82. The audit should report intervals, use a larger evaluation sample for R2 (more test years, or pooled out-of-time folds), and treat "no significant gap" as "not yet shown", not as "fair".

(d) Report selection rate (demographic parity), TPR among repayers (equal opportunity), FPR (equalized odds) and precision/calibration per group (predictive parity), and state in advance which one is the binding criterion and why (P11.18 shows they cannot all be equal when default rates differ). For proxies: remove the protected attribute from the inputs but keep it for auditing; measure how well each input (postcode, employer, shopping data) predicts region or other protected attributes (P11.15); drop or constrain strong proxies; and check whether the historical labels themselves reflect past exclusion (negative legacy, P11.17), for example applicants who were never given loans and so have no outcome.

(e) Every rejection must come with the main reasons (adverse-action reasons), so either use an interpretable model (scorecard or logistic regression, P11.20) or show that a black box is significantly better (P11.21) and validate its explanations. Document data sources, metrics, subgroup results and known limitations; name an accountable owner; keep version-controlled model and data; and have an independent team reproduce the audit.

(f) Monitor the input distribution, the approval rates and default rates per group, and calibration over time; set alert thresholds; re-audit on a fixed schedule and after any retraining; and provide a channel for applicants to contest decisions.

Key insight: A deployment-grade evaluation is a protocol, not a number: honest splits, cost-based metrics with intervals, per-group error analysis with its own uncertainty, a proxy and label audit, explanations, a named owner and monitoring after launch.

P11.24 L5 · Mastery

When is a black box acceptable?

(a) On the MNIST test set of 10,000 images, a multinomial logistic regression reaches 92.0% accuracy and a convolutional network 99.2%. Compute both 95% confidence intervals and the number of misread digits for each. Is the gap in doubt?

(b) For each scenario, say whether a black-box model is acceptable, and what you would require:

(i) sorting handwritten postcodes on letters in a mail centre;

(ii) deciding whether to approve a home loan, in a jurisdiction that requires reasons for every rejection;

(iii) an early-warning score for sepsis in an intensive-care unit, where a nurse decides whether to call a doctor;

(iv) a bail recommendation shown to a judge.

(c) A colleague says: "Explain the black box with its feature-importance chart and we have the best of both worlds." Explain why a random forest's feature-importance ranking is not an explanation of an individual decision in the way a linear model's coefficients are.

(d) Give two ways of reducing the trade-off rather than just choosing a side.

Hint

Ask in each scenario: who bears the cost of an error, can a human check or override it, and is there a legal or ethical right to a reason?

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ 0.920 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.92 \times 0.08}{10000}} = 0.920 \pm 0.0053, \qquad 0.992 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.992 \times 0.008}{10000}} = 0.992 \pm 0.0017. \]

So [0.915, 0.925] versus [0.990, 0.994], with 800 versus 80 errors. The intervals are far apart; the gain (a tenfold reduction in errors) is not in doubt. This is the "high-performing models tend to be less interpretable" picture of slide 748.

(b) (i) Acceptable. Errors are cheap and recoverable (a letter is re-sorted), no one has a right to know why a digit was read as a 7, and the performance gain is huge and certain.

(ii) Generally not, unless it can give faithful reasons. The law requires reasons, and the stakes for the applicant are high. Use an interpretable model unless a black box is significantly and materially better (P11.21), and then only with validated per-decision explanations and a fairness audit.

(iii) Acceptable with conditions. Missing sepsis is very costly, so performance matters greatly, and a human is in the loop. Require external validation on this hospital's patients, subgroup error analysis, calibration, and an explanation of which vital signs drove the alert so staff can sanity-check it and detect failures.

(iv) Not acceptable as an opaque score. The decision affects liberty, the labels carry negative legacy (P11.17), and the defendant has a right to contest the evidence. A transparent model with audited, published error rates by group is required; COMPAS-style secrecy is exactly the accountability failure FAccT addresses (P11.25).

(c) A linear model gives, for each applicant, the signed contribution \(w_j x_j\) of every feature, and these add up exactly to the score (P11.20). A forest's importance is global (averaged over all predictions), unsigned (it says that income matters, not whether more income helps), not additive for a given case, and can be split between or distorted by correlated and high-cardinality features (P11.22). Two applicants with the same importance chart can be rejected for completely different reasons.

(d) For example: (1) check whether the gap is real first: on many tabular tasks a regularised logistic regression or a small tree is within noise of the black box; (2) make the simple model better with feature engineering (binning, interactions, monotone constraints) so that it closes the gap; (3) use the black box for triage and a human or an interpretable model for the final decision; (4) use per-decision explanation methods for the black box, validated against the model and used with care.

Key insight: Whether a black box is acceptable depends less on the model than on the decision: stakes, reversibility, a human in the loop and a right to reasons determine how much measured performance gain is needed to justify giving up transparency.

P11.25 L5 · Mastery

A COMPAS-style dispute: calibrated, yet unequal

A commercial risk tool labels defendants "high risk" or "low risk" of reoffending within two years. A journalist obtains outcomes for 1000 defendants from each of two groups:

Group TP FP FN TN Total
A 375 125 125 375 1000
B 150 50 150 650 1000

(Positive = reoffended; "high risk" = predicted positive.)

(a) Compute the base rate, selection rate, precision, FPR, FNR and accuracy for each group.

(b) The vendor says: "The tool is fair: a high-risk label means the same 75% chance of reoffending in both groups." The journalist says: "The tool is biased: non-reoffenders in group A are wrongly labelled high-risk three and a half times as often as in group B, while reoffenders in group B are twice as likely to be wrongly labelled low-risk." Check both claims against your numbers.

(c) Could the vendor fix the problem the journalist describes without creating the problem the vendor cares about? Use the result of P11.18.

(d) Race is not one of the tool's 137 input features. Give two reasons why its error rates can still differ by race.

(e) Dressel and Farid (2018), cited on slide 738, reported that a simple model using two features (age and number of prior convictions) predicted reoffending about as accurately as the 137-feature tool, at around 65%. What does this add to the critique?

(f) Write a short recommendation for a court considering this tool.

Hint

Both parties are reading the same table correctly; they are conditioning on different rows or columns of it.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

Metric Group A Group B
Base rate 0.50 0.30
Selection rate (high risk) 0.50 0.20
Precision \(\frac{TP}{TP + FP}\) 0.75 0.75
FPR \(\frac{FP}{FP + TN}\) 0.25 0.071
FNR \(\frac{FN}{FN + TP}\) 0.25 0.50
Accuracy 0.75 0.80

(b) Both claims are true. The vendor conditions on the prediction: among people labelled high-risk, 75% reoffend in both groups (predictive parity). The journalist conditions on the outcome: \(\frac{0.25}{0.0714} = 3.5\), so non-reoffenders in A are flagged 3.5 times as often, and \(\frac{0.50}{0.25} = 2\), so reoffenders in B are missed twice as often (equalized odds fails). Group A bears more false "high-risk" labels, which can mean detention; group B bears more false "low-risk" labels.

(c) Not while base rates differ (0.5 versus 0.3). By P11.18, PPV rises with the base rate when TPR and FPR are equal across groups. Equalising FPR and FNR would make a high-risk label less reliable in group B than in group A, breaking predictive parity; keeping predictive parity forces unequal error rates. Society, not the algorithm, must decide which error matters more in a bail decision.

(d) (1) Proxies: features such as neighbourhood, prior arrests, age at first arrest and family history can be correlated with race, so the model can partly reconstruct it (P11.15, P11.16). (2) Negative legacy in the label: "reoffended" is measured by re-arrest, which depends on how heavily a group is policed (P11.17), so the base rates themselves may be inflated for one group. (3) Even with no proxies, different base rates alone produce different error rates (part (c)).

(e) If two transparent features match 137 opaque ones, the tool's complexity buys no accuracy, while it costs transparency and accountability: the defendant cannot inspect or contest the score. About 65% accuracy also means roughly one prediction in three is wrong, which is weak evidence for a decision about liberty. (With roughly 7000 defendants in such a study, a 95% interval on 65% is only about ±1 point, so the similarity is not a small-sample accident.)

(f) Use the score, if at all, only as one input to a human decision; require the vendor to publish the model or use an equally accurate interpretable model; require published per-group error rates (FPR, FNR, precision) with intervals; audit the labels for policing bias; decide explicitly which fairness criterion the court prioritises; and assign accountability for errors.

Key insight: In the COMPAS dispute neither side was miscalculating; with different base rates, calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold, so the real questions are which errors society will accept, how biased the labels are, and whether an opaque tool is justified at all.

P11.26 L5 · Mastery

Six tempting statements about evaluation and fairness

Each statement below was made in a real-sounding project meeting. Say what is wrong with it and what should be said instead, using numbers where given.

(a) "The defect detector is 99% accurate, so it is ready to ship." (Defects occur in 1% of parts.)

(b) "We removed gender and age from the inputs, so the model cannot discriminate on gender or age."

(c) "On our 100,000-case test set, Model B beat Model A with \(p < 0.001\), so B will beat A in production." (Only A right: 1350 cases; only B right: 1650 cases.)

(d) "The model has the same accuracy, 80%, in both groups, so it treats both groups equally."

(e) "We tried 50 architectures and kept the one with the best test score. We never trained on the test set, so the test score is an unbiased estimate."

(f) "The black-box model is 0.5 points more accurate, so we must use it."

Hint

For (c), compute the McNemar statistic and the size of the accuracy gap separately; for (d), recall that a confusion matrix has more than one ratio.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Accuracy paradox. A detector that never flags a defect scores exactly 99%. Say instead: "It catches X% of defects (recall) and Y% of its alarms are real (precision), with ROC-AUC Z, and here is the cost of misses versus false alarms" (P11.6).

(b) Fairness through unawareness fails. Other inputs (job title, part-time status, years since graduation, first name) can act as proxies for gender and age, and historical labels may encode past bias. Say instead: "We kept the protected attributes for auditing, measured proxy strength, and report selection rates and error rates per group" (P11.15, P11.16).

(c) McNemar gives \(\chi^2 = \frac{(1650 - 1350)^2}{3000} = \mathbf{30.0}\), \(p \approx \mathbf{4 \times 10^{-8}}\), so the difference is real on this test population. But the gap is only \(\frac{300}{100000} = \mathbf{0.3}\) points. Statistical significance is not practical importance, and it says nothing about production if the deployment data differ from the test data (new customers, seasonality, drift) or if the test set was reused for selection. Say instead: "B is reliably 0.3 points better on data like our test set; we will confirm the gain with an A/B test or shadow deployment and monitor it."

(d) Equal accuracy hides unequal errors. In P11.25, accuracies were 0.75 and 0.80 while FPRs were 0.25 versus 0.07 and FNRs 0.25 versus 0.50; in P11.14, accuracies were 0.80 and 0.82 while selection rates were 0.56 versus 0.34. Say instead: "Here are TPR, FPR, precision and selection rate for each group."

(e) Selection on the test set is tuning on the test set. The best of 50 noisy scores is optimistically biased (P11.7 found about 5 points of bias for 20 models on 200 cases). Say instead: "We selected by cross-validation; the test set was used once for the final model", or, if it was already used, "we need a fresh test set".

(f) A gap must be shown to be real and material before it outweighs transparency. Test it (P11.21: a 1.5-point gap on 2000 cases had \(p = 0.083\)), put it in cost terms, and weigh it against the need for reasons, audits and contestability (P11.24). Say instead: "If the gain is significant and worth more than the loss of explainability for this decision, we use the black box with safeguards; otherwise we use the interpretable model."

Key insight: Most evaluation failures are not arithmetic errors but category errors: confusing accuracy with usefulness, absence of an input with absence of bias, significance with importance, and a test score with a production guarantee.

PART 14 — Cross-Module Capstones

Each capstone below draws on three or more modules, the way a real machine-learning project does: data preparation from M2 feeds a model from M3–M10, and the result is judged with the evaluation and fairness tools of M11. The capstones deliberately reuse the big ideas of Part 2.1 (loss as likelihood, bias–variance, Bayes' theorem, distance, the linear score, ensembles, and test-set discipline) rather than repeat the module problems, so attempt them only after finishing the module sets. Every number in the answers was computed from the data stated in the problem; carry at least four significant figures through intermediate steps and round only the final answer.

C.1 L5 · Mastery

A churn model from split to sign-off (M2 + M4 + M11)

A telecom company has 1000 customers, of whom 100 churned last quarter. A data scientist holds out 20% of the customers as a test set and trains a logistic regression on two z-scored features, monthly charge \(x_c\) and tenure in months \(x_t\). The scaler was fitted on the training set only and stored \(\bar{x}_c = 70\), \(s_c = 20\), \(\bar{x}_t = 30\), \(s_t = 15\). The fitted model is

\[ z = -2.0 + 0.9\,\tilde{x}_c - 1.1\,\tilde{x}_t, \qquad \hat{p} = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \]

where \(\tilde{x}\) denotes a standardised feature. A missed churner (false negative) costs ₹500 in lost revenue; a retention offer sent to a customer who would have stayed (false positive) costs ₹50. A correct decision costs nothing.

The scores on the 200 test customers fall into four bins:

Score bin Churners Stayers
\([0, 0.1)\) 2 110
\([0.1, 0.3)\) 4 45
\([0.3, 0.5)\) 5 15
\([0.5, 1]\) 9 10

(a) How many churners and stayers should a stratified 80/20 split put in the test set? Under a simple random split of the same size, the number of test churners is hypergeometric with standard deviation 3.80; the probability that it falls outside 16 to 24 is 0.235. What does that mean for the reliability of a recall measured on this test set?

(b) Score a new customer with monthly charge 95 and tenure 6 months. Then show what a pipeline bug that forgets to apply the scaler would output for the same customer.

(c) Derive the cost-minimising threshold \(t^*\) for a calibrated model. Then compute the total test cost of flagging every customer with score at least \(t\), for \(t = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5\), and for the two trivial policies "flag nobody" and "flag everybody". Which threshold wins, and why does it differ from \(t^*\)?

(d) At the winning threshold, give the confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall and \(F_1\). Compute the test AUC from the binned scores (count tied bins as one half).

(e) The baseline "predict nobody churns" is 90% accurate. Give a 95% confidence interval for the model's accuracy at the winning threshold, and run McNemar's test of the model against the baseline. Write the one-paragraph recommendation to the product owner.

Hint

(c) Flag a customer when the expected cost of not flagging, \(500\,p\), exceeds the expected cost of flagging, \(50(1 - p)\). (e) The baseline is right on every stayer and wrong on every churner, so the discordant cells are the model's false positives and true positives.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Stratification keeps the 10% churn rate in both parts: the test set gets 20 churners and 180 stayers, the training set 80 and 720. Under a random split, roughly one split in four would give 15 or fewer, or 25 or more, test churners. With only about 20 positives, a single churner moves recall by 5 points, so an unstratified split adds avoidable noise to exactly the metric the business cares about.

(b) Standardise with the training statistics:

\[ \tilde{x}_c = \frac{95 - 70}{20} = 1.25, \qquad \tilde{x}_t = \frac{6 - 30}{15} = -1.6 \]

\[ z = -2.0 + 0.9(1.25) - 1.1(-1.6) = 0.885, \qquad \hat{p} = \sigma(0.885) = \mathbf{0.708} \]

Without the scaler, \(z = -2.0 + 0.9(95) - 1.1(6) = 76.9\) and \(\hat{p} = \mathbf{1.000}\): every customer with a non-trivial charge looks like a certain churner. The weights were learned in standardised units, so the scaler is part of the model and must be saved and applied with it.

(c) Flag when \(500\,p > 50(1 - p)\), that is

\[ t^* = \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}} = \frac{50}{550} = \mathbf{0.0909} \]

Policy TP FP FN TN Cost (₹)
Flag nobody 0 0 20 180 10000
\(t = 0.5\) 9 10 11 170 6000
\(t = 0.3\) 14 25 6 155 4250
\(t = 0.1\) 18 70 2 110 4500
Flag everybody 20 180 0 0 9000

\(t = 0.3\) wins. The rule \(t^* = 0.0909\) assumes the scores are calibrated. The observed churn rate in the \([0.1, 0.3)\) bin is \(4/49 = 0.082\), which is below 0.0909, so flagging that bin costs more in offers (\(45 \times 50 = 2250\)) than it saves (\(4 \times 500 = 2000\)). The bin \([0.3, 0.5)\) has rate \(5/20 = 0.25 > 0.0909\), so it should be flagged. Thresholds must be checked against observed rates on held-out data, not only derived from formulae.

(d) At \(t = 0.3\): TP = 14, FP = 25, FN = 6, TN = 155.

\[ \text{accuracy} = \frac{169}{200} = \mathbf{0.845}, \quad \text{precision} = \frac{14}{39} = \mathbf{0.359}, \quad \text{recall} = \frac{14}{20} = \mathbf{0.70}, \quad F_1 = \mathbf{0.475} \]

For the AUC, count over all \(20 \times 180 = 3600\) churner–stayer pairs the pairs in which the churner sits in a higher bin, plus one half of the tied pairs. This gives \(3027.5\) favourable pairs, so

\[ \text{AUC} = \frac{3027.5}{3600} = \mathbf{0.841} \]

(e)

\[ SE = \sqrt{\frac{0.845 \times 0.155}{200}} = 0.02559, \qquad \text{CI} = 0.845 \pm 1.96 \times 0.02559 = \mathbf{(0.795,\ 0.895)} \]

The baseline is right where the model is wrong on the 25 false positives (\(b = 25\)), and the model is right where the baseline is wrong on the 14 true positives (\(c = 14\)).

\[ \chi^2 = \frac{(25 - 14)^2}{25 + 14} = \frac{121}{39} = \mathbf{3.10}, \qquad p = \mathbf{0.078} \]

The continuity-corrected value is 2.56 (\(p = 0.109\)). At 5% there is no significant accuracy difference between the model and the trivial baseline, and the point estimate even favours the baseline.

Recommendation: accuracy is the wrong yardstick here. On the 200 test customers the model at \(t = 0.3\) costs ₹4250 against ₹10000 for doing nothing, a 57.5% saving, while catching 70% of churners with about one offer in three reaching a real churner. Ship the model with threshold 0.3, the stored training-set scaler, and a plan to re-check calibration in the \(0.1\)–\(0.5\) score range as new labels arrive.

Key insight: An end-to-end classifier is a pipeline: stratified splitting keeps the rare class measurable, the scaler is part of the model, the threshold comes from costs and calibration, and the final comparison must use the business metric. A model can lose on accuracy, fail McNemar against a trivial baseline, and still be the clearly right decision.

C.2 L4 · Analysis

Same data, four learners, four answers (M2 + M4 + M5 + M6 + M7)

A lender has nine past borrowers, described by annual income \(x_1\) (in thousands) and number of late payments in the last year \(x_2\). The label is \(y = 1\) for default.

Borrower 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
\(x_1\) 30 35 45 85 58 62 65 40 90
\(x_2\) 3 4 3 4 0 1 0 1 3
\(y\) 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 0 0

A new applicant has \(q = (75, 3)\). Min-max scaling uses the training range \(x_1 \in [30, 90]\) and \(x_2 \in [0, 4]\).

(a) Classify \(q\) with 3-NN and Euclidean distance, first on the raw features and then on the min-max scaled features. List the three neighbours each time.

(b) Grow a depth-1 decision tree on the raw features using entropy and midpoint thresholds. Report the best split, its information gain, and the tree's prediction for \(q\) with the leaf's class proportion. Would scaling the features change the tree?

(c) A soft-margin linear SVM (\(C = 10\)) trained on the scaled features gives \(w = (-1.60,\ 4.26)\), \(b = -1.80\), with labels coded \(\pm 1\). Compute \(f(q) = w^\top \tilde{q} + b\), the prediction, and the margin width. Which training points lie on or inside the margin?

(d) A logistic regression (\(C = 10\)) trained on the same scaled features gives \(w = (-1.85,\ 4.12)\), \(b = -1.74\). Compute \(P(y = 1 \mid q)\) and the prediction. Both models classify all nine training points correctly. At income 75, find the late-payment count at which each linear model's boundary sits.

(e) Summarise the five predictions. For each learner, name the inductive bias that produced its answer, and say what you would tell the credit officer.

Hint

The raw income range is 60 and the late-payment range is 4, so in raw Euclidean distance income dominates. For (d), set \(w_1 \frac{75 - 30}{60} + w_2 \frac{x_2}{4} + b = 0\) and solve for \(x_2\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Raw distances from \(q = (75, 3)\): borrower 4 at \(\sqrt{10^2 + 1^2} = 10.05\) (\(y = 1\)), borrower 7 at 10.44 (\(y = 0\)), borrower 6 at 13.15 (\(y = 0\)). Raw 3-NN predicts 0, by a 2–1 vote.

Scaled, \(\tilde{q} = (0.75,\ 0.75)\). The nearest are borrower 9 at \(\sqrt{0.25^2 + 0^2} = 0.250\) (\(y = 0\)), borrower 4 at 0.3005 (\(y = 1\)) and borrower 3 at 0.500 (\(y = 1\)). Scaled 3-NN predicts 1, by a 2–1 vote. In raw units a gap of one late payment counts the same as a gap of ₹1000 of income, so the raw neighbours are simply the borrowers with the closest income.

(b) The parent has 4 defaulters in 9, so \(H = 0.9911\). The best of the eleven candidate thresholds is \(x_2 \le 2\) (midpoint of 1 and 3): the left node holds borrowers 5–8 (all \(y = 0\), entropy 0), the right node holds 1–4 and 9 (4 of 5 defaulters, entropy 0.7219).

\[ IG = 0.9911 - \frac{5}{9}(0.7219) = \mathbf{0.590} \]

The best income split, \(x_1 \le 37.5\), gains only 0.320. \(q\) has \(x_2 = 3 > 2\), so the tree predicts 1 with leaf proportion 0.8. Scaling does not change the tree: a monotone rescaling of a feature moves every threshold with it and leaves the ordering of the points, and hence every entropy, unchanged.

(c)

\[ f(\tilde{q}) = -1.60(0.75) + 4.26(0.75) - 1.80 = \mathbf{0.195} > 0 \]

so the SVM predicts 1. The margin width is

\[ \frac{2}{\lVert w \rVert} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{1.60^2 + 4.26^2}} = \frac{2}{4.551} = \mathbf{0.440} \]

in scaled units. The values \(y_i f(x_i)\) are 1.395, 2.327, 0.995, 0.993, 2.547, 1.588, 2.733, 1.002 and 0.205. Borrowers 3, 4 and 8 sit on the margin (\(y_i f \approx 1\); the small departures are rounding of \(w\) and \(b\)), and borrower 9 is inside it with slack \(\xi_9 = 1 - 0.205 = 0.795\). These four are the support vectors; the other five could move freely without changing the SVM.

(d)

\[ z = -1.85(0.75) + 4.12(0.75) - 1.74 = -0.0375, \qquad P(y = 1 \mid q) = \sigma(-0.0375) = \mathbf{0.491} \]

so logistic regression predicts 0, essentially at a coin-flip. At income 75 the boundaries are

\[ x_2^{\text{SVM}} = \frac{4\,(1.80 + 1.60 \times 0.75)}{4.26} = \mathbf{2.82}, \qquad x_2^{\text{LR}} = \frac{4\,(1.74 + 1.85 \times 0.75)}{4.12} = \mathbf{3.04} \]

The applicant's 3 late payments fall between the two boundaries.

(e)

Learner Prediction Inductive bias that decided it
3-NN, raw 0 Similar means close in the metric; the unscaled metric is effectively income only
3-NN, scaled 1 Local majority with both features weighted equally by their ranges
Depth-1 tree 1 (0.8) One axis-aligned test on the single most informative feature; income is ignored
Linear SVM 1 Widest-margin hyperplane, fixed only by the four support vectors
Logistic regression 0 (0.491) Hyperplane that maximises the likelihood of all nine points, so borrower 9's high income pulls it

All five learners fit the training data perfectly or nearly so; they disagree because \(q\) sits in a region with no training points, where the answer comes from the inductive bias, not the data. The raw k-NN answer is a preprocessing bug and should be discarded. Among the rest, the honest report is "borderline": logistic regression says 0.49, the tree's leaf says 0.8 on only five borrowers, and the SVM is 0.195 inside a margin of half-width 1. Tell the credit officer the model cannot decide this case and it should go to manual review, then collect more borrowers with high income and several late payments.

Key insight: Different learners agree where the data are dense and disagree where they are sparse. A disagreement between learners is a useful sign of where the inductive bias, rather than the evidence, is making the call. Only distance-based and margin-based learners care about feature scaling; trees do not.

C.3 L4 · Analysis

Every loss is a likelihood in disguise (M3 + M4 + M8)

This capstone derives three losses used in the course from probability models and then checks them on small data.

Regression data. Five points follow the through-origin model \(y_i = \theta x_i + \varepsilon_i\):

\(x\) 1 2 3 4 5
\(y\) 2.1 3.9 6.2 7.8 10.1

(a) Assume \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) independently. Write the log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta)\), show that maximising it is the same as minimising the sum of squared errors, and find \(\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}\). With \(\sigma^2 = 1\), evaluate \(\ell(\hat{\theta})\). Also give the MLE of \(\sigma^2\).

(b) Put the prior \(\theta \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) on the slope, with \(\sigma^2 = 1\) and \(\tau^2 = 0.5\). Show that the MAP estimate minimises a ridge objective, identify \(\lambda\), and compute \(\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}}\). What happens as \(\tau^2 \to \infty\) and as \(\tau^2 \to 0\)?

(c) Classification. A logistic model gives \(\hat{p}_i = P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i)\) for five labelled points:

\(y\) 1 0 1 1 0
\(\hat{p}\) 0.8 0.3 0.6 0.9 0.2

Treat each label as Bernoulli(\(\hat{p}_i\)). Show that the negative log-likelihood is the summed cross-entropy loss, and compute the likelihood, the negative log-likelihood and the mean cross-entropy. Compare the cross-entropy and squared-error penalties for a single point with \(y = 1\) and \(\hat{p} = 0.01\).

(d) Naïve Bayes tables. Among 10 churners, the categorical feature Plan takes the values Basic, Standard, Premium and Family with counts 6, 3, 1 and 0. Use a Lagrange multiplier to show that the MLE of each class-conditional probability is the relative frequency. Then show that Laplace (add-one) smoothing is the MAP estimate under a Dirichlet(2, 2, 2, 2) prior, and compute both sets of estimates.

(e) Change the noise. The point \(x = 5\) is mis-recorded as \(y = 20.1\). Recompute the least-squares slope. Then assume Laplace noise, \(p(\varepsilon) \propto e^{-\lvert \varepsilon \rvert / b}\), derive the loss it implies, and find the new MLE of \(\theta\). Which assumption would you trust for data with occasional recording errors?

Hint

Every part is the same recipe: write the likelihood (times the prior, for MAP), take the log, drop the terms that do not involve the parameter, and read off the loss. For (e), \(\sum \lvert y_i - \theta x_i \rvert = \sum x_i \lvert y_i / x_i - \theta \rvert\) is minimised at a weighted median.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)
