\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(y_i - \theta x_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}} = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \theta x_i)^2 \]

The first term does not involve \(\theta\) and the second is \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\text{SSE}(\theta)\), so maximising \(\ell\) is minimising SSE. Setting \(\frac{d\,\text{SSE}}{d\theta} = 0\) gives

\[ \hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2} = \frac{110.2}{55} = \mathbf{2.0036} \]

\(\text{SSE}(\hat{\theta}) = 0.10927\), so with \(\sigma^2 = 1\), \(\ell(\hat{\theta}) = -\frac{5}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \frac{0.10927}{2} = \mathbf{-4.649}\). Maximising over \(\sigma^2\) as well gives \(\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n} = \mathbf{0.02185}\), which divides by \(n\), not \(n - 1\).

(b) The log-posterior is the log-likelihood plus the log-prior:

\[ \ln p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \text{const} - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum (y_i - \theta x_i)^2 - \frac{\theta^2}{2\tau^2} \]

Multiplying by \(-2\sigma^2\), the MAP estimate minimises

\[ \sum (y_i - \theta x_i)^2 + \lambda\,\theta^2, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2} = \frac{1}{0.5} = \mathbf{2} \]

which is the ridge objective. Therefore

\[ \hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2 + \lambda} = \frac{110.2}{57} = \mathbf{1.9333} \]

As \(\tau^2 \to \infty\) the prior becomes flat, \(\lambda \to 0\) and MAP becomes MLE. As \(\tau^2 \to 0\) the prior insists on \(\theta = 0\), \(\lambda \to \infty\) and \(\hat{\theta} \to 0\): maximum underfitting. Choosing \(\lambda\) is choosing how strongly you believe small weights a priori.

(c) For Bernoulli labels, \(P(y_i \mid x_i) = \hat{p}_i^{\,y_i}(1 - \hat{p}_i)^{1 - y_i}\), so

\[ -\ln L = -\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i \ln \hat{p}_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \hat{p}_i)\right] \]

which is exactly the summed cross-entropy. Here

\[ L = 0.8 \times 0.7 \times 0.6 \times 0.9 \times 0.8 = \mathbf{0.2419}, \qquad -\ln L = \mathbf{1.419}, \qquad \text{mean cross-entropy} = \mathbf{0.2838} \]

The five terms are 0.2231, 0.3567, 0.5108, 0.1054 and 0.2231. For a confident mistake (\(y = 1\), \(\hat{p} = 0.01\)) cross-entropy charges \(-\ln 0.01 = \mathbf{4.605}\), while squared error charges only \((1 - 0.01)^2 = \mathbf{0.980}\). The log-likelihood punishes confident errors without bound, which is what a probability model should do, and combined with the sigmoid it is convex in the weights.

(d) Maximise \(\sum_k n_k \ln p_k\) subject to \(\sum_k p_k = 1\). With the Lagrangian \(\sum_k n_k \ln p_k + \mu\left(1 - \sum_k p_k\right)\), setting the derivative to zero gives \(n_k / p_k = \mu\), so \(p_k \propto n_k\), and the constraint gives

\[ \hat{p}_k^{\text{MLE}} = \frac{n_k}{n} = (\mathbf{0.6,\ 0.3,\ 0.1,\ 0}) \]

Counting is maximum likelihood. Under a Dirichlet(\(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_K\)) prior the log-posterior is \(\sum_k (n_k + \alpha_k - 1)\ln p_k\), so the same argument gives

\[ \hat{p}_k^{\text{MAP}} = \frac{n_k + \alpha_k - 1}{n + \sum_k \alpha_k - K} \]

With every \(\alpha_k = 2\) and \(K = 4\), this is \(\frac{n_k + 1}{n + 4}\), which is Laplace smoothing: (0.5, 0.2857, 0.1429, 0.0714). The MLE of 0 for Family would make any churner on the Family plan impossible, whatever the other features say. The prior removes that zero, just as the Gaussian prior in (b) pulled \(\theta\) towards 0.

(e) With \(y_5 = 20.1\), \(\sum x_i y_i = 160.2\) and the least-squares slope jumps to \(\hat{\theta} = 2.9127\). Under Laplace noise,

\[ \ell(\theta) = \text{const} - \frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert y_i - \theta x_i \rvert \]

so the MLE minimises the sum of absolute errors. Writing it as \(\sum x_i \lvert r_i - \theta \rvert\) with ratios \(r_i = y_i / x_i = 2.1, 1.95, 2.0667, 1.95, 4.02\) and weights \(x_i\), the minimiser is the weighted median. Sorted, the ratio 1.95 carries weight 6 of the total 15 and the ratio 2.0667 brings the running total to 9, past half, so \(\hat{\theta} = 2.0667\). The outlier moves the least-squares slope by 0.91 but leaves the absolute-error slope close to the clean value. For data with occasional gross recording errors the heavy-tailed Laplace assumption, and its absolute loss, is the more honest model.

Key insight: Squared error, cross-entropy and frequency counting are not arbitrary choices; each is the negative log-likelihood of a noise or label model (Gaussian, Bernoulli, categorical). Adding a prior turns MLE into MAP, which shows up in practice as ridge regularisation or Laplace smoothing. Choosing a loss means choosing an assumption about the data.

C.4 L5 · Mastery

One trade-off, four knobs (M3 + M5 + M6 + M9)

Data are simulated from \(y = \sin(2\pi x) + \varepsilon\), with \(x \sim U(0, 1)\) and \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, 0.3^2)\). A team draws a training set of 40 points and a validation set of 200 points, and fits four model families, each with one complexity knob. The mean squared errors are:

Polynomial degree 1 3 5 9 15
Train MSE 0.244 0.058 0.056 0.055 0.051
Validation MSE 0.289 0.092 0.088 0.092 0.103
Regression-tree max depth 1 2 3 4 6 unlimited
Train MSE 0.163 0.117 0.053 0.035 0.001 0.000
Validation MSE 0.191 0.171 0.135 0.142 0.157 0.157
\(k\) in \(k\)-NN regression 1 3 5 9 15 40
Train MSE 0.000 0.045 0.059 0.082 0.135 0.491
Validation MSE 0.157 0.119 0.103 0.120 0.164 0.615
Gradient-boosting rounds (depth-2 trees, learning rate 0.3) 1 10 50 200 1000
Train MSE 0.300 0.038 0.003 0.000 0.000
Validation MSE 0.392 0.125 0.140 0.156 0.157

(a) For each family, say in which direction the knob increases model complexity, and label each setting as underfitting, about right, or overfitting. Explain the \(k = 40\) row and why the unlimited tree, \(k = 1\) and 1000 boosting rounds have almost the same validation MSE.

(b) Choose each family's hyperparameter and the overall model using the validation set only. What is the smallest expected squared error any model can achieve on these data, and what does that say about the winner's validation MSE?

(c) The team writes in its report: "Expected error in production: 0.088." Explain why this is optimistic, and state what should have been done. (The winner's MSE on a separate 1000-point test set, used once, is 0.087.)

(d) To study bagging, 300 independent training sets of size 40 are simulated. On each, a depth-1 stump, an unlimited-depth tree, and bagged versions of both (100 bootstrap trees each) are fitted. Averaged over a grid of \(x\) values, the results are:

Model \(\text{bias}^2\) Variance
Stump 0.0660 0.0450
Bagged stumps 0.0636 0.0225
Deep tree 0.0007 0.0944
Bagged deep trees 0.0015 0.0465

Compute each model's expected test MSE. Explain why bagging rescues the deep tree but not the stump, even though it halves the variance of both. Use \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{h}) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2\) to estimate the correlation \(\rho\) between two bootstrap deep trees.

(e) Which ensemble method should be applied to the stump instead, and what evidence for it is already in the boosting table? Why is the number of boosting rounds itself a bias–variance knob?

Hint

Complexity rises with degree, depth and rounds, but falls as \(k\) grows. Expected test MSE is \(\text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \sigma^2\), and here \(\sigma^2 = 0.09\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

Family Complexity rises with Underfitting About right Overfitting
Polynomial degree 1 3, 5, 9 15 (mild)
Tree depth 1, 2 3, 4 6, unlimited
\(k\)-NN smaller \(k\) 15, 40 3, 5, 9 1
Boosting rounds 1 10 50, 200, 1000

Underfitting shows as train and validation errors that are both high and close together. Overfitting shows as training error near 0 with validation error rising. With \(k = 40 = N\), every prediction is the global mean of the training \(y\), so both errors are near \(\operatorname{Var}(y) \approx 0.5 + 0.09\): maximum bias. The unlimited tree, 1-NN and 1000 boosting rounds all interpolate the training data, reproducing each training \(y\) on a piecewise-constant map of \(x\), so they make nearly the same predictions and share a validation MSE of about 0.157.

(b) By validation MSE: degree 5 (0.088), depth 3 (0.135), \(k = 5\) (0.103), 10 rounds (0.125). The overall choice is the degree-5 polynomial, which is natural because a smooth sine is well approximated by a low-degree polynomial.

The noise variance \(\sigma^2 = 0.3^2 = \mathbf{0.09}\) is the irreducible error: even the true function \(\sin(2\pi x)\) has expected squared error 0.09. A validation MSE of 0.088 is therefore as good as it gets; being slightly below 0.09 is sampling noise in a 200-point estimate, not a model that beats the noise.

(c) 0.088 is the minimum of about 22 validation scores. Choosing the smallest of many noisy estimates biases it downwards (a winner's curse), so the validation set is no longer an unbiased estimate of the chosen model's error. The team should freeze the choice and then score the winner once on an untouched test set. That gives 0.087 here; the optimism is small because the validation set is large and the four families are not very different, but the procedure, not the luck, is what makes the reported number trustworthy.

(d) Adding \(\sigma^2 = 0.09\):

Model Expected test MSE
Stump \(0.0660 + 0.0450 + 0.09 = \mathbf{0.2010}\)
Bagged stumps \(0.0636 + 0.0225 + 0.09 = \mathbf{0.1761}\)
Deep tree \(0.0007 + 0.0944 + 0.09 = \mathbf{0.1851}\)
Bagged deep trees \(0.0015 + 0.0465 + 0.09 = \mathbf{0.1380}\)

Bagging averages, and averaging reduces variance only; the mean prediction, and so the bias, is essentially unchanged. The deep tree's error is almost all variance, so halving it gives the best model in the table. The stump's error is dominated by bias: one split cannot draw a sine wave. Even infinitely many bagged stumps cannot get below \(0.0636 + 0.09 \approx 0.154\), which is worse than the bagged deep trees already achieve.

For the deep trees, \(\frac{0.0465}{0.0944} = 0.4926 = \rho + \frac{1 - \rho}{100}\), so

\[ \rho = \frac{0.4926 - 0.01}{0.99} \approx \mathbf{0.49} \]

Bootstrap trees grown on the same 40 points are strongly correlated, so the variance cannot fall below about \(0.49\sigma^2\) however many trees are added. That floor is what Random Forest's random feature subsets lower, by decorrelating the trees (with one feature here there is nothing to subsample).

(e) The stump needs boosting, which adds learners sequentially, each fitted to the current residuals, and so reduces bias. The boosting table shows it: one depth-2 tree has validation MSE 0.392, and ten boosted trees reach 0.125. But each round also adds capacity, so after about 10 rounds the training MSE heads to 0 and the validation MSE climbs back to 0.157. The number of rounds (together with the learning rate) must be tuned on validation data, usually by early stopping.

Key insight: Degree, depth, \(k\) and boosting rounds are the same knob under four names: they move a model from high bias to high variance. Read the train–validation gap to tell which side you are on, tune on validation only, and match the ensemble to the problem: bagging for a high-variance learner, boosting for a high-bias one.

C.5 L4 · Analysis

One boundary, three routes: Naïve Bayes, the GMM E-step and the sigmoid (M4 + M8 + M10)

A single sensor reading \(x\) is recorded for ten machines; \(y = 1\) means the machine later failed.

Class Readings
\(y = 0\) (healthy, 6 machines) 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.5, 0.5
\(y = 1\) (failed, 4 machines) 3.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5

Use maximum-likelihood estimates throughout (variances divide by the number of points).

(a) Fit a Gaussian Naïve Bayes model with a separate variance for each class. Compute \(P(y = 1 \mid x = 3.5)\). Find every decision boundary, and explain the boundary that lies far to the right.

(b) Refit with one shared (pooled) variance. Compute \(P(y = 1 \mid x = 3.5)\) again. Show that the posterior has the form \(\sigma(w_0 + w_1 x)\), give \(w_0\), \(w_1\) and the boundary.

(c) Now hide the labels and treat the ten readings as unlabelled data from a two-component, tied-variance GMM, initialised at the parameters of (b): \(\pi = (0.6, 0.4)\), \(\mu = (2.0, 4.5)\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Carry out one E-step, and show that each responsibility \(\gamma_{n1}\) equals the posterior of (b). Then carry out the M-step and report the new \(\pi_1\), \(\mu_0\), \(\mu_1\), \(\sigma^2\) and the new boundary. Did the log-likelihood rise?

(d) Fit a logistic regression by maximum likelihood (no regularisation) on the labelled data; it gives \(w_0 = -8.084\), \(w_1 = 2.342\). Compute its boundary and \(P(y = 1 \mid x = 3.5)\). Why do the generative model of (b) and the discriminative model differ, although both are sigmoids of a linear function of \(x\)?

(e) In a new plant failures are believed to be as common as healthy machines (\(\pi_1 = 0.5\)). Update the boundary of (b) and the logistic regression of (d) without refitting either.

Hint

For a shared variance, the \(x^2\) terms of the two log-densities cancel, leaving \(w_1 = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{\sigma^2}\) and \(w_0 = \frac{\mu_0^2 - \mu_1^2}{2\sigma^2} + \ln\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\). The E-step uses exactly the same Bayes formula, with mixing weights in place of class priors.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\hat{\pi}_0 = 0.6\), \(\hat{\pi}_1 = 0.4\), \(\hat{\mu}_0 = 2.0\), \(\hat{\sigma}_0^2 = 1.0833\), \(\hat{\mu}_1 = 4.5\), \(\hat{\sigma}_1^2 = 0.875\). At \(x = 3.5\):

\[ \pi_0\,N(3.5 \mid 2.0, 1.0833) = 0.08141, \qquad \pi_1\,N(3.5 \mid 4.5, 0.875) = 0.09634 \]

\[ P(y = 1 \mid 3.5) = \frac{0.09634}{0.08141 + 0.09634} = \mathbf{0.542} \]

Setting the log-posterior ratio to zero gives a quadratic, \(-0.10989x^2 + 3.2967x - 10.024 = 0\), with roots \(x = 3.434\) and \(x = 26.57\). Between them the model predicts failure. Because class 0 has the larger variance, its density eventually dominates in both tails, so far to the right (beyond 26.57) the model predicts "healthy" again. That second boundary is an artefact of the Gaussian assumption in a region with no data at all (at \(x = 30\) the posterior is already \(4 \times 10^{-5}\)).

(b) The pooled variance is

\[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{6(1.0833) + 4(0.875)}{10} = \mathbf{1.0} \]

The log-odds is linear in \(x\):

\[ \ln\frac{P(y = 1 \mid x)}{P(y = 0 \mid x)} = \underbrace{\frac{\mu_0^2 - \mu_1^2}{2\sigma^2} + \ln\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}}_{w_0} + \underbrace{\frac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{\sigma^2}}_{w_1}\,x \]

\[ w_1 = \frac{4.5 - 2.0}{1} = \mathbf{2.5}, \qquad w_0 = \frac{4 - 20.25}{2} + \ln\frac{0.4}{0.6} = -8.125 - 0.4055 = \mathbf{-8.5305} \]

so \(P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(-8.5305 + 2.5x)\). At \(x = 3.5\), \(z = 0.2195\) and \(P = 0.5547\). The boundary is

\[ x^* = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2 \ln(\pi_0/\pi_1)}{\mu_1 - \mu_0} = 3.25 + \frac{0.4055}{2.5} = \mathbf{3.412} \]

The prior pushes the boundary 0.16 towards the rarer class.

(c) The E-step responsibility is

\[ \gamma_{n1} = \frac{\pi_1 N(x_n \mid \mu_1, \sigma^2)}{\pi_0 N(x_n \mid \mu_0, \sigma^2) + \pi_1 N(x_n \mid \mu_1, \sigma^2)} \]

which is the Bayes posterior of (b) with the mixing weight as the prior, so \(\gamma_{n1} = \sigma(-8.5305 + 2.5x_n)\). For the sorted readings:

\(x_n\) 0.5 1.0 2.0 2.0 3.0 3.0 3.5 4.5 5.0 5.5
\(\gamma_{n1}\) 0.0007 0.0024 0.0285 0.0285 0.2630 0.2630 0.5547 0.9382 0.9815 0.9946

The two readings of 3.0 get the same responsibility although one came from each class; without labels the model cannot tell them apart. The M-step uses \(N_1 = \sum_n \gamma_{n1} = 4.0549\):

\[ \pi_1 = \frac{4.0549}{10} = \mathbf{0.4055}, \quad \mu_1 = \frac{\sum \gamma_{n1} x_n}{N_1} = \mathbf{4.497}, \quad \mu_0 = \mathbf{1.979}, \quad \sigma^2 = \mathbf{0.9713} \]

The new boundary is \(x^* = 3.386\). The log-likelihood rises from \(-18.321\) to \(-18.315\), as EM guarantees. The parameters barely move because the labelled fit was already near a stationary point of the unlabelled likelihood.

(d) The boundary is \(x^* = \frac{8.084}{2.342} = \mathbf{3.451}\), and \(P(y = 1 \mid 3.5) = \sigma(-8.084 + 2.342 \times 3.5) = \mathbf{0.528}\). Both models are sigmoids, but they are fitted to different objectives. Gaussian NB estimates \(\pi\), \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) by maximising the joint likelihood \(p(x, y)\), and its \(w\) follows from those. Logistic regression maximises the conditional likelihood \(p(y \mid x)\) directly, without assuming that \(x\) is Gaussian within each class. When the Gaussian shared-variance assumption holds, the two converge to the same \(w\) as the data grow. When it does not, logistic regression is usually more accurate with plenty of data, and Naïve Bayes with little.

(e) Only the prior term changes, by \(\ln\frac{0.5}{0.5} - \ln\frac{0.4}{0.6} = +0.4055\). For (b), \(w_0\) becomes \(-8.125\) and the boundary moves to the midpoint, \(x^* = 3.25\). For logistic regression, \(w_0\) becomes \(-8.084 + 0.4055 = -7.678\), giving \(x^* = 3.278\). The correction is exact for the generative model. For logistic regression it is valid only if the class-conditional distributions \(p(x \mid y)\) are the same in the new plant (a pure prior shift).

Key insight: Bayes' theorem is one formula used three ways: as the Naïve Bayes posterior, as the GMM E-step responsibility, and, with Gaussian classes and a shared variance, as the logistic sigmoid. The priors appear as an additive term \(\ln(\pi_1/\pi_0)\) in the log-odds, so a change of base rate is a shift of the intercept.

C.6 L5 · Mastery

Clustering, then classifying, without leaking (M2 + M5 + M10 + M11)

A shop describes eight training customers by visits per month \(x_1\) and items per visit \(x_2\) (both on similar scales, so no rescaling is needed), and records whether each responded to a promotion (\(y = 1\)).

Customer P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6 P7 P8
\(x_1\) 1 2 2 3 6 7 8 5
\(x_2\) 2 1 3 2 5 7 6 4
\(y\) 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0

The analyst plans to segment customers with K-means (\(K = 2\), Euclidean distance) and use the segment as a feature for a classifier.

(a) Run K-means on the eight training customers from the initial centroids \(c_1 = \text{P1} = (1, 2)\) and \(c_2 = \text{P3} = (2, 3)\). For each of the first two iterations, give the assignments, the SSE of those assignments to the current centroids, the new centroids, and the SSE after the update. Show that the third iteration changes nothing.

(b) Compute the silhouette coefficient of P4 and of P8 for the final clustering. The mean silhouette over all eight customers is 0.628. Which customer is the worst clustered, and why?

(c) Grow a depth-1 entropy tree using only the segment as a feature. Compute its information gain and compare it with the best single split on the raw features. What does this say about using unsupervised segments as features?

(d) Four new customers form the test set, and all four responded: T1 \(= (4, 3)\), T2 \(= (4.5, 3.5)\), T3 \(= (4, 4)\), T4 \(= (3.5, 3.5)\). The segment rule from (c) predicts "respond" for the high-activity segment only. Compute its test accuracy (i) when test customers are assigned to the nearest training centroid, and (ii) when K-means is refitted from the same initial centroids on all 12 customers, train and test together. Also score the best raw-feature tree from (c).

(e) Explain why (d)(ii) is leakage even though no test labels were used, and write the correct pipeline for 5-fold cross-validation.

Hint

(a) SSE is the sum of squared distances to the assigned centroid, and it can only fall at each half-step. (b) \(s = \frac{b - a}{\max(a, b)}\), with \(a\) the mean distance to the other members of the point's own cluster and \(b\) the mean distance to the members of the other cluster.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

Step Cluster 1 Cluster 2 SSE
Iteration 1, assign to \((1, 2), (2, 3)\) P1, P2 P3–P8 120.0
Iteration 1, update \(c_1 = (1.5, 1.5)\) \(c_2 = (5.1667, 4.5)\) 45.33
Iteration 2, assign P1–P4 P5–P8 27.11
Iteration 2, update \(c_1 = (2, 2)\) \(c_2 = (6.5, 5.5)\) 14.0
Iteration 3, assign P1–P4 P5–P8 14.0

In iteration 2, P3 and P4 move to cluster 1: P3 \(= (2, 3)\) is at squared distance 2.5 from \(c_1\) against 12.28 from \(c_2\). The third assignment step reproduces the same partition, so the centroids stop moving and K-means has converged with SSE = 14.0. The SSE sequence \(120 \to 45.33 \to 27.11 \to 14.0\) never increases, which is the convergence argument of 10.2.2.

(b) P4 \(= (3, 2)\): its distances to P1, P2, P3 are 2, 1.414, 1.414, so \(a = 1.6095\); to P5–P8 they are 4.243, 6.403, 6.403, 2.828, so \(b = 4.9693\).

\[ s_{\text{P4}} = \frac{4.9693 - 1.6095}{4.9693} = \mathbf{0.676} \]

P8 \(= (5, 4)\): \(a = \frac{1.414 + 3.606 + 3.606}{3} = 2.8751\) and \(b = \frac{4.472 + 4.243 + 3.162 + 2.828}{4} = 3.6764\).

\[ s_{\text{P8}} = \frac{3.6764 - 2.8751}{3.6764} = \mathbf{0.218} \]

P8 is the worst clustered (every other customer has \(s > 0.6\)). It sits between the two groups, nearly as close to the low-activity customers as to its own cluster.

(c) Segment 1 (P1–P4) has 1 responder in 4, segment 2 (P5–P8) has 3 in 4. Each child has entropy 0.8113, so

\[ IG_{\text{segment}} = 1 - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}(0.8113) + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.8113)\right) = \mathbf{0.189} \]

The best raw split, \(x_1 \le 2.5\) (P1–P3 all non-responders on the left; 4 of 5 responders on the right), has \(IG = 0.549\), almost three times as large. K-means groups customers by geometry, not by the label. A segment is a useful feature only if the label happens to follow the cluster structure, and here it does not: the responder P4 and the non-responder P8 fall on the wrong sides.

(d) (i) With the training centroids \((2, 2)\) and \((6.5, 5.5)\), the squared distances are T1: 5 vs 12.5, T2: 8.5 vs 8, T3: 8 vs 8.5, T4: 4.5 vs 13. Only T2 joins the high-activity segment, so the rule predicts (0, 1, 0, 0) and the test accuracy is 1/4 = 25%.

(ii) Refitted on all 12 customers, K-means converges to \(c_1 = (2, 2)\) and \(c_2 = (5.25, 4.5)\), with SSE 35.5. The training customers keep the same segments, so the rule learned from their labels is unchanged. But the four test customers have pulled \(c_2\) towards themselves, and all four now join segment 2: the test accuracy becomes 4/4 = 100%.

The raw tree \(x_1 \le 2.5\) sends all four test customers right and predicts "respond" for each: 4/4, with no leakage.

(e) In (ii) the test customers' features helped to define the feature that is then used to score them. The model was effectively allowed to see the test set and adapt to it. In deployment, customers arrive one at a time and cannot move the centroids, so the 100% cannot be reproduced; the honest estimate for this pipeline is the 25% of (i). Labels are not the only thing that can leak: any fitted preprocessing step (scaler, imputer, PCA, clustering, SMOTE) leaks if it is fitted on data that includes the evaluation set.

Correct pipeline for each of the 5 folds:

  1. Split into training folds and the held-out fold.
  2. Fit K-means (and any scaler) on the training folds only.
  3. Assign each held-out customer to the nearest training centroid.
  4. Fit the classifier on the training folds and score it on the held-out fold.

Average the five scores. After model selection, refit the whole pipeline on all training data and score the untouched test set once.

Key insight: An unsupervised step inside a supervised pipeline is still a fitted model. It must be fitted on training data only, or it will quietly use the test set. Cluster labels are geometry, not the target, so they earn their place as features only if a validation score, computed honestly, says so.

C.7 L5 · Mastery

Shipping a fair, auditable credit model (M5 + M9 + M11)

A bank compares two loan-approval models on the same 1400 test applicants: 1000 from group A (600 of whom would repay) and 400 from group B (160 would repay). "Positive" means approve, and the truth is "would repay". The group attribute \(G\) was not an input to either model.

Model, group TP FN FP TN
Gradient boosting, A 540 60 120 280
Gradient boosting, B 112 48 53 187
Depth-2 tree, A 510 90 130 270
Depth-2 tree, B 120 40 60 180

The tree's two levels test debt-to-income ratio and then income; postcode does not appear. The gradient-boosting (GB) model uses about 40 features, including postcode region \(Z\).

(a) For the GB model, compute each group's selection rate, TPR, FPR, precision and accuracy. Report the demographic-parity difference, the disparate-impact ratio (compare it with the four-fifths rule) and the equal-opportunity (TPR) gap.

(b) An audit finds that the GB model approves 75% of applicants in region \(Z = 0\) and 30% in \(Z = 1\), in both groups, and that 20% of group A and 75% of group B live in \(Z = 1\). Show that this alone reproduces the selection rates of (a). How well does \(Z\) predict \(G\)? Explain why "fairness through unawareness" failed.

(c) Repeat (a) for the tree. Compute both models' overall accuracies with 95% confidence intervals. On the same applicants, GB is right where the tree is wrong 95 times, and the tree is right where GB is wrong 56 times. Run McNemar's test.

(d) What demographic-parity difference would a perfect classifier have on this test set? Use the answer to say which fairness criterion should be binding here, and compare the two models on it.

(e) The bank tries a group-specific threshold for GB, lowering it for group B only, which gives TP = 144 and FP = 84 in group B (group A unchanged). Compute the new group-B TPR, FPR, selection rate and precision, the new gaps, and the overall accuracy. Then make a recommendation, including what must be recorded for accountability.

Hint

Selection rate is \(\frac{TP + FP}{n}\), equal opportunity compares \(TPR = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\), and the disparate-impact ratio is the lower selection rate divided by the higher. For (d), a perfect classifier approves exactly the repayers.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

GB Selection rate TPR FPR Precision Accuracy
A 0.660 0.900 0.300 0.818 0.820
B 0.4125 0.700 0.221 0.679 0.7475

Demographic-parity difference \(= 0.660 - 0.4125 = 0.2475\). Disparate-impact ratio \(= 0.4125/0.660 = 0.625\), well below 0.8, so the four-fifths rule is violated. Equal-opportunity gap \(= 0.900 - 0.700 = 0.20\): one in ten repayers in A is refused, against three in ten in B.

(b)

\[ \text{sel}_A = 0.8(0.75) + 0.2(0.30) = \mathbf{0.660}, \qquad \text{sel}_B = 0.25(0.75) + 0.75(0.30) = \mathbf{0.4125} \]

which are exactly the rates of (a). Region \(Z = 1\) holds 200 A and 300 B applicants, and \(Z = 0\) holds 800 A and 100 B, so \(P(G = B \mid Z = 1) = \mathbf{0.60}\) and \(P(G = B \mid Z = 0) = \mathbf{0.111}\). Guessing \(G\) from \(Z\) alone is right for \(\frac{300 + 800}{1400} = \mathbf{78.6\%}\) of applicants, against 71.4% for always guessing A. Removing \(G\) did not remove the information: postcode encodes it redundantly, and the model, trained on historical outcomes in which region \(Z = 1\) fared worse, learned to use it. Unawareness fails whenever any input, or combination of inputs, is a proxy for the protected attribute.

(c)

Tree Selection rate TPR FPR Precision Accuracy
A 0.640 0.850 0.325 0.797 0.780
B 0.450 0.750 0.250 0.667 0.750

Demographic-parity difference 0.19, disparate-impact ratio 0.703, equal-opportunity gap 0.10, half that of GB.

Overall accuracies: GB \(\frac{1119}{1400} = \mathbf{0.7993}\), CI (0.778, 0.820); tree \(\frac{1080}{1400} = \mathbf{0.7714}\), CI (0.749, 0.793).

\[ \chi^2 = \frac{(95 - 56)^2}{95 + 56} = \frac{1521}{151} = \mathbf{10.07}, \qquad p = \mathbf{0.0015} \]

(continuity-corrected 9.56, \(p = 0.002\)). GB is significantly more accurate, by 2.8 points, although its confidence interval overlaps the tree's. The paired test sees what the two separate intervals cannot.

(d) A perfect classifier approves exactly the repayers, so its selection rates equal the base rates, 0.60 and 0.40: a demographic-parity difference of 0.20. The tree's 0.19 is already below that, so pushing demographic parity further would mean approving non-repayers in B or refusing repayers in A on purpose. With base rates this different, equal opportunity (equal TPR, so that a person who would repay has the same chance of approval in either group) is the more defensible binding criterion, assuming the repayment labels are themselves trustworthy. On it, the tree (gap 0.10) clearly beats GB (gap 0.20).

(e) In group B: \(TPR = \frac{144}{160} = \mathbf{0.90}\), \(FPR = \frac{84}{240} = \mathbf{0.35}\), selection rate \(\frac{228}{400} = \mathbf{0.57}\), precision \(\frac{144}{228} = \mathbf{0.632}\). The equal-opportunity gap is now 0, the demographic-parity difference falls to 0.09, and the FPR gap reverses (0.30 in A against 0.35 in B). Group-B accuracy is \(\frac{144 + 156}{400} = 0.75\), so overall accuracy becomes \(\frac{1120}{1400} = \mathbf{0.800}\): fairness on this criterion costs nothing in accuracy here.

The price is elsewhere. The bank now needs \(G\) at decision time, which may count as disparate treatment under lending law. It also bears more defaults in B, because precision falls from 0.679 to 0.632. And GB remains a black box that reconstructs group from postcode.

Recommendation: if group-specific thresholds are lawful, ship GB with them, otherwise ship the tree. The tree gives up 2.8 points of accuracy for half the opportunity gap, rules a loan officer can explain to a refused applicant, and no postcode dependence. In either case, record the accountability items:

  • the protected attribute kept for auditing only;
  • the chosen fairness criterion and why it was chosen over demographic parity;
  • the per-group confusion matrices and confidence intervals;
  • the proxy analysis of \(Z\);
  • a schedule for re-auditing as the applicant mix shifts.

Key insight: Fairness is measured per group from the confusion matrix, and different criteria (parity of selection, of TPR, of precision) cannot all hold when base rates differ. Deleting the protected attribute does not remove a bias that proxies can reconstruct. The choice between an accurate black box and an interpretable tree is a trade-off to be quantified, with paired tests for accuracy and per-group gaps for fairness, and then documented.

14.7 Final self-assessment: can you do each of these from memory?

Tick a box only if you can do it without notes in under 5 minutes.

  • [ ] State a learning problem as \(\langle T, P, E \rangle\), and say whether it is supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement or semi-supervised, and instance-based or model-based (1.1–1.3)
  • [ ] Apply the IQR and \(3\sigma\) outlier rules, choose between min-max and z-score scaling, and choose between one-hot and label encoding (2.3, 2.5)
  • [ ] Design a train/validation/test split, stratified where needed, in which every fitted preprocessing step (scaler, imputer, SMOTE, clustering) sees training data only (2.4, 6.5, 11.1)
  • [ ] Solve the normal equations and run one batch gradient-descent step by hand, and explain how the learning rate and feature scaling change the descent (3.2–3.3)
  • [ ] Write the ridge, lasso and elastic-net objectives and explain why lasso gives exact zeros and ridge does not (3.5)
  • [ ] Derive least squares as the Gaussian MLE, cross-entropy as the Bernoulli MLE, and ridge as MAP with a Gaussian prior (3.1, 4.2.1, 8.1)
  • [ ] Compute a logistic-regression probability, its decision boundary and the odds ratio \(e^{w}\), and run one gradient step on the log-loss (4.1–4.2)
  • [ ] Build a confusion matrix, compute precision, recall, \(F_1\) and AUC, and choose a threshold from a cost matrix (4.4, 11.1)
  • [ ] Grow a split by entropy, Gini or gain ratio on categorical and continuous attributes, and explain pre- and post-pruning (5.2–5.3)
  • [ ] Compute Minkowski and Gower distances, classify with \(k\)-NN before and after scaling, and choose \(k\) by validation (6.2–6.3)
  • [ ] Check a given \((w, b)\) against the SVM constraints, compute the margin \(\frac{2}{\lVert w \rVert}\), identify the support vectors, and explain the effect of \(C\) and of a kernel (7.1–7.4)
  • [ ] Apply Bayes' theorem in the right direction, and train discrete and Gaussian Naïve Bayes with Laplace smoothing by hand (8.2–8.3)
  • [ ] Show that Gaussian Naïve Bayes with a shared variance gives a logistic sigmoid, and contrast generative with discriminative training (8.4)
  • [ ] Explain bagging versus boosting through bias and variance, and run one AdaBoost round (\(\varepsilon\), \(\alpha\), reweighting) by hand (9.1–9.3)
  • [ ] Run K-means iterations with SSE, compute a silhouette coefficient, and read an elbow plot (10.2, 10.4)
  • [ ] Perform one EM iteration for a 1-D two-component GMM, and explain why the E-step is Bayes' theorem (10.5)
  • [ ] Compute a confidence interval for an accuracy, and compare two models with a two-proportion \(z\) test or McNemar's test as the sampling design requires (11.2)
  • [ ] Compute demographic-parity, disparate-impact and equal-opportunity measures per group, explain why fairness through unawareness fails, and weigh interpretability against accuracy (11.3–11.4)
